after they had twice entered into communion through deceit, they were in sorrow, mourning, and endless distress,
with lamentations and bitter turmoil. Then, finally, they resolved and decreed for themselves
that they would never again have any communion whatsoever with those who professed two natures, even if they should face death by sword or fire.
Because of this too, fierce fury and great anger arose against them, and all three were thrown into exile, each in his own region.
Thus they were separated from one another by no small distance, and harsh and bitter sentences were passed against them, as we have already explained.
They suffered bitter distress, deprived of their acquaintances and separated from those close to them, until they even came to the point of death.
Now those bishops made an agreement among themselves and firmly resolved that they would never again have any communion at all with the Synodites.
They resisted and stood courageously against the authorities, while countless things were done and said between them in the struggle of this great conflict.
Then, in bitter rage, a sentence of exile was passed mercilessly against every one of them.
First, the patriarch Paul was sent to the monastery called Abraham’s and imprisoned there. While he was imprisoned, he found
some room and a little light in his prison, and began writing about what John the Sarmian had done in the church. He was watched and caught while writing.
The writing was taken away from him before it was finished, and they brought it to John.
In bitter rage, he took it, went in, and read it before the emperor. When the emperor too heard that Paul had written about him and the patriarch,
and about what they had done to the Orthodox community, he too became filled with great anger and was furious with Paul.
He ordered them to take the writing, go to Paul, and demand that he acknowledge whether he had written it.
If he acknowledged it, they were to demand of him, demand of him, that he put his signature to it, confirming that he had written it.
But if he denied it and would not acknowledge it, he was to be tortured to the point of death until he acknowledged it, and then left in prison.
Those who received these orders took the writing, went to him at the monastery in great fury, and showed it to him.
They demanded that he acknowledge whether he had written these things. But he, so that he would not be caught in a lie, acknowledged that he had written it.
They demanded that he write an acknowledgment on the document in his own handwriting: “I, Paul, acknowledge that I wrote with my own hand everything contained in this document.”
So they left him imprisoned there and went away, taking the document to the patriarch and the emperor.
From then on, threats of death hung over him, since the matter of the accusations from Rome had also been added to this.
Indeed, both he himself and everyone else gave up hope for his life. They thought that he would die a terrible death and depart from this earthly life.
Stephen, who was a bishop and whom the account mentioned earlier, was the man whom John, bishop of the imperial city, had wanted
to depose and ordain anew. He disputed with John and stood against him firmly and forcefully, and hurried to the emperor,
crying out and protesting against him over this. The emperor himself rejected the practice and strongly condemned it. He gave orders, and a pragmatic decree was issued
that no one should ever again dare to engage in this unlawful and godless practice. Stephen enjoyed great freedom to speak openly with the emperor,
and the emperor appointed him to go as bishop to the island of Cyprus, honored him in many ways, and also granted a substantial remission on that island for his sake.
From then on, having gained freedom to speak, he presented a petition on Paul's behalf, asking that he be pardoned
and released from the severe distress he was in. The emperor showed consideration for Stephen and promised him that, if Paul came in and received communion with him,
all the offenses he had committed would be forgiven. So Stephen went to him and told him these things.
Because of the terror of death that had gripped him, he surrendered, went in, and once again received communion. He was received into the bishop's residence.
But John, wanting to humiliate him before everyone, arranged for many senators and Alexandrians to assemble,
because he was Alexandrian by birth. In front of them all, John made him receive communion from him again,
so that, even if he wanted to turn back—to turn back, as John supposed—he would not be able to.
From then on, the emperor received him every day and discussed many things with him, for he was a wise, knowledgeable, and widely read man.
The emperor now sought his advice on affairs, and often spent time with him and spoke with him confidentially,
to the point that this alarmed John considerably: [?] he might dismiss him and bring in Paul in his place.
John was now in great anxiety and fear. He began sounding out the emperor, saying,
"If you command it, my lord, let them send Father Paul to Jerusalem as bishop, or to Thessalonica, since both sees are vacant."
But the emperor, knowing his timidity and wanting to make him tremble still more, said to him, "Leave Father Paul alone,
because we need him here." This alarmed him even more. From then on, he was firmly gripped by this suspicion and became bewildered.
So he gave Paul freedom to leave if he wished and left him without a guard.
Anyone who wished could visit him, for John was hoping that he would have an opportunity to escape. And this is exactly what happened: Paul escaped, and John was relieved.
Now, when Paul had gone in through Stephen's intervention and had been received, and the Synodites had become very confident of him,
Stephen was also sent by the emperor and the patriarch to John, who was called the man in charge of the pagans and the breaker of idols,
along with senators and the rest of the others, to the hospice called Eubulus's—Eubulus's establishment, where, after the two had been confined in the bishop's residence
and after they had all been separated from one another, John himself was confined in its infirmary,
with none of his acquaintances being seen with him at all. The men who had been sent therefore came to him and said,
"Our lords the victorious emperors and the patriarch—and the patriarchs—send you their very affectionate greetings and urge you
to free yourself from this distress and come in to your brothers, Mar Paul the patriarch and Mar Elisha, and bring joy to them,
as well as to the merciful emperors and the holy patriarch, and discuss unity once again."
When John himself, amid the distress and hardship of his harsh imprisonment, heard these things,
He was stirred by zeal to confront those who came to him angrily and harshly, with anathemas, insults, curses, and many other things of this kind.
These seemed too excessive to be put into writing. And so they left him, embittered and distressed over him.
Then, a day later, they were sent to him again, appealing to him in a conciliatory manner on behalf of the emperors and the patriarch, saying:
“For the sake of the church’s unity, yield and come, and let us talk. Do not persist like this in quarreling over unity.”
But again they heard from him things even harsher than the earlier ones, as he said, “God and human beings have had enough of that first union,
which was proclaimed and became a cause of overthrow, uprooting, and downfall,” along with other things of this kind.
After they had gone back and forth many times and he had neither yielded nor been persuaded by them, they finally said to him, “Because we know what awaits you,
and we hear threats of death against you—that you are not destined to be destroyed by an ordinary death—
we are concerned about you. We say this to clear ourselves of responsibility for the sufferings you are going to endure.”
When he heard this, he boiled with zeal and cursed them: “If only you would eat me roasted, and I could be spared the sight of you, and then be handed over to a bitter death!”
In short, they left him. Then Stephen himself came to him secretly, alone,
informing him about the deadly measures decreed against him. He said to him, “For my part, I am leaving now, so that I do not see the sufferings coming upon you. Look after yourself.”
Although many things happened and were said, it proved impossible to weaken his resolve. And so Stephen left them and departed for Cyprus.
While John himself was subjected to the harsh and bitter affliction of imprisonment, he also fell into another affliction: bitter pain in his feet and hands caused by gout.
From then on he was like a dead man, unable to turn over or move either a hand or a foot, and deprived of human care, especially that of his acquaintances.
Along with this, he was tormented night and day by the ordeal of various crawling creatures. First, he was infested with countless lice.
Besides these, there were fleas, which filled the cell where he was imprisoned. Night and day they wore his life away.
Besides these, throughout the day countless swarms of flies and mosquitoes gathered on him because of the filth of the infirmary,
while he was completely unable to move his hands and drive them away.
Nor did he have anyone to drive them away from him. At night another ordeal was added to his sufferings, a fourth and more bitter than all the others: bedbugs.
All night long they would come out and cover him, his entire bed, his face, and his eyes,
until his face and eyes became swollen and puffy, and he could not wipe them away.
Then there was another ordeal, a fifth: mosquitoes, which, together with these, fastened on him like fire throughout the night,
especially on his face and wherever they could find any exposed part of his body. He wept and wailed because of all this distress.
And there was the burning from these five plagues, which surrounded his whole body on every side, within and without, and there was no one to come to his aid.
Neither at night nor during the day, for throughout all these trials he was burning from the vermin. Besides these, there was also the sixth trial [?] that Satan brought upon him.
These were mice, which came up and made themselves a nest beneath the pillow under his head. All night long they dug and squeaked beneath his head.
All these afflictions were added to his confinement and illness—were added to him [?]—and there was no one to help.
Yet it happens that those who have not been tested and fallen into these things even treat the written record of their remembrance—their remembrances [?]—as something to laugh at and mock.
These people should, according to our Lord’s words, stay awake and pray that they may not enter into temptation.
So, from the depth of his miseries, amid all that burning of his body from all the varied and vicious vermin that were making him burn:
This John whom we have mentioned came, through the bitter pains that were also tormenting him, to look for someone to feel sorry for him, but there was no one;
and for someone to comfort him, but none was found. That is, he came to despondency under the pressure of his trials, as he himself afterward used to relate.
For both in many letters and in a declaration in the Spirit that he made to the eastern synod and to all the ranks of the faithful,
he wrote about all these things, including this vision that he saw, declaring in the Spirit before God that he was not going beyond the bounds of truth
and adding a single word to what he had endured, or to this vision that had plainly appeared to him. He spoke as follows before everyone:
“While I was being tormented by all these trials, my spirit grew distressed, and I lost heart and despaired of my life.
One day a handsome young man, wearing a beautiful white tunic decorated with [?], suddenly came in to me.
It seemed to me that he was one of the attendants who cared for the sick.
It was after the meal, at midday, when everyone had gone to sleep, the doors had been shut, and everything was quiet on every side.
While I was burning under the torment of all those different kinds of vermin, together with bitter pains, he suddenly came in to me and said,
‘Peace to you, Father! How are you feeling? How are you? Do not be afraid.’ But I was still in that same despondency,
and in my great distress I said to him, ‘Why do you ask me, my son, when you see me in all this torment?’
But that young man said to me, ‘Take courage, Father, and do not lose heart. Give thanks to God, who has not abandoned you, for he has not forgotten your affliction.’
I answered him again, ‘What encouragement or comfort can there be for me? Look, I am dying a bitter death,
not only under the pressure of the severe pains laid upon me in keeping with my sins, but also from all these vermin that surround me and are destroying me.
And I have no one to remember me, so that I might at least be comforted by seeing them.’ After this he said to me,
‘We know that you are afflicted and that there is no one to care for you, and especially that you are afflicted by pain and vermin.
That is why I have now come in to visit you and encourage you. I also know that you are thirsty and that there is no one to give you water.
I will bring you a mixed drink. God will help you; be strong. And know that, in proportion to all this affliction that holds you, God will also increase your reward.’”
“Do not be distressed, and do not lose heart.” After saying these things and many others, he went outside.
He returned carrying a vessel of wonderful mixed drinks that shone like light. He gave it to me, and I drank with pleasure and delight.
My soul was refreshed, and I thanked God, while also expressing my gratitude to that young man.
I said to him, “May God have mercy on you, my son, because you have shown me this kindness, visited me, comforted me, and encouraged me.”
After comforting me with many words, he said, “Tomorrow I will visit you again,” and left.
I was so encouraged by that young man’s appearance and words that all my pains and afflictions became lighter.
The next day he came again at the same time. Once again he asked me, “How have you been?”
“Be strong and do not be distressed, for you have a great reward to receive from God in return for all this suffering.
You will be released from this hardship, and your own people will gather around you.
God is with you; do not let your spirit be distressed.” He said many other things to me as well, and then left again.
On the third day, although my eyes were now fixed in expectation of his coming, he did not come. I became deeply distressed and was filled with great sorrow.
On the fourth day he came again at the same time and said, “I know that you were distressed because I did not come to you yesterday.
Do not be distressed; I will not abandon you.” After again advising and encouraging me with many words, he left me once more. In this way he kept coming and going for eight days.
I marveled at the dignity, beauty, and features of that handsome young man, and at his speech and knowledge.
After these eight visits, when he had come to me and gone away, the patriarch’s assistant finally came to pressure me.
After he had said many things, I answered him, “This is in keeping with your divided faith—that you should behave like pagans.
So now you are carrying out the deeds of pagans: you see me in all this hardship,
yet you have no fear of God that would lead you to give me even one of my servants whom you are holding prisoner, so that he might attend to me.”
He recounted many things that had been said between them, and how he had spoken harshly to him and rebuked him. The man left him
in a surge of anger, went and brought him one of his servants, and said, “Here is your servant to attend to you. Do not curse us.” Then he went out angrily and left.
After his servant came, that young man no longer came to him, nor did he appear to him again.
As he wondered and tried to find out about him, supposing that he was an attendant, he said to the officer who was guarding him,
“A young man, one of your attendants, used to come in to me, encourage me, and visit me. But now, for several days, ever since this servant of mine came to me, he has not come to me again.
What can have happened to him? [?] Has he fallen ill?” The officer then questioned him about what sort of young man he was.
He told him, “He is a handsome young man, and he was very tall in stature.”
His face was bright and fair, and he was wearing a beautiful tunic with a patterned fringe.
It had roundels containing figures, both above and below. The superintendent said to him:
“None of the attendants has any of these features you have described to me.” But he answered him again, saying, “You should know
that for eight days he kept coming in and out to see me, comforting and encouraging me, and speaking with me wisely and sensibly.” Then the superintendent said again:
“We have no young man at all like the one you have described.” Then he went out, gathered all the young men, and brought them before him,
saying, “Here are all our attendants. We have no others. See whether he is one of them.”
But after looking closely at them all, he said, “He is not any one of these.” Then, when the superintendent heard this, he said:
“A vision from God has appeared to you and visited you, Father. One of the angels or one of the saints was sent to you to strengthen and encourage you.
There is no one here like the one you have described.” And so John was astonished, bewildered and amazed,
reflecting on the words, wisdom, and sayings of that extraordinary young man, so extraordinary in appearance.
He said, “I regarded him as one of the attendants. But God knows what and who he was.
He helped me in many ways. He brought me medicinal mixtures in a [?], and I marveled at how clear and wonderful they were.
All my pains were relieved. And I was also astonished at the words of wisdom and good sense that came from his mouth,
that someone like this should be serving the sick in your hospice.
So from now on, as we marvel at the grace shown to us, we must give thanks to God, who in his mercy cares for everyone,
who himself knows what that young man's appearance was—for through his hands he cared for us and brought us relief in our afflictions.”
For when this John had completed twelve months and nine days confined in this way, after his two earlier periods of imprisonment in the bishop's residence,
even then the malice of John of Sirmium had still not subsided. He gave orders, and they took him from the hospice and sent him out again to the island in the sea.
There too they confined him in the same way, under harsh conditions. He ordered that none of his acquaintances should any longer be allowed to speak with him at all.
When he had completed twenty-eight months on that island as well, the chastisement from God overtook both parties—a terrible, astonishing, and grievous chastisement.
And so, finally, by order of Caesar Tiberius, they sent for him, took him from there, and brought him into the city.
He then lived in the city under guard for more than three years, until the end of John of Sirmium, the persecutor.
All these things are also found in the many letters he wrote to many people,

together with the vision of that young man who used to care for him. Anyone who reads these earlier and later accounts should not be surprised to find that they differ from one another, with omissions and additions.
For he himself did not speak of these things either, except for a few of them, for the glory of God.
Although I have neglected and passed over many things because of their great length, in some places I have dealt at greater length with some of these things that were mentioned [?].
And especially in certain matters [?], whether concerning the vision or the other remaining matters.
So here too I shall write only briefly, so that these things may serve as short reminders.
And by not recounting the stories at great length, they will not seem excessively wearisome to those who encounter them afterward.
Now Paul of Antioch himself supposed that he had by then become firmly established in the doctrine of two natures.
But John the patriarch, who was very weary of him, was glad that the thought should occur to him to escape, and he was no longer kept under guard.
After spending some time in the bishop’s residence, he went down one night among the people, escaped, and went and hid in a concealed place.
At the appointed time he was sought but could not be found. Then John, afraid of the emperor, immediately went in and informed him of Paul’s escape.
When he heard, he was astonished and was filled, was filled, was filled with anger. He ordered all the crossings to be secured and all the boats to be searched.
And all the houses on the other side of the entire city, all the suburban estates and monasteries—even the tombs were being opened.
They searched for him inside [?] full of corpses. Finally, urgent letters were written to every region and city,
to the bishops and governors, with his distinguishing features also described, so that he might be recognized and arrested. But he was not found.
Finally his brother, who was the official in charge of the ships, was arrested and subjected to harsh treatment.
But he himself remained hidden inside the city, as they say, in a cabinet built into a wall, for nine months.
Then afterward he left and went into hiding in the land of Arabia, with the knowledge of the household of Mundhir son of Harith, until the time of the terrible punishment mentioned above.
At that time, then, when everyone was gripped by fear, many were shaken by the emperor’s harsh and terrifying threats,
and were being driven into communion. For on the feast day the emperor had also commanded, saying, “Anyone who does not receive communion with me must not greet me.”
Many were shaken by this and were led into communion with them, apart from only a few.
These had accepted a sentence of death upon themselves. And so many were gripped by fear.
But Andrew the treasurer, who has been mentioned, had from his youth been ardent and burning with zeal for the faith, and diligent in virtuous conduct.
He persevered in fasting and prayer. From the very beginning of the persecution, when many of the male and female chamber attendants,
out of fear—including the empress’s own chief chamberlain, whose name was Stephen—
who had been orthodox since the days of Empress Theodora, were led away and driven into communion with the adherents of the council who sided with the emperor,
he alone remained resolute and stood courageously, confident in that struggle with death,
while the sovereigns themselves, together with all the rest of the chamber attendants of both households, who wanted to please them, were drawn up against him in battle and debate.
He was not at all afraid of any of them, nor did he cease or slacken in his struggle against them all.
Thus the king himself constantly addressed him with terrible and harsh threats of death.
But he would not give way at all, even on a single point, or bow to him or shrink from him, until the king became enraged.
Once the king himself struck him in the liver with his own hands, because he was boldly opposing him in public as they exchanged words.
The king demanded that he receive communion from those who adhered to the synod, but he disputed with him and opposed him, saying:
“I acknowledge that you are my masters and that I am your servant. My body is in your hands,
so that you may do whatever you wish with it. But you have no authority over my soul, because it is in God's hands.
And neither you nor anyone else will ever change my faith, because I have believed in God.”
There were countless other things said between them every day. And because both rulers loved him for his noble character and virtue,
and also for his intelligence and knowledge, they were all the more eager to bring him into submission rather than expel him from their palace.
The king himself would say in front of many people, “What are we to do with this insolent man who opposes us and will not obey us? For an intellect and a mind like his
we have nowhere else here. We do not want to expel him, yet there is no way to leave him here when he will not obey us.”
So they put up with him for a considerable time, hoping to turn him around. But when he neither yielded to them nor relented,
they finally gave him an ultimatum, saying, “Either obey us and receive communion with us, or leave our palace.”
When he saw this, he immediately took off his robes and threw them down before them, saying:
“You have never done me a greater kindness than this: you are releasing me from service and slavery to human beings,
and enabling me to stand in the service and slavery of the one who created me and brought me into the world, and to serve him alone as a slave.”
Thus he left the palace and went and was confined under harsh conditions in the palace called Hormizd's.
After many days, the king's administrator was sent to him to unsettle and frighten him, and to see whether he had relented and would receive communion with them rather than lose his position.
He went and tried many approaches with him, admonishing, coaxing, and pleading with him. When he saw that he would not relent, he began making threats and trying to frighten him, saying:
“Watch yourself, [?] I am compelled to do to you what I have been ordered.” But he immediately bent his neck and stretched it out before him,
saying, “May you not be among the living, and may God not accept your kindness, if you have not brought your sword with you.
Here is my neck: cut it off. But do not be mistaken, either you or those who sent you.
I have never had any fellowship whatsoever with those who divide our Lord Jesus Christ into two, nor will I ever have it again—God forbid!
And may God not accept your kindness unless you immediately take off my head and enable me to escape this miserable life.”
When the curator heard these things, he went in and reported them to the sovereigns. When they heard, they were astonished at him and were also distressed on his account.
Again, in the hope that he could be persuaded, they ordered that, in the monastery called that of Dalmatius—
that of Dalmatius, which stands above all the monasteries in the city and throughout its surroundings—he should go and be imprisoned.
So they brought him out and led him away in daylight, in everyone's sight, as an act of intimidation.
But he was joyful and cheerful and gave thanks to God as they held him and he passed through the city among all the people, going to be imprisoned for the truth of the faith.
Great crowds ran to see the empress's treasurer, who had stripped off and thrown away his worldly authority and was being led to imprisonment for the true faith.
Thus, while everyone was astonished at him, many praised God, who had strengthened him to despise the world in this way.
Many were strengthened in the faith as they saw him so cheerful and joyful, and they praised God.
His own people and the others who were leading him kept tugging at the covering on his [?], so that he would cover his head.
But he kept uncovering it, saying, “It is a great honor for me to die for the truth of Christ. Let no one deprive me of my honor.”
So he went and was imprisoned in that monastery for three years. Finally, after this chastisement, he was released and left outside the palace.
Now, from the days of the late Empress Theodora, her maternal aunt, the merciful Empress Sophia herself,
from her youth until three years before she became empress, used to receive communion with the orthodox.
She entirely avoided all communion with the adherents of the council, that is, those who profess two natures. Everyone knows this openly.
A priest named Andrew also used to come in [?] and celebrate the Eucharist in her house, giving communion to her and everyone in her household.
When he finished the Eucharist, she would tell him to leave one eucharistic particle on the plate and place it under the veil.
No one else knew who took that particle which was left, except the patrician Sophia herself.
From this, everyone supposed that the merciful Justin took it secretly, since he too avoided communion with those who profess two natures.
We cannot testify to the truth of this. We have put it on record only on the basis of the report commonly believed by everyone.
Her coming into communion with those who profess two natures happened for the following reason.
They were urging many people to persuade the late Justinian to make Justin, his sister's son, Caesar.
But he paid no attention to this and brushed everyone aside. Finally Theodore, who had been made bishop of Caesarea, went to her—
a man whose sentence of judgment for his many wicked deeds is known to God alone—and said to her:
“You should know that it is not without reason that, up to now, your uncle has not listened to anyone and made his sister's son Caesar.
He is upset with you because you have acted against him: you receive communion with those who oppose him, but you do not receive communion with him.”
And how can he bring you to share the rank of royalty with him, when you are seen to be opposed to him?
But listen to me: go and receive communion in the church. You will please the emperor, and he in turn will give you relief.
And so she was persuaded by this—“you were persuaded” [?]—and just three years before she became empress, she received communion—“you received communion” [?]—with the synod, for many years.
Now these three consuls, whose names were John, Peter, and Eudaemon, held their bodily lives in contempt for the sake of spiritual life, in defense of the true faith in Christ.
They stood firm, took their stand, and declared that they would not share communion with those who divide Christ. Deadly wrath and hostility were directed against them.
From then on they were constantly expecting trials and the destruction of their estates, their houses, and everything they owned.
And although everyone had condemned them to utter destruction, God protected them, seeing that for his name and in defense of the truth of faith in him, they were struggling with death.
For many senators, chamberlains, and other officials had been driven by fear into communion with the Chalcedonians.
And the emperor heard the murmuring about the force and compulsion imposed on many people. Finally, wishing to present himself before the senators
as someone who compelled no one—although everyone was being subjected to compulsion harsher than any other—God put it into his mind to speak as follows:
“We have not compelled anyone, nor do we compel anyone. Those who would not be persuaded by us to receive communion with us, we have left to their own choice.”
This thought and declaration brought relief to these men, and they were subjected to no further trials over the matter of faith.
Instead, they eventually attained high offices and great freedom to act openly. Thus the illustrious Eudaemon became count—count of the private estates.
And the illustrious John, who was related to Emperor Anastasius and was also the grandson of Empress Theodora through her daughter,
together with Peter, who likewise belonged to the family of Peter, the patrician and curator of the empress’s estates—
these men were eventually sent to negotiate a treaty with the Persians on behalf of the entire Roman state.
They maintained their firm position as they had from the beginning, with great openness. Patriarch John, however, had removed their names from the diptychs.
The diptychs. And this itself gave them great joy, for they said, “Now we know that God is pleased with us
and has looked upon us, so that we are not commemorated at the offering of those who divide Christ into two after the true and indivisible union.”
But against these two well-known women, along with many other women of patrician rank and others, a fierce campaign was mounted from every side.
They were subjected to harsh threats of fire and menaced with death. The others grew weak in the struggle because of the severity of the suffering caused by the persecution.
For the sake of their movable possessions, their houses, their children, and their estates, they were driven into communion, though only outwardly.
But these two stood firm and faced death, surrendering their lives to death and holding possessions, children, and houses in contempt.
One of them, whose name was Antipatra, was the mother-in-law of John the consul,
who was mentioned in the preceding account, together with her daughter, who was herself a consul’s wife and zealous for the faith. Her name was Georgia, the wife of John.
The other woman, whose name was Juliana, was the daughter of Magnus the consul, who himself had once been sent into exile with his sons, and Juliana was with him.
She too was there, for he himself belonged to the family of Emperor Anastasius. She was also the sister-in-law of Emperor Justin himself, the wife of his brother.
So, after much conflict and a heroic struggle, they put both this woman and Antipatra into convents across the water at Chalcedon.
Harsh orders were issued concerning them and sent to the convents in which they were confined:
if they would not agree to receive communion, they were to be tonsured and dressed in the black monastic habit.
They were to be required to perform every menial task of monastic life. Indeed, even harder tasks than these were imposed on them.
They required them to sweep the convent, carry out the refuse, and scrape and wash their latrines,
to serve in the kitchen, and to wash lamps and pitchers, along with other such tasks that were harshly demanded of them.
Thus, when they could no longer bear and endure all these afflictions, they too were driven into Chalcedonian communion, though only outwardly,
so that they might be released and escape the oppressive confinement of these convents—if indeed they deserve to be called convents.
In this way they were released and returned to their homes, thereafter retaining their former rank.
Then the time of chastisement from God overtook both sides, and so relief came to these women and to everyone.
Now this Sergius was a priest and the author's syncellus, together with another Sergius, a priest who was also his disciple.
While John himself was in prison, in the confinement rooms of the hospice of Eubulus, to which they were brought after they had repeatedly struggled, been arrested, and been imprisoned,
at last, through treacherous betrayal by others—that is, by someone close to them who was ostensibly imprisoned with them—
this very betrayer, who resembled Judas, was himself also arrested and dragged off to the bishop's residence.
As they stood up to those who were holding them, disputed with them, and argued vigorously with them,
their captors became enraged with them. Before a large crowd, they stripped them, stretched them out, and flogged them severely in full view of everyone.
But they could not weaken their resolve. When they stood firm and struggled so powerfully and courageously
that even their persecutors marveled at them, they imprisoned them in the sacristy of that same hospice of Eubulus,
after other earlier imprisonments, oppressive and harsh, twice in the bishop's residence
and once in the monastery called the Monastery of Rabbula—that is, this Sergius, the syncellus mentioned above.
They remained there for forty days during the harsh cold and frost of February.
Patriarch John used to send for Sergius the syncellus and have him brought to him. He would admonish him, trouble him, and urge him to stay with him in his episcopal residence
and become his cleric—a cleric—swearing to him, “I will not force you to receive communion with us.”
But since I have heard that you are a chaste man and a monk, stay with us and live as you wish.
And if you commit yourself and join us, I will immediately make you bishop of whatever city pleases you.” But he fought bravely,
and so neither by promises nor by threats could he make him relax his firm adherence to the truth,
so that, when he saw his determination and his refusal to yield, he immediately sent him away and confined him in the monastery called the House of Rabbula.
These were not corrupt in their faith like the other monasteries. They did not favor the Council of Chalcedon, nor did they proclaim it at all.
Then, while this same Andrew the priest was again imprisoned outside the city wall in the [?], he sent clergy and Roman soldiers against him.
They broke open his place of confinement and brought him out. Pulling at him and dragging him along, they led him into the middle of the city.
When he saw a large crowd, he began shouting, “Help! Help! People, I am a Christian, and orthodox too!
And if these men who are pulling at me are not pagans, but say that they are Christians, why have they become persecutors and murderers of Christians?
And why are they dragging me through your midst, while you remain silent instead of showing zeal for Christ?”
Along with many other things like these, he shouted—[?] he was shouting things like these.
Consequently, a large crowd gathered and looked at those who were holding him with such fierce zeal that they were ready to kill them.
But when they saw the anger and zeal of the whole crowd against them, they fled and hid.
Thus they rescued the blessed Andrew from them. Eventually, however, they seized him again and sent him away to be confined in the monastery of the Sleepless Monks.
Of the Sleepless Monks. After he had been there for some time and many things had happened, he escaped from there too.
Afterward they again lay in wait for him, seized him, and confined him in the bishop’s residence. After much contention, he escaped from there too.
For although various charitable establishments for men and women can be seen in this great imperial city, there were two large and well-known charitable establishments.
Both belonged entirely to the orthodox. One was the first and largest, the one founded by the godly Paul of Antioch,
who with great zeal also created and established charitable institutions in the large and well-known cities of both the East and the West.
In these, the saying of our Lord is seen and fulfilled: “This is my rest: give rest, that I may give rest to the weary.”
Not a single person who accepted the Council of Chalcedon was admitted into any of them.
Now, when this time of persecution arrived, a great, celebrated, and well-known man named Thallus was in charge of one of them.
He had especially expanded and enlarged this ministry through many spiritual and godly activities, about which there would be much to tell and write.
While it was flourishing in this way, as it still does even now, through the envy of the devil it was denounced before the emperor and the bishop:
“They are all opposed to the Council of Chalcedon, and many monks and clergy are mixed in among them.”
Assemblies, gatherings, and much activity took place there. From that time the blessed Thallus was compelled, so as not to give those who hated good things a pretext,
to send away all the clergy and monks who were with him. Thus the laypeople alone carried out the service.
When these things became known to those in authority, they left him alone throughout his lifetime, also out of respect for him, since they admired the man's conduct.
His life came to an end recently, in the year eight hundred and eighty-eight. After him, a moneychanger named Romanus took his place.
At this same time, a cleric who was also named Comitas was in charge of the other of the two charitable establishments.
He too was diligent and virtuous. He had been a cleric at the church of Our Lady Mary at Blachernae.
At Blachernae, he had left because of the faith, together with others. He also gathered many people together and required them to live according to the monastic rule,
while he himself attended to all their needs. A large house was therefore left to him as an inheritance, so that a charitable establishment might be set up in it.
This indeed happened, and all the service to the poor was carried out in that house.
During the persecution, however, he too was accused of holding gatherings, and that house was taken away from him.
Imperial seals were affixed to it—imperial seals—and the charitable establishment was removed from it.
He himself was sent into exile on an island in the sea, and all those with him, down to the little ones, were scattered.
A few of them, however, persevered. They went and obtained another place for themselves, and continued their service in an orderly way, bathing the poor.
Because of this persecution, then, which had arisen in the imperial capital and was being carried out so zealously, forcibly, and relentlessly,
a fierce persecution now arose throughout all the territories of the Romans, wherever the orthodox were to be found.
Persecution was therefore stirred up against them through letters from John the patriarch and the others.
It rose like the waves of the sea and like the furnace of the Babylonians with its great blaze. But unlike that furnace, it was not fueled by reeds, twigs, and other combustible materials;
rather, this one was fueled by anger, fury, and a zeal for destruction and killing. It burned and blazed terribly and fiercely,
with everything that accompanied all these things: the plundering of household goods and the seizure of property under this pretext;
and secondly, imprisonment—in cramped prisons—and harsh bonds, tortures, floggings, banishments, and the rest, in every region and city and their surrounding districts.
Now, concerning the things that we witnessed, being close to the frequent ordeals involved in them and resulting from them throughout the period we have described,

we undertook to write only about these. But now we have thought it right to include, as a written record for remembrance, also those things which were recounted not by ordinary and insignificant people,
but before many people in our Roman imperial capital, concerning what had also happened in the territories of the Persians.
Although we ourselves did not see these things or know them firsthand, and cannot testify to their truth, since we were far from the places where they happened,
nevertheless, they were recounted before everyone by the great catholicos himself of Dvin, the great city in Persian Armenia, and by the other bishops who were with him.
When they fled, came, and took refuge in the Christian kingdom, they were received with great honor by the victorious kings.
They related the following things, solemnly swearing to their accuracy and taking great pains over their account.
They said that when their magi and the nobles of the Persian kingdom learned that, at the command and desire of the Roman emperor,
he required everyone throughout his realm, in every region and city of his entire dominion, to submit and embrace his faith,
and ordered all who resisted and would not obey his command and desire to be persecuted, imprisoned, and plundered,
and finally to be handed over to death: “Look,” they said, “these things are happening throughout Roman territory.
Now we too ought to act in this way in our own territories and convert all the religions under our authority to our religion.”
Then, they said, all the magi assembled and said to Khosrow their king, “O king, live forever!
We have learned that the Roman emperor demands, compels, and forces everyone throughout his dominion to embrace his religion and his faith.
He demands that the many people throughout his territories worship—that they worship according to his religion.
He expels and persecutes throughout his dominion all who will not obey him.
Let your own divinity likewise command that the same be done in your dominion, so that all religions may embrace your religion,
and everyone in your dominion may practice your worship. Those who dare to oppose your command must not live.”
When King Khosrow heard these things from the magi, they said, he yielded to their words and accepted their advice.
Immediately he too began with the Christians. First, they said, he sent and seized three bishops, together with many clergy and a large crowd of people [?].
He commanded them to renounce their faith and join him in worshiping fire, the sun, and the other objects of his worship.
But they resisted him and stood courageously against him, declaring, “We are Christians belonging to the kings [?].
We worship and honor God, the maker of heaven, earth, the seas, and everything in them. We will not abandon him,
who is the creator of everything, and worship his creatures. Do not be mistaken, O king! You have authority over our bodies, to do whatever you wish with them.
But our souls belong to him and are in his hands. You have absolutely no authority over them.”
When the king heard these words, together with many others worthy of the bishops’ testimony, they said, he gave the order, and they were immediately flayed and died.
This was in addition to the many other evils he inflicted on the Christians. He demolished many monasteries and churches, bound and imprisoned many people, and became arrogant.
He blasphemed Christ, saying, “Let us see what Christ, the Christians’ God, will do to me! I do not know who or what he is.”
These bishops recounted these things, along with many others that the Persian king said and did at this time, before Armenia surrendered to the Romans.
It was for this very reason, they said, that he ordered fire temples to be built throughout Persian Armenia.
After all these things, as the catholicos and those with him related, he sent a governor to our country, accompanied by two thousand armed horsemen.
He first came to us, to our city, carrying an order to build a fire temple there for the king’s worship.
As the catholicos went on to relate: “When he showed me and the townspeople the order,
I burned with zeal and stood against him, together with all the townspeople. We said, ‘We are servants of the King of Kings,
and we pay him tribute. But we are Christians, and in matters of faith we will not submit, even if we must die for the truth of our faith.
For this also happened in the days of Shapur, King of Kings. He wanted to build a house of worship here, and the people of the country assembled.
There was war for seven years. Then he established a law and issued us an order that the matter of Christianity should never again be prosecuted or investigated.
We even showed him a copy of that order of King Shapur, but he was not persuaded.
Instead, in accordance with his orders, he forcibly set about marking out the site, digging, and laying foundations. He began building, while also making thorough preparations for battle.
Although I pleaded with him at length, he would neither listen to me nor pay me any attention at all. Finally, I sent word of this everywhere, to all the people of the country.
When they heard, they burned with zeal for faith in Christ. They all assembled as one man, about ten thousand of them, armed for battle,
determined either to live or to die for Christ, and never to allow a temple of Magian religion and paganism to be built in their country.
When all the nobles and leaders of the country had assembled, we went together to that governor, to the place where he had begun building the fire temple.
We spoke with him at length, standing against him and saying, ‘We are Christians and subjects of the King of Kings.
But in matters of faith we cannot and will not submit to human beings. As for a pagan temple in our country, even if the king himself came,
it would never, ever be built before we had all died. So leave the country without war or bloodshed, and go to the king.
Tell him how firmly our resolve is set concerning our faith. He has the authority to do whatever he commands.
For until we are all dead, we will not allow a temple of Magian religion to be built in our country.’”
After they had spoken at length with one another, the governor, who was preparing to build as he had been ordered, argued with the people of the country and warned them, saying:
“Look, you are resisting the command of the King of Kings and insulting him.
He can sentence you to a cruel death. Consider what you are doing.”
But when the governor saw their resolve and their readiness to oppose him, and saw also that they were stronger than he was, he left, threatening and warning them.
He went in great anger and reported all these things to the king. When the king learned of them, he was roused to anger and became fiercely enraged.
He pronounced a death sentence on all the people of the country and sent fifteen thousand men against them for battle, together with the governor.
He ordered that, if they resisted his command, they should be put to the sword, and that the shrine of the fire temple should be built there.
When the people of the country learned these things, they all gathered together as one, about twenty thousand men prepared for battle, ready to fight to the death for their Christian faith.
When the others arrived and all drew up for battle against them, these men called on the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and went out against them.
Christ shattered them before the people of the country, who slaughtered them all to a man. They killed the marzban,
cut off his head, and brought it to the patrician Justinian, who was then stationed on the frontier in the city of Theodosiopolis.
All these things happened, along with the other events that followed, about which there would now be much to say and recount.
For when these things happened, and the whole country of Greater Armenia saw that a fierce war had been stirred up against them by the wicked Persian kingdom,
the entire country gathered together as Christians, and they hurried to seek refuge in the Christian empire, saying,
“From now on we are servants of the Christian empire, and we have hurried to seek refuge in the Roman Empire,
so that it may deliver us from the barbarity of Magianism.” Along with many other things, which, before our merciful emperors
and before the entire senate, the catholicos himself and the other bishops with him recounted, these were the things of which we have used only a few brief recollections.
They recounted the battles and the great slaughter that took place there at various times, and how afterward the armies again fell upon one another,
and many times the Persians were defeated and their elephants were taken from them. For the present, however, we have passed over these events because they are so numerous.
All these things, then, together with many others, the catholicos of Dvin, in the country of Persian Armenia,
recounted in the capital of our Roman Empire—he and the bishops and the many nobles with him—in the presence of many people.
When he arrived with the other bishops and some of the leading men of Armenia, they were all received with great honor,
and they received imperial gifts and honors. Great offices were granted to all those who had come with him from there,

as well as large houses and imposing imperial residences. Much gold and appointments to office were sent to those still in the country, along with a three-year remission of taxes from the Roman emperor.
Orders were given to help them and fight the Persians on their behalf and on behalf of the whole country of Armenia, while holding the country.
This continued for a long time, and the Magian people fell before the Christians on many occasions when they attacked them.
They continued waging these wars for six years. As for the events that followed, we shall recount a little out of much when we reach their time.
After two years, the catholicos himself died in the capital without returning to his own country.
From the very beginning of the arrival of the catholicos of Armenia and the other bishops and leading men with him,
as people who had fled from the wicked, pagan kingdom of the Magi and had come to seek refuge in the Christian empire,
as soon as they entered and were received and greatly honored, they made no inquiries but confidently entered into communion with the patriarch of the city, without investigation.
They were unaware of the cause of the division and dispute that existed throughout all the churches in the territories of the Romans because of the wrongdoing of the council held at Chalcedon.
So when this was heard in their own country, the rest of the bishops and all the people of the country became angry with them.
They wrote harsh things to them, which the circumstances require should be covered over in silence.
And so they withdrew and separated. From then on, they all formed a congregation together in one of the large residences that had been granted to one of their leading men.
There they used to gather in a large congregation after the death of their catholicos.
Now, as we consider how many things have happened in our times and in our days, and especially just recently,
and how they have transgressed boundaries and written agreements, especially those events after the surrender of Persian Armenia to the Romans,
which took place in the year eight hundred and eighty of Alexander, and how, because of this, continual and frequent wars broke out on every side,
and the sword devoured and much blood was shed; and how, again, the Magian advanced in his cunning and attacked the Roman forces in Armenia,
as—as he hoped—to destroy and annihilate them; and when he could not accomplish this, he turned away from them and crossed into Roman Armenia,
hoping to conquer Caesarea in Cappadocia and take its people captive. But when the armies surrounded him and checked his advance from Cappadocia as well, they turned and attacked him.
They carried off his entire baggage train, and he returned in disgrace. Had the commanders of the armies been in agreement with one another, he would not even have returned alive.
And how, again, the Roman emperor enriched and exalted the Armenians—Armenia [?]—with presents and gifts and offices and service;
and how, again, all Persian Armenia surrendered, was conquered and was seized—surrendered, was conquered and was seized [?]—by the Romans;
and although they had often triumphed, won victories and conquered other powerful nations, in the end, because of the leaders’ bad management,
or because they had angered God in many ways, although they numbered no fewer than a hundred thousand, before a single contemptible marzban,
who did not have thirty thousand men with him, the entire Roman army trembled and fled. They lost their weapons and their horses and were disgraced.
After these events, the Persian advanced and grew strong, seizing and conquering all Armenia. The whole country asked him for his pledged word, and he gave it to them.

The whole country once again surrendered to him, except for those of its people who were in Constantinople, after a period of seven years during which they had rebelled against him and fought with him.
And how, again, after these events, high-ranking envoys from both kingdoms were sent to examine the matters
that had arisen between the two kingdoms, and also to discuss peace once more. This did indeed take place.
For more than a year they sat opposite one another, talking, considering and debating with one another, without accomplishing anything.
At first the Persian demanded that he receive gold and then make peace. In response, the Roman emperor rose up boldly, saying,
“This man demands gold from us as though from someone who fears him and is subject to him.
Let him know that he will not receive a single mina during our lifetime, not even what he has been receiving from us until now.
If he will not act with the equal respect due from one kingdom to another, we will not make peace with him.” In the end, the Persian was brought to accept this too.
And nothing happened, along with many other things like these, whose stories many books could not contain.
And the remaining events concerning wars, the world, and the church—we have left some of these out because they are so numerous.
At this time, then, the power and fulfillment of the apostolic teaching are fittingly seen in action, when it says:
“For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all the injustice and wickedness of human beings who suppress the truth through injustice,” and the rest.
For at this time Christians, on frivolous pretexts, launched harsh and severe persecutions against Christians, without mercy and entirely without fear of God,
brutally and barbarously, not as Christians, resembling a lion roaring to tear apart, and a young lion sitting in hiding.
For this reason the Lord stood against them and brought them to their knees, as was openly revealed and made known before everyone's eyes.
These men, who, with every kind of lawless cunning toward their own flesh and blood—that is, toward the entire orthodox people—and with angry zeal,
were behaving neither peacefully nor justly nor as Christians, stirred up fierce and merciless persecutions,
and ordered bitter confinement in dark, cramped prisons for God's servants, men who were elderly, sick, weak, and respected.
They also decreed impious sentences of exile, entirely devoid of the fear of God, ordering
that those whom they arrested and imprisoned should be tormented with hunger and thirst and deprived of their acquaintances.
And those in the places where they cast the exiles were instructed to treat them mercilessly,
pressuring them by every means, so that through coercion, harsh afflictions, and trials they would be forced to submit to the will of their oppressors.
Others they coerced, subdued, and subjected to their will. Even the priesthood that orthodox men had held for many years
they were dissolving unlawfully and entirely outside canonical order, and they were ordaining them anew
as priests and bishops. And there were many other things like these, which we have too little time to recount.
These things, as indeed became known, even God's justice did not bear and endure.
Instead, swiftly and urgently, a sentence of judgment and wrath from heaven against all this impiety and brutality
was sent—that is, against those who practiced it without the restraints of the fear of God,
namely, against John the patriarch and against the emperor, who was being stirred up by him and was ordering him to act in these ways.
Both were struck with one rod of wrath and received one sentence of being handed over to evil spirits,
along with the many other terrible and grievous things that happened in the meantime, which, out of respect for the priesthood and the imperial office, we will conceal in silence for the moment.
These things were being done, displayed, and spoken over no short period by the demons to whom each and every one of them had been completely handed over.
Though these things are very terrible and grievous, they are not false, according to the testimony of all the people of these times.
But after the terrible punishment that had been sent upon the bishop and upon the emperor,
Bishop John himself, through the activity and urging of the one who was working within him, prepared all the more to persecute the faithful.
Every day he prepared savage and harsh attacks against them from every direction, without understanding or orderly thought.
And although he was repeatedly afflicted by an evil spirit, so that the righteous Judge became still more angry with him,
and sent upon him further internal affliction and pain in his bowels, together with the bitter pain of gout,
so that he now languished beyond any cure, and pain upon pain and affliction upon affliction
were added to him every day. Although he received abundant care from many physicians, no relief or improvement at all could be seen in him.
But just as the magicians acknowledged before Pharaoh, “This is the finger of God,” so this man too, even if compelled by necessity,
now recognized the punishment that had been sent upon him from heaven, and began to say to the physicians with sorrowful tears,
“Why, my sons, are you still wearing yourselves out over me in my misery? You cannot cure my afflictions,
because all these afflictions have been sent upon me from heaven by a righteous sentence, because I provoked anger. Human beings cannot cure them.
For only now have I learned and understood that, just as I struck many people without mercy, so now I alone have been struck without mercy by that one.”
The physicians had stopped treating him some time before, as he himself had urged them to do, since he could no longer take any food.
Even if he drank mixed drinks, he quickly vomited them up. Finally, even his internal organs were breaking apart and passing out of him.
His torment was not only bitter and severe but also prolonged. Weeping over himself, he would say in the presence of many people, “I know, my Lord, that I have done evil before you,
and the curses of your servants, elderly and honorable men, have overtaken me and stirred up your anger against me, because I treated them without mercy.”
This man had been continually afflicted since after the first year of his persecution, unable to raise his head.
Yet even so he did not desist from the cruelty of his schemes. Finally, after severe diarrhea and all this bitter torment had worn him down
for about two years, he departed from this earthly life in the thirteenth year of the reign of Emperor Justin.
He remained in these illnesses, and although he occasionally experienced some relief, he was continually afflicted again until the day of his death.
We have already dealt briefly with his memory earlier in this chapter. But now it is right for us to show
God’s righteous sentence: he has shown that deeds receive their recompense not only at the judgment to come, but even here.
For when John of the imperial city, who was mentioned above, was driven by savage impetuosity and carried away by pride and restlessness like a young boy,
and was also crazed and drunk with power, persecuting and seizing monasteries and even the churches of the orthodox Church,
he would take down and remove all the images of the orthodox fathers, and set up and install his own images everywhere.
While he did not expect to die, the end of his life suddenly overtook him. Eutychius, who had previously been expelled, was summoned and installed in his place.
When this man had died and the other had been summoned and installed, although he had put aside and overlooked everything that had previously happened between them at the emperors’ urging,
the portraits of John himself, which were numerous everywhere—
Eutychius himself erased and removed from the bishop’s residence and from all the churches, even the individual ones that had been overlooked and were found here and there.
Indeed, in all the cities and districts, once people learned Eutychius’s wishes, they erased all John’s portraits, both paintings and those on panels, so that they would not be accused.
They removed his portraits and installed those of Eutychius, as we have said, even the small ones left scattered about.
God repaid Abimelech for the evil he had done: he killed—and they killed [?]—his brothers, seventy men on one stone.
And so this became a source of astonishment, amazement, and wonder to everyone:
how quickly God repaid John, already in this life. As he had done, so it was done to him. And the Lord brought Nabal’s retribution back upon his own head.
Thus John’s portrait was erased after his death, just as he had dared to take down the portraits of the saints and put up his own.
He occupied his see for approximately thirteen years.
Now this Theodulus, a deacon of the church from his youth, appeared gentle, humble, and quiet.
Thus many people considered him virtuous. When he gained access to Emperor Justinian, and the emperor saw his gentleness and quietness,
he entrusted him with a large amount of gold to distribute to the poor, to prisoners, and to the monasteries around the city and in all the surrounding regions.
He would even give him hundred-pound sums of gold and send him to distant places to distribute them. Thus, little by little, he too kept hundred-pound sums for himself.
[?] In the same way, Justin too continued to trust him. When the persecution broke out, in an effort to win favor,
as a trusted man, he joined John and the others in inflicting many sufferings on the whole body of the faithful.
He himself was sent to the monasteries first. He misled many with deceitful oaths, but in the end he was exposed as a liar.
Thus he was filled with angry zeal, even more than John, on behalf of the council and the entire heresy of the two natures.
With his authority he seized, imprisoned, and tortured people as he pleased, while slandering all the faithful before both the emperor and the patriarch,
and inciting them to fierce anger. He received orders and authority and acted as he pleased.
Indeed, even John himself was very much afraid of him and kept clear of him. He had also been given authority over all the Arians everywhere.
While he too was rising so high and engaging in persecution, God sent severe afflictions upon him as well, so that he could no longer walk upright.
While he was still behaving so insolently and pursuing the persecution furiously, even his own relatives and his wife’s relatives, and his guard along with the others,
boarded a boat to cross to the other side of the sea. Their boat sank, and they drowned in the sea.
Only two or three of them escaped. After this destruction and the calamity that overtook him, his wife also died.
He himself also became bedridden in a state of severe weakness, suffering torment for three years.
Then, under the distress of these severe afflictions, he confessed with bitter tears, saying:
“Woe to me! The curses of the persecuted have overtaken me, and the cry of those whom I oppressed has risen before God.
All this misery has been sent upon me in wrath from heaven.” For a short time earlier, moreover, because of some matter that had arisen for him
and had upset his treasurer, who held everything he possessed, the treasurer went in secretly and informed the emperor about the hundred-pound measures of gold that he owned.
According to what was being said—for we do not know for certain—there were twenty-four or thirty.
After the emperor had secretly sent and taken them, he sent for Theodulus and said to him, “Since we need money to spend on wars, deacon,
if you have two or three hundred-pound measures of gold, give them to us, and we will repay you.” But he said to him, “My lord, where would I get hundred-pound measures of gold?”

He said to him, “By my life and my salvation, have you none?” But he denied it and swore that he did not possess a hundred-pound measure of gold. The emperor then gave an order, and the hundred-pound measures of gold were brought in together with his treasurer.
The emperor said to him, “Do you recognize these? How could you swear falsely by us and by God? Your shame is punishment enough for you. Get out of here!”
And so, like a thief ashamed when he is caught, he went out in shame and hid himself because of his disgrace. He became an object of reproach and contempt to everyone who encountered him.
Thus, when this disgrace was added to all his misery, from that time onward he lay prostrate and cast down, even to the present day.
For this imperial quaestor was himself also of Samaritan descent.
When the Samaritans were brought to trial in Palestine by Photius, they made him a [?].

A record of proceedings was drawn up against him and reached the emperor. But he ran here and there and distributed bribes on every side, and the record was suppressed, and no investigation was made against him.
He too was a hater and bitter enemy of all the faithful, and he threatened them harshly.
He accused them and constantly stirred up trouble against them, taking the place of John the patriarch when he was away.
But whenever John came in, the two of them would pester the emperor. And when the emperor sent for them and accepted what they said,
he would become inflamed with anger and issue terrible and harsh orders against the party of the faithful.
For, as everyone knows, he was constantly receiving considerable amounts of gold from John.
He was an adviser and instigator of every kind of evil, like his accursed teacher Aetherius,
who had been removed [?]. This man had long been in agreement with him and was eager to follow in all his footsteps.
When longsuffering justice would no longer tolerate this man's wickedness either—for although he presented himself as a Christian,
like the pagans and Samaritans, he used his authority as a pretext to strike secretly at Christians by every means and under every excuse.
He was secretly in league with the rest of the pagans to destroy the unity of the church.
Thus, when God saw the deceitfulness of his schemes, and that he thought he could deceive God and human beings, he exposed his deceit before the eyes of the entire church.
For on the day of the veneration of the holy cross of our Savior, when it was brought out and placed in the Great Church,
the whole senate and the entire city gathered to venerate it. The quaestor had entered with the senate to make an outward show that he too was a worshiper.
As the ranks stood in order and approached in procession, he reached the holy cross, and before he could bow down, a demon entered him
and lifted him up and dashed him to the ground before the holy cross, which he was approaching to venerate deceitfully rather than sincerely, mocking Christianity.
He began foaming at the mouth, tormented by the demon, thrashing about and crying out for a long time, until the patriarch gave orders, and a number of people gathered around and carried him away.
They brought him in and threw him into an inner room in the church, while the entire congregation cried out, “Lord, have mercy,” for a long time.
They marveled at the exposure of this man's fraud and at the rebuke that the Lord of the cross had administered to him before the eyes of the great crowds.
Fear fell upon many pagans and hypocrites. As for him, he never raised his head again.
Instead, continuing to be tormented in this way by that demon, he lived for about a year and a half, more or less, and then departed from this earthly life.
Now, when those who held authority, both secular and ecclesiastical, had chosen and approved this course:
that they should tear down the meeting places of the believers and overthrow their altars, shortly afterward, at that very time,
the nation of those shaggy-haired barbarians called the Avars mobilized and came against the city, as far as its outer wall.
All the churches throughout the land of Thrace were plundered, and they were driven out before them, along with the whole country. Their altars were stripped and torn down,
and the tombs were uprooted and demolished, right up to the city wall. Thus some of them, reflecting on this just judgment, said:
“What the members of our own party unjustly did to those who do not agree with us, tearing down their churches,
has now been done to us by God in his anger: our own churches too have been torn down and devastated.”
Everyone marvels at these things and praises God, who repays everyone according to their deeds.
After the death of Patriarch John, Eutychius, who had preceded him, was summoned from his monastery in Amasea, in the northern region.
He entered and was received with great ceremony by the rulers and the whole city. Great things were also being reported about him: that he worked miracles and performed mighty deeds.
The whole city rejoiced at his arrival, as though they had found relief from all John's dishonesty, deceitfulness, and [?],
which had been disorderly, since he was a young man and had belonged to the lawyers. Only a short time before, he had received the tonsure and become a cleric,
and then suddenly became bishop of the imperial city as well. He had not changed from his youthful ways or from all the ways of the lawyers.
Eutychius was a chaste monk. He had occupied the throne of the imperial city for twelve years before his removal.
After he left, John held office for another twelve years, and had even entered his thirteenth year.
Thus Eutychius returned, thinking that he would not sit on his throne before he had anathematized John and abolished his commemoration from the church of God.
Now, after John of Sirimis had died and Eutychius had been recalled and returned, the archdeacon of Rome spoke as follows before the emperor with great boldness:
“Let it be known to Your Clemency that, according to the ecclesiastical canons and regulations, if John was patriarch,
and performed everything as patriarch throughout his life, Eutychius is not patriarch. He cannot possibly enter the church and occupy the throne.
But if Eutychius is received again and enters as patriarch and occupies the throne, John and everything done by him are outside the entire church.
Everything done by him is invalid, whether the appointment of a bishop or all his other ordinations.
Whether he administered baptism, consecrated a church or an altar, or performed any other such acts, they are annulled and invalid.
His own name is likewise erased, he is publicly proclaimed excluded from the church of God, and he is removed from the entire priestly order.
This is especially so because the two of them deposed and anathematized one another from the church, together with everyone in communion with them.
According to the canons, one of them is deposed and deprived of office—deprived of office and excluded from the church.”
When the archdeacon had said all these things before the emperor, and declared that the pope of Rome would accept no other arrangement, he was sternly rebuked
and told to be silent and set aside the strict application of the canons. So he fell silent and let the matter go, and the canonical order was trampled down and transgressed.
For everyone had thought that Eutychius would undertake a thorough inquiry when he was recalled and returned.
Their wrongdoing came down upon their own heads: he went up and sat on the throne without dispute, while the turbid dregs of their mutual anathemas—

that is, John's and his own—were drunk and drained by both parties, together with those in communion with them, just as they had pronounced their anathemas. Everyone was seized with amazement at these things.
When Eutychius returned and took office, he neglected a canonical inquiry, fearing that some opposition might arise against him from it and that he would lose his stall.
He did, however, display his hatred and resentment toward John by ordering that all his portraits be torn down and removed from the episcopal residence,
which John himself had magnificently rebuilt after it burned down. His portraits were erased and torn down there and everywhere else.
He also stopped John's name from being proclaimed, until the emperor expressed his displeasure at this suppression of his name.
He expelled and degraded all John's close associates and relatives, and poured insults and abuse upon him.
Everyone who wished to please him, seeing his lack of restraint, would abuse John in his presence.
He listened with pleasure. Finally, he went to such lengths of recklessness that he openly declared before everyone:
“John was not the bishop of Constantinople. He was only keeping my place, while he himself was an outsider.”
Everyone who heard these words mocked them, knowing that he himself had left and been cast out, and that John had taken his place, occupied the throne, and carried out his deposition.
For while Eutychius was away in exile in his monastery, he selected and compiled writings consisting of extracts from the Fathers as a persuasive argument,
teaching a quaternity instead of the Holy Trinity, like the Council of Chalcedon and the wicked Tome of Leo.
That is, he too taught in the same way as these, saying, “There are two natures in Christ, even after the union.”
“This,” he said, “is also what all the Fathers confess.” Thus, immediately after he entered and took his seat on his throne,
he eagerly and diligently began sending his writings to all the leading men and prominent women,
urging them to read and consider them, so that they would confess two natures. He sent these writings with particular zeal
to those who took offense at the confession of two natures and who, together with all the Fathers, confessed one incarnate nature.
Thus, when many read them and were appalled by his laxity, including his own bishops and the others, the whole city began to be disturbed.
Especially all those who had not drunk the turbid dregs of Nestorius’s gall grumbled bitterly against him, particularly his own bishops,
until they were stirred to great agitation and uproar against him. They gathered at the bishop’s residence and said to him,
“You should know that unless you withdraw your writings and abandon this opinion, you will create a division in the Church of God and among us ourselves.”
So he withdrew his writings, and the disturbance ceased, although he persisted in his opinion.
After these things, however, this headstrong Eutychius, who originally came from the heresy of the Sabbatians,
did not delay in throwing himself into another pit, that of those who deny the resurrection of the body. Shamelessly and zealously, he also embraced this teaching,
openly professing and teaching it, saying, “These human bodies do not come to the resurrection.
Rather, other bodies, newly created, are the ones that rise at the resurrection.”
He taught these things not merely by ordinary speech, but also composed written discourses and published them publicly. He persisted in arguing about these matters.
Because of this too, agitation, grumbling, insults, and abuse arose against him throughout the city, especially from his own people and those who shared his faith.
They said to him, “Unless you stop this teaching, we will all anathematize you.” Yet even in this way they did not turn him from his opinion.
But he stopped teaching, while everyone regarded him as a heretic and a fool.
Out of empty conceit, Eutychius became filled with hatred and implacable hostility toward the entire community of the faithful.
He pursued them and set his mind on wiping them out and destroying them. Against each one of them, church advocates, imperial guards, Romans, and clerics,
along with members of the imperial bodyguard and others, would descend upon them during their worship services like brigands and barbarians, not like Christians.
They would seize them, tear at them, and drag them away, overturn their altars, throw away their offerings, and spill their consecrated gifts.
They would plunder and seize their liturgical equipment, all the other utensils they could find that they used, and their books.
They even seized their clothing and footwear, as well as the money for their necessities.
They did not disdain anything they could find, but plundered, seized, and stole it.
Finally, they dragged them away, together with everyone they found with them, and took them off to prison.
There they handed over what they possessed and what they did not possess, and only then did they leave that place. In this way, every day they seized one congregation after another.
When many people reproached them because, like pagans, they threw down and trampled on the Christians’ Eucharistic offering,
they finally began throwing it into the fire and burning it. All these evils continued without restraint, until no congregation could be found meeting openly anywhere in the city.
The cause of all these evils was a certain Pharbina, a slave of Andrew.
