When the persecution began, Andrew, who was the empress’s treasurer, left the palace and his service and departed for the sake of the true faith.
He was robbed and imprisoned in the monastery of Dalmatius, [?], but did not give in. He had a shameless barbarian slave whom he himself had raised and taught to read.
He had been trusted throughout his household, but in the end he rebelled against him and went and surrendered himself to Eutychius.
He appointed him to be an informer and [?], and [?] against all the priests and all the congregations.
Thus, to his master’s hurt, he would lead church advocates, excubitors, Romans, and clerics,
and go and drag everyone away, taking them off and putting them in prison after they had been barbarously plundered.
They carried off and took everything they had, even taking large amounts of gold from many of them.
Even if someone had gone in and hidden in a hole, so to speak, this man would cunningly make his way in and seize him,
rob him, and imprison him. This man became a trial and an adversary to all the priests, all the congregations, and all the faithful in the imperial city,
including us along with the rest. The evils this man inflicted on the whole church of the faithful are beyond telling and without end.
Now these sisters were sisters by birth. While they were still little girls, their mother died.
She died, and their father placed them in a convent. He too died and left them—that is, their convent—everything he owned.
As time passed, they grew up and reached maturity. Then the persecution under John overtook them, and afterward the persecution under Eutychius.
When they were forcing the whole convent to receive Communion from them, they seized some of the women and distributed them among the convents in the city.
But these two sisters stood firm as diamond, especially the elder.
They subjected her to every kind of torture and every affliction of harsh imprisonment, hunger, and thirst.
But she grew ever stronger, more radiant, and more fervent in faith. She rebuked and reproached all the women in whose convent she was imprisoned,
saying, “You, all your priests, and everyone who shares your views are strangers to the Holy Trinity.”
As people who uphold a quaternity in its place, you also side with the Council of Chalcedon,
which condemns Nestorius in appearance, but in practice and in truth holds to his faith and confesses two natures, just as he does.
And you side with it, along with everyone who agrees with it.” Thus she defeated them all, and they went in to complain to the bishop, crying out:
“Unless you order this trial to be taken away from us, you should know that we will all leave our convent.
For we cannot endure her insults, her abuse, and her arguing.” So he sent word to the exarch of the convents to send for her, judge her, and have her tortured,
and to take her out and put her in another convent, stricter than that one. The women there were to be ordered to torment her until they brought her into submission.
So when the exarch’s inspector went to her [?], and they began accusing and threatening her, she laughed at them boldly,
mocking them and saying, “What is this, you pagans and murderers? Are you threatening me, a weak woman? If you have come only to threaten,
and do not kill, as is your custom and that of the man who sent you, you are not men, and I do not even count you among the living.”
So while they angrily beat her with a staff as though she were a camel, she mocked them still more,
condemning them and calling out to them, “You pagans, persecutors and murderers of Christians!” She challenged them to kill her,
saying, “You are pagans, not Christians! For Christians do not persecute Christians.
But you show yourselves to be pagans, and you display the deeds of your paganism.”
So when these men too were defeated by her, they dragged her away and imprisoned her in another convent, ordering the women there to torment her harshly.
But after she had spent a few days there, [?] these women too began crying out and fleeing from her.
They put her in many convents in this way, but could not overcome her strength.
Then Eutychius ordered, “Bring her here to the church; bring her.” When the exarch’s people heard this, they went in and said to Eutychius,
“You should know, my lord, that if she comes to you, unless you cut out her tongue or take off her head, there is no insult or mockery she will leave unsaid to your face.
And when she is beaten and flogged, she only does it all the more, ready to be killed and eager for death.”
Finally, when they brought her into the church, many people took turns confronting her and heaped intimidation and threats upon her. She mocked them all as though they were lifeless corpses,
and rebuked them at length, until they were all defeated by her on every count. Finally they released her to return to her convent.
Thus she brought relief to her whole convent, for they no longer put pressure on its women. Shuddering at her struggles, they said,
“If one sister from that convent stood firm through all these struggles without weakening, who could withstand their strength when they all stand together?”
Now the mighty Eutychius, as in his other dealings, arrogantly [?], intending to show himself a teacher,
and schemed to abolish and put an end to the established practices of the church services that had existed from the beginning, and to establish and confirm his own destruction:
He was the one who wrote it out on notices on the Thursday of the Mysteries, sent it to all the churches, and ordered that, once the anthem used from the beginning was abolished,
his own should be used, threatening and intimidating those who dared to use the original one and abandon his.
As a result, not only the clergy of all the churches and of the monasteries for men and women were disturbed and troubled by this, but also the whole city and the entire senate.
It nearly came to a great uprising against him, not only from the churches and monasteries, but also from the whole city.
These matters were even brought to the emperor’s attention by some members of the senate.
But when the bishop hurried in to the emperor in a fit of anger to complain to him about these things,
the emperor rebuked him severely, saying, “How long will you refuse to control yourself and remain quiet?
Look, you have disturbed and troubled the whole city! How can you change their ancient customs?
And take care that they do not stone you!” He said to him, “My lord, I composed one of my own that is far more suitable than the original.”
The emperor said to him, “You should know that even if you had brought your anthem down from heaven, they would not accept it at all.
Go, remain in your church, and follow what was established in it by the early fathers.” Thus he restrained his impetuosity, and his threats ceased and fell silent.
Now this John, who was called “the one over the pagans” and was bishop of Ephesus, after all the trials, imprisonments, persecutions, and exiles he had endured,
was finally required to hand over the document for an estate that had been given to him by Callinicus the praepositus, the emperor’s praepositus and a patrician.
When John received it, he spent a great deal on it and renovated it. He built a church on it, made three cisterns there, and designated it a monastery.
When persecution arose from John, he took away from him the place he had designated a monastery, installed adherents of the council there, and sent him into exile on an island in the sea.
When John died and Eutychius took office, he demanded that he hand over his deed of gift for the estate and the rest of his documents relating to the estate.
And not only that, but also the church furnishings, books, and other possessions. After many days of persecution and oppression,
he seized him and put him in prison, demanding and taking from him all the documents for the estate.
While he was imprisoned, he assembled against him the whole company of church legal officers and laymen, who brought proceedings against him over the church furnishings and the other things.
But he was strengthened by grace and said to them, “What church furnishings and what possessions are you demanding?
Those that you or someone else gave there? Whoever gave me church furnishings is the proper person to come, demand them, and call me to account.
For look, you have unjustly and forcibly taken all the title deeds for the estate that I possessed, without any fear of God.
Read them and see. Is the name ‘monastery’ in them? Is it written in them that I received church furnishings? Yet that is what is being demanded of me.
For I acted unwisely when I designated it a monastery. Otherwise, it was not a monastery at all.”
Thus, with God’s help, he refuted them, and they all left him alone concerning these matters. But they demanded and took five loaves from him.
which had been bought for him for three hundred darics. They say “darics” [?]: “I bought these in the monastery’s name.”
While he was in prison, he provided a surety, and then he was released and escaped the distress of imprisonment.
Paul’s story, then, deserves great sorrow. He was a sincere, quiet, humble, and innocent man,
and, like Jacob, he had long lived in the tent of his monastery in the village district.

When John of Sirimis learned about him, he immediately sent to Asia. He had him brought in, bound and fettered with iron chains, and imprisoned him under harsh conditions in his own episcopal residence.
Through those bonds and many torments, he forced him to submit to him and receive communion from him.
Out of shame before the man’s gray hair and dignity, however, he did not reveal the deceit in his heart or what he had plotted against him.
But after he had brought him into submission and appeared to be favorably disposed toward him, he sent him to the bishop of Aphrodisias. And he wrote, and wrote [?] of Aphrodisias.
to him: “Depose this man from his episcopate and ordain him anew. Appoint him in the city of Antioch, which is under your authority.”
As soon as that bishop received Paul and the letters, he seized him, while Paul remained unaware of their deceit.
He said to him, “The patriarch has ordered me to depose you from your episcopate and ordain you anew.”
When he heard this, he began to wail and said, “You people! You are pagans!
I was ordained many years ago and have been a bishop ever since. I was ordained by three bishops, in accordance with the canonical order.
Why, then, am I now being deposed contrary to the canons and wickedly ordained anew?
If you are annulling my priesthood and ordaining me anew, then first annul my baptism too, and baptize me anew!”
They were not persuaded, but instead became filled with anger against him. They seized him tyrannically and forcibly, deposed him, and ordained him anew.
He beat his face, and his eyes grew dim, and he became blind.
Afterward he wept, lamented, and wailed over himself, and tried to find a way to flee to the refuge of repentance. In this condition, the appointed time of death overtook him,
and his old age went down to Sheol in torment, grief, and sorrow. His judgment, however, is reserved for the righteous Judge.
John’s advisers took a document and wrote it as though it came from Paul himself, putting these words into it: “I, Paul, who was astray and lost,
when I came to understand the true faith, turned back and came willingly and of my own free choice,
without compulsion or force, to the church of God, to you yourself, my lord John, ecumenical [?] patriarch.
I acknowledge in this document that I assent to the council of the six hundred and thirty holy fathers who assembled in the city of Chalcedon,
and to the letter of the holy and blessed pope of Rome, in accordance with the confession of Peter, chief of the apostles, until my last breath.
May I never again dispute it, turn away from it, or change my position. I have acknowledged these things and signed them with my own hand.”
I, Paul the bishop, acknowledge that I agree with and accept everything written in this document.
They therefore brought this to him for his signature, but did not allow him to read and learn what they had written in his name and as though it came from him, falsely and deceitfully.
And they bore false witness against him, without fear of God.
This Deuterius, diligent and upright in his conduct, who from his youth until his old age, throughout a period of thirty-five years,
labored with John, who was making disciples of the pagans in the regions of Asia, Caria, Phrygia, and Lydia,
and together with him established ninety-nine new churches and twelve monasteries—John relied on him and trusted him more than the others.

John also appointed him bishop of the orthodox in the region of Caria and made him his successor, since he himself had grown old and advanced in years and had become caught up in the struggle of persecution.
He appointed him over all the churches and monasteries, and he labored, visited them, and supported them all until the end of his life,
which came in the imperial city. This Deuterius, aided by divine grace, ran the race of his ministry with strength,
diligence, and courage. And when the Synodites were pursuing him to seize him and do to him as they had done to Paul,
and install him in that man's place in Antioch, the Lord did not deliver him into their hands. Thus he completed his struggle and departed in a good old age.
As for this group, these are the people who oppose the treatise that Theodosius of Alexandria composed
while he was in the imperial city, against the two heresies, namely those of the Tritheists and the Sabellians.
They take offense at certain statements in it and suppose that he too introduces a plurality of substances and natures.
For this reason they separate themselves and assemble on their own, although they have no leader and no one to ordain priests for them.
These people often sought to unite with the faithful, and discussions were held with them. Some of them did unite,
those who had the understanding to judge what was right. Others, however, without understanding, foolishly and without any valid reason, stubbornly persisted in this state.
Now these Cappadocian monks, at the height of the persecution, as I also mentioned them in the earlier account,
were repeatedly persecuted and left the large and strong monastery in Cappadocia called Gordison.
They numbered no fewer than seventy men, venerable and zealous elders. After building and establishing many places,
and being driven again from place to place, they went and found a good, secure place, suitable in every way for their monastery,
called Cardonian, near the hot springs called Pythia, on the southern side of the imperial city.
A certain chamberlain, one of the faithful, bought it for them, and they settled there. They planted a vineyard there and built a large church.
That entire company of venerable elders died, and the younger generation remained.
Finally, when Emperor Justin and the empress and the entire senate were passing by on their way to the hot springs, they entered and stayed at the monastery.
And through promises and gifts they brought them into submission, while he ordered that their former monastery, from which they had been driven out, should also be restored

to them, and that they should be granted exemption from taxes. In this way they brought them into submission and stamped them with their seal, after twenty years in which they had struggled through the trials of persecution.
They divided: half of them returned and took possession of their former monastery, while half remained in that same place.
They were thrown into confusion and dismay, so to speak, so that their ship was wrecked at the entrance to the harbor. And they turned away completely from all orthodoxy.

As for these monasteries, then, both the large ones and the small ones for women, some of them were subjected to pressure and submitted, while others held out—or, even if they eventually turned back, remained in this condition:
those who had submitted and those who had not submitted joined together in their entire service, except for receiving communion together.
Even at the Eucharist that the clergy celebrated in each of them,
during the waving they stood together and took part in the service, performing the whole order of worship, and they could not separate.
But those who did not receive communion also had other, orthodox priests who celebrated the Eucharist and gave it to them.
Because of the distress of the times, they could not act otherwise, lest they immediately be expelled and scattered.
And the leaders of the orthodox were compelled to remain silent and overlook these things, so that orthodoxy would not disappear altogether.
Now it may perhaps be easy for some people to mock this, and it may be taken as a joke,
that in these narratives we make use of an account concerning unsightly animals, namely elephants.
We bring this to remembrance not casually or, so to speak, contemptuously, but first of all for the glory of God,
and secondly as a rebuke and a disgrace to pagans, Jews, and the rest of those who are astray,
who deny the cross and reject the work of our salvation, which was accomplished through the sign of the cross.
For these elephants, through the victory that God gave the Christians over the accursed people of the Magi,
were taken from them and brought up to the imperial city. They remained there for a long time.
Whenever they passed in front of churches, the first one, which went at the head, would turn toward the east, lower its head and trunk, and bow down.
Immediately it would raise its trunk, move it around, and make the shape of a cross. It would make the sign and then pass on.
The one behind it followed and acted in the same way, and so did the rest, one after another, however many there were.
We saw this many times with our own eyes, marveling and giving thanks to God, who had given knowledge of Christianity
even to dumb animals, as a rebuke to rational beings who neglect Christianity and reject the grace of the Savior of our race.
Another thing of the same kind, also worthy of wonder and great amazement, was continually done by these animals.
Whenever there was a hippikos—that is, the customary horse race—
Those elephants used to enter regularly [?], with a man riding on each one to guide it.
They would stand in the middle of the Hippodrome, facing the emperor. As far as they could, and as their nature allowed them to bend down,
they would bow down and pay homage to him. Each one would make the sign of the cross with its lip and trace it facing the emperor.
The crowds gathered there were astonished and amazed at how they made the sign of the cross as perfectly as human beings.
Then, after receiving gifts from the emperor, they would leave.
Now, at the end of Tiberius’s reign and the beginning of Maurice’s, a disaster—that is, a great fire—occurred throughout the center of the imperial city.
There was complete destruction: many properties, large, medium, and small alike, were laid waste.
Even those who escaped were stripped and deprived of all their possessions and all their wealth, which, as they watched, became food for the flames in a single day.
Now, since it happens that some people [?], deficient in knowledge, who come across these histories and read them,
may pour blame on the writer because the account of a single event sometimes appears in several chapters, mixed together and scattered about,
let those who find fault with these things know this: most of these accounts were written during a time of persecution and distress, amid every kind of opposition.
Under the pressure of necessity, the sheets on which these chapters were being written were carried away to various places, along with the remaining papers and other books.
Sometimes they remained hidden in different places for as long as two or three years.
It happened that matters arose which the writer wished to put on record, and some of them had already been recorded in earlier chapters.
But the earlier notebooks were not at hand for him to read and determine whether these matters had been written down.
Nor did he remember that they had already been written down, so he subsequently recorded them again. For this reason,
sometimes an account of the very same subject is found repeated in several chapters.
Time did not even allow a later comparison of them to be made readily and easily.
Now, the arrogance of Patriarch Eutychius’s heart led him astray in many ways, since from the beginning he had belonged to the heresy of the Sabbatians.
When he became bishop, he wanted to conceal his heresy and please those who had appointed him,
who held the Chalcedonian position. At first he stood up and vigorously championed the doctrine of two natures, beginning to persecute harshly.
When he was removed from his see and went into exile, he undertook to compose a large book of divisive teaching about two natures.
When he was recalled and returned to his see after John’s death, as we also explained in the preceding account,
he began sending this book to the great senatorial households, to men and women, especially those who recoiled from the confession of two natures.
He wrote to them: “Read and learn that the Church confesses two natures in Christ after the union.”
While they were laughing at his foolishness, they sent him his book. Then again, after a short delay, he heard about the heresy of Athanasius:
He was the one who, in the heresy of those who count substances—that is, beings and natures—in the Holy Trinity,
had been made its head and founder, and who also went astray by following the error of John the Grammarian of Alexandria.
He said that these human bodies do not rise at the resurrection of the dead, but that other bodies come into being and rise instead.
As a result of this madness of paganism and Manichaeism, a division arose among them, and they anathematized one another in writing.
When Patriarch Eutychius learned of these things, he immediately joined them, became entangled with them, and became one of them. He began composing teaching on this subject.
He wrote and published books, until even his own bishops and clergy were stirred up and rose against him, and much was said between them.
Thus he was refuted and fell silent, and he suppressed his book, although he did not abandon that belief.
As he also tells us in another chapter, that excellent Eutychius was zealously and fiercely opposed to the words, “You were crucified for us.”
He wrote everywhere and issued threats, pressing the bishops to remove this confession from their churches and cities.
From the other bishops whom he newly appointed, he demanded pledges that they would abolish this confession in their territories.
As they took care to do as they had been commanded, scandal and blasphemy arose in the cities and rural districts—that is, in the villages and throughout the regions—
especially those of Syria, Asia, and Cappadocia, which had held to this confession from the beginning. Consequently, in many villages
and cities they disputed and rose up, saying, “Even if we are cut to pieces and burned, we will not deny God, who was crucified and suffered for us.”
This dispute and struggle persisted everywhere, even after the death of Eutychius.
The second book of the Ecclesiastical History ends here. It contains fifty-two chapters.

Book Three of the Third Part of the Ecclesiastical History, concerning the histories of the church, and so forth.
Since, therefore, we have already given a sufficient account in the preceding narrative of the events at the beginning of the reign of the victorious Justin II,
and of how he initially showed himself eager to bring about unity, and until the sixth year of his reign was gentle and at peace with the entire body of believers,
and also of how he eventually turned to harsh and lawless persecution—we have briefly sketched a little of these many matters in the two other books preceding this one.
And concerning the chastisement sent upon him from heaven to help him and to check the impetuous course of his wicked deeds,
we made brief, veiled references, withholding precise details so that it would not be thought
that we had dared to write openly in order to disgrace or dishonor the high dignity of kingship,
and to mention God’s merciful stroke, which had justly been sent upon him. For this reason we restrained ourselves at that time.
But now, in order to instill fear in those who afterward assume the great powers of rulership,
and so that the judgment of God’s power that overtook King Justin may be depicted and imprinted on the hearts of all people to inspire fear,
It seemed good to us to give a brief account of these things as a written record.
Now the merciful God, who does not desire the destruction of his creation and cares for the lives of human beings,
when he saw that Emperor Justin, in the exercise of his royal authority, had plunged and ventured into excesses and things foreign to the fear of God,
so that the measure of his sins would not become full, engulf him, and utterly destroy him—when he saw that he was wickedly engaged in shedding people's innocent blood,
and had plunged into plundering and seizing property without restraint or any check arising from the fear of God, gathering and heaping up unjust spoils,
more than many who had been before him; and besides these things, he sinfully committed every kind of evil and provoked God,
even turning to the persecution of Christians, cruelly, ruthlessly, and without natural compassion,
overthrowing the altars of the orthodox with bitter malice through Bishop John, and devastating the churches of the faithful everywhere,
and arresting, oppressing, and crushing priests and chief priests, imprisoning them in prisons, government headquarters, monasteries, and various harsh hospices,
men who were old, advanced in years, and weak, so that many of them perished under these afflictions and departed from this present life,
and suffered torment and died from afflictions, tortures, fetters, and bitter, harsh confinement in cramped prisons.
For there were also many other unspeakable evils that he wickedly committed,
which we have no wish at all to bring to remembrance, or even to bear witness about.
God's justice does not forget the perpetration of these things and others like them. Yet it also had pity on him, so that he would not perish utterly,
but would be disciplined and restrained from the violent rush of his wickedness. So God sent upon him, as it is written, wrath, anger, and affliction,
and sent them through an evil angel, who suddenly entered and possessed him, taking control of him cruelly and terribly, and revealing in him the filth of his wickedness.
Suddenly he lost his reason, and his soul became confused and darkened.
His body was handed over to hidden and visible tortures and severe torments, so that he made the sounds of animals.
He would bark like a dog, sometimes bleat like a goat, sometimes meow like a cat, and at other times crow like a rooster,
and do many such things beyond human reason, which came from the ruler of darkness to whom he had been handed over,
who had darkened his understanding and taken him captive, and was working in him everything that was happening. He would also drive him into agitation and panic,
so that he would flee from place to place in a savage frenzy, managing to get under his bed and climb the walls.
At other times, whenever bewilderment seized him, he would rush out in a panicked, savage frenzy and run to the windows to throw himself down.
Since they feared him as emperor, they would run and seize him so that he would not throw himself down and die.
The empress was therefore compelled to order carpenters to come up, install bars, and board up all the windows of the palace throughout the wing where he lived.
Young, strong chamberlains were chosen to guard him, so that, when they were compelled to run after him and seize him, as is reported,
because he was a strong man, he would turn around, seize them one by one, and bite them with his teeth, injuring them.
He bit two of them on their necks, severely wounding them; [?] they were in a bad state.
It reached the point that a report spread through the city that the king had eaten two chamberlains.
Eventually, as was reported, they were compelled—indeed compelled—to bind him even with ropes.
He would shout and howl and speak words of madness. They would shout at him, “Look! Al-Harith son of Jabalah is coming for you! Be quiet!”
Immediately he would flee, go inside, and crouch down. If they mentioned anyone at all to frighten him, he would likewise flee, become quiet, and hide under the bed.
Many other things, even more disgraceful and unlawful than these, were also being recounted fearlessly by everyone throughout the city.
We have now recorded some of these from what we heard from many people, since these things were constantly being recounted.
He remained tormented and afflicted not for just a few days, but for as long as five years.
We have made use of only a few accounts of these things, although we were neither close at hand nor eyewitnesses to them.
But the whole senate and the whole city, insiders and outsiders alike, bear witness to their truth:
they really and certainly happened, along with many other things that are not fit to be put in writing.
Eventually, wishing to entertain the king and bring his mind back to him and restore him, they made a small cart for him to sit in, with a chair on top of it.
They would seat him in it, and the chamberlains would pull him, making him race back and forth for a long time.
He would become bewildered and dazed by the force of the movement and would stop many of his mad antics.
They also distracted him with the sound of an organ. An organ would play night and day near [?] the place where he was,
apart from a short interval [?], whether at night or during the day. Sometimes, as he listened to the sound and melodies of the organ, he would become quiet.
But it would happen that he suddenly became bewildered, shouted, and behaved in disorderly ways.
For the patriarch came in to visit him. When he approached him and bowed to him, he saw that he was confused and made the sign of the cross over him.
But he raised his hand and struck the patriarch on the neck, sending him falling a considerable distance away from him.
He said to him, “May you come to a bad end if you do not go and make the sign of the cross over yourself, so that your own demons may come out!” The patriarch then pulled himself together,
while others took hold of him and helped him stand. For a considerable time he remained dazed from the blow he had received on the neck.
Later, since it was customary and the patriarch could not avoid entering the palace, he again went in to see him, taking care and guarding himself against him.
When he saw him, he began laughing at him. He approached him, reached out his hands, and took his cloak off his shoulder.
That is, the scarf of his episcopal office. He spread it out and placed it over his head like a woman's veil.
He said to him, “How fine you would look now, my lord Patriarch, if you put tassels on it, like the threads women wear on their heads!”
Again, he would look down toward the seashore and shout like those who go around selling earthenware [?]. He would shout like them and say:
“Who is selling earthenware [?]?” There were also many other things he did that cannot be recounted or spoken of, through the working of the devil,
to whom he had been handed over. Thus, in all our cities and all the villages, and in the houses, streets, and all the shops of the city, outside and inside,
and even along the roads, everyone spoke of these things with great amazement and astonishment.

While the emperor was undergoing discipline through all this humiliation and bitter trial, many people were forming opinions and speaking about him, foremost among them his own wife, the empress Sophia.
Not only did she fail to learn discipline and feel fear [?] through his affliction, trial, and chastisement, but she became even more conceited, saying:
“The imperial power was mine and came to me. This man was chastised on my account and fell into this trial
because he despised me and treated me with contempt.” Not everyone understood the matter this way; rather, everyone regarded her words as wicked.
We will also record these matters later, at their proper time. But what everyone believed to be the true explanation
was that God had sent wrath upon him from heaven [?] for no other reason than these three things:
the innocent blood he had shed; the persecution of Christians, and the tortures, afflictions, chains, and harsh imprisonments
and exiles that he had inflicted on priests, bishops, and the rest of the faithful, both men and women;
and also the seizure and plundering of people's property, since he would not allow orphans to inherit from their fathers.

The cry of the orphans and widows rose before the Lord, along with these other things. He became angry with him and handed his empire over to another while he was still alive and could see it with his own eyes.
After the emperor Justin had endured this trial and his other illnesses and afflictions for five years,
and had entered the sixth, still being chastised and afflicted by demonic activity, all business had by then come to a standstill,
all the affairs of the entire state were obstructed, and attacks by barbarians were frequent on every side.
Then the whole senate consulted with the empress about advising the emperor to appoint a Caesar to succeed him and attend to the affairs of the state.
He himself yielded to their words, for he had intervals when his reason returned to him, though only to a limited extent,
and at such times he would speak sensibly. After consulting with him at length, they chose Tiberius and appointed him Caesar.
He had long been the emperor Justin's bodyguard, even before Justin became emperor.
When he summoned Tiberius and had him stand before him to clothe him in the insignia and garments of imperial office, as he himself declared,
an angel appeared to him, standing beside him and telling him in his ear what he should say to Tiberius Caesar.
And that king began to speak astonishing and astounding words, as though his mind had never been impaired. With weeping and choking tears, he said:
“My son Tiberius, come and receive the kingdom of the wretched Justin, who angered God. God rejected him and cast him out of his kingdom while he was still alive.
Come, my son, enter and remove the man who wronged his Creator, who had made him worthy of kingship. Before his own eyes he is being rejected and falling from his kingdom.”
He cried these things aloud before many thousands, so that bitter weeping and violent sobbing seized everyone who heard him.
This happened especially when he turned around, waved his hand toward all the troops standing there, and said to them in a loud voice:
“Let the guards open all the gates of the royal palace [?], and let everyone enter to see the wretched Justin,
as he is stripped of his authority and falls from his kingdom, because he angered and embittered that true King whose kingdom never passes away, who made him king although he was unworthy.
And now, Tiberius, let me be a warning to you. Tremble and fear before the Lord, the eternal King. Be on your guard before him, and do not anger him by your evil deeds,
as I angered him by all my deeds and conduct, so that all this harsh and terrible punishment was sent upon me.
And now, look: while I am still alive, I am being stripped of my authority and rejected from the kingdom, because I governed it unjustly.
Take care that this royal clothing and appearance do not deceive you, as they deceived me, lifting you up, leading you astray, and making you arrogant,
and bringing wrath upon you from heaven, as happened to me, so that you too are stripped of your authority and fall from your kingdom, as I have today.
Look, my son, at this one who stands beside me and speaks into my ears. He teaches me all these things that I say to you, teaching you, commanding you, and warning you.
Know, understand, and realize within yourself that these things I am now saying to you are not my own, but come from this angel of God.
Even if neither you nor anyone else sees him, look: he stands beside me and teaches me these things that I am saying to you,
so that you may tremble and fear the terrible sentence of justice that was decreed and sent upon me, as you and everyone else can now see.
And because I did not keep his commandments, look: he is stripping me of my authority and casting me out of the kingdom, and now he is handing it over to you.
Look at me now, my son, and take from me an example to fill your heart with dread and trembling at this sentence pronounced against me. Do not let yourself be drawn into doing evil deeds,
evil deeds such as I used to do, lest wrath be sent upon you too from heaven, as it has now been sent upon me, and he reject you too from your kingdom.
But take care not to be persuaded—persuaded by evil people who advise you to do evil and lead you astray, just as they led me astray, and I angered God by all my deeds.”
These things, then, and very many more than these—of which we have used only these few because they were so numerous—
were spoken by the king himself with anguish and weeping, in a loud voice before everyone.
The illustrious Tiberius himself had completely removed his covering and thrown himself face down on the ground
at the king’s feet, and he too was bellowing like a bull with choking, bitter weeping.
Together with the entire senate and the rest of the crowds gathered around, they cried out in great anguish as they heard all these things.
And they saw him handing over his kingdom, and the man called to receive it, both overcome by cries of grief.
And as they lifted Tiberius up and set him on his feet, he would fall on his face again, crying out.
Then all the crowds together cried aloud with one voice, with a mighty cry from their hearts,
and no one could restrain or check his tears over what he heard from the emperor, who spoke as he wept over his fallen state.
Then at last he gave the order, and they stood him up. And he continued speaking with him amid many sobs.
Then he clothed him with the insignia, robes, and dress of royalty, saying to him, “From now on your name shall be called Constantine,
since in you the reign of Constantine the Great has been renewed,” and the rest of the other words
of boundless sobbing and grief that were spoken there, as many thousands wrote them down.
Tiberius became Caesar on the seventh day of the month of December, in the year eight hundred and eighty-six, on Friday morning.
Thus it became known and certain to everyone that all these words were truly spoken with him by an angel of God, and did not originate with the emperor himself.
Thus, afterward, when portraits of the two of them were put up, an angel was depicted between them,
standing with his mouth close to the ear of Emperor Justin. And so everyone accepted this as trustworthy.
Everything he said was immediately taken down in shorthand by many people and committed to writing.
For many notaries and scribes stood there, making accurate records and [?]. Because of their great number, we have left these out and passed them over.
After Emperor Justin appointed Tiberius Caesar, he lived with him for four years, while both he and everyone else still hoped for his recovery.
This was especially because, from time to time, they would support him and he would go up to the hippodrome, in the morning only, so that all the people of the city could see him.
Sometimes, too, he would sit and receive the homage of the senate. At other times he would distribute gifts of money,
while they placed gold in his hand and he dropped it into the hands of the recipients. Then he would return again to his affliction,
as other pains and afflictions were added to the painful urinary disorder that tormented him along with everything else. And he continued to decline.
By then all affairs were being administered by the God-loving Caesar, especially the wars against the barbarians and the Persians.
He would consult him, and whenever he was well and spoke a word while in his right mind, he would act on it.
But when the period mentioned above had passed, and the recovery that he and many others had expected did not come,
but instead still more pains and bitter torments were added to him, he often cried out and implored them,
“Bring a sword and kill me with it! For death is far better for me than this life of torment and misery.”
At other times he would cry out for all the palace gates to be opened, so that everyone might come in and see an emperor begging for death.
And he longed for it more than for life, but could not obtain it. Afterward, he suffered still more from painful cramps and from stones that obstructed his bowels.
When he was in distress and the physicians came to operate on him, they were afraid, as physicians usually are, and persuaded him to take the knife himself and hand it to them.
But he put them under oath not to spare him, so that he might depart this life, saying, “Do not be afraid.
You will be in no danger if I die.” Then he underwent a severe operation in both his groins, until all his [?] had wasted away.
And, as they say, even his penis wasted away and was cut off. While he was suffering and wailing, he said in a loud voice, “Your judgments are just, O God!
For look: already here, for all my sins and the evil things I did with my body, I have openly received punishment in wrath in the very limbs with which I committed sin.”
When he had finally given up hope of living and was certain that he was dying, he summoned Caesar. He gave him many instructions and warnings, saying,
“My son, I am dying. But come now, receive the crown of the kingdom and look after yourself. Do not engage in evil deeds and anger God.
Take care of the Roman Empire.” And so Tiberius received the crown on the twenty-sixth day of the month of September, a Monday,
in the year eight hundred and ninety. After Justin placed the crown on him, he lived with him for nine days.
He departed this world on the fourth day of October of that same year.
After the death of Emperor Justin, his wife, Empress Sophia, remained [?] in the palace with Emperor Tiberius.
He promised her great honors, although she did not understand her own honor, as it is written.
For before they made him Caesar, they required a formal undertaking and many oaths from him,
that if the emperor died, Caesar would keep Sophia in honor and do her no harm.
He observed this very carefully, as is evident, and when Emperor Justin died, he kept her with him in the palace in honor.
He said to her, “You are my mother. Stay here and give orders, and command me to do whatever you wish.”
After he became emperor, he began pleading with her about his wife, asking that she might come and join him—her [?].
But she was not pleased and would not relent. Even while Justin was alive, he had said to her, “Allow Caesar’s wife to come in to him.
He is a young man and cannot bear his body’s demands.” But she turned on him and insulted him,
saying to him, “You fool! Do you want me to act as foolishly as you, who clothed your servant in your imperial robes?” She declared with oaths,
“I will not give my imperial position and my robes to another woman while I am alive. No other woman will enter here during my lifetime.”
And so Caesar’s own wife remained outside: during those four years before Justin’s death in which he held the position of Caesar, she would not allow his wife to enter the palace.
Eventually he was compelled to bring his wife and her two daughters and settle them in the House of Hormizd, below the palace.
Every day he would go down and spend the night with them, and early in the morning he would go up to the palace.
O women, how wicked you are! And, as the story was told, he had been approached through another intermediary [?] and through the patriarch,
with the proposal that Caesar should leave his wife and marry one of them—either Sophia or her daughter, who was also a widow.
When he heard this, he was deeply distressed. According to what was being said, he replied in great distress to those who had been sent to him, saying:
“Would it be right before God and before you for me to abandon the wife by whom I have three children, who entered into a marriage partnership with me, marrying me when I had nothing?
And now that God has raised me up, should I abandon her and marry another?” Thus he would not be persuaded to agree to commit this injustice.
Now Caesar’s wife, whose name was Ino, had previously been married to another man, whose name was John.
He was a Roman, a junior officer of the Romans. She was from the fortress of Daphnudion.
They had a daughter, whom they betrothed to Tiberius when he was still only a private citizen and an ordinary Roman.
It happened that the girl’s father died [?], and she too died before Tiberius married her.
Take note: when she herself had died and her mother was left a widow, perhaps through some providence of God as well,
he married the girl’s mother, and he had three children by her.
When he sent for her and brought her to the Palace of Hormisdas, she lived in anxiety and fear, uncertain whether her life was safe while she stayed at Hormisdas.
No one dared to go to her and see her. For all the senators’ wives had gathered together,
because they were afraid to go and pay their respects to her, lest the empress become angry with them. Then they went in to consult Empress Sophia,
asking whether she thought fit to command them to go and pay their respects to Caesar’s wife, lest they be blamed afterward.
When she heard them, she looked at them angrily and answered them harshly,
saying, “Go away! Be quiet, be quiet! This is none of your concern.” After that, no one dared to go and see her.
As a result, she fled, left the city, and went back to Daphnudion.
Consequently, when she also fell ill, Caesar himself was obliged to go out to see her and then return.
But when Justin died, after Tiberius had received the imperial crown, as we explained above,
he persuaded Empress Sophia to let him send for his wife and bring her in, so that she too might reign as empress.
When Sophia heard this, she was displeased and would not accept it. Nevertheless, she could not prevent it.
The praetorian prefect was sent to fetch her, together with the other senators, many [?], and a large military force.
They went out in a grand procession to bring in the emperor’s wife, so that she too might reign as empress.
When they reached Daphnudion and she learned of it, she sent word to them: “Come—come in the morning, and we will enter together.”
When they received this answer, lodgings were prepared for them, and they went in and stayed there.
But she immediately sent one of her trusted servants, saying, “Go and prepare a ship for us.
For I want to send an answer ahead through you during the night, without anyone knowing.”
When the ship was ready, at midnight she took two of her maidservants [?] and one trusted servant,
and went down and boarded the ship with them, taking no one else. She left the others to tell the prefect and the rest, “Do not linger here.
The woman you are looking for will be in the city before daylight.” When they learned this, they were deeply upset.
They returned to the city, concealing the fact that they had come back empty-handed. She, meanwhile, was taken immediately to the palace.
The bishop entered with the entire senate and the emperor, and they clothed her too in the robes and all the regalia of imperial rule.
She went out in the imperial carriage to go to church, accompanied by the senate and the chamberlains, while the factions were making their preparations.
When they began acclaiming her, the Blues called her Anastasia, but the Greens called her Helena.
While the former were shouting “Anastasia,” the others were shouting “Helena.” There was such a great and terrifying uproar that she and everyone with her were alarmed.
She entered the church and worshiped, then returned to the palace and assumed imperial power.
As for the many things that happened among them afterward, it is not our task to recount them.
Indeed, we would not have needed to include even these things, except that we interweave [?] imperial histories with ecclesiastical ones,
and because there was a change of ruler, and so that it might be made known to everyone, to the glory of God.
Now Empress Sophia, after the death of Emperor Justin, was preparing, with no small amount of scheming,
to act against Emperor Tiberius, who was also called Constantine, with bitter resentment and wicked plots.
She was embittered at seeing him and his wife enter, take possession, and exercise imperial power,
while she herself had now lost, during her lifetime, the imperial authority that she had exercised neither justly nor in the fear of God.
She had neither learned discipline nor been moved by her husband’s ordeal and punishment. It was as though she had not realized that she too ought to fear God,
accept discipline, and become like one of the righteous. Instead, as the apostolic saying [?] addressed to such people declares, “Because of your hard and unrepentant heart,
you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and the revelation of God’s righteous judgment, when he will repay everyone according to their deeds.”
This was fulfilled in her case as well: because of the hardness of her heart and the arrogance of her thoughts, she neither repented nor feared God,
and she too fell from her imperial position, which she had sworn with oaths that she would not give to another woman during her lifetime.
Yet before she had been laid to rest, her imperial authority was taken from her too and given to another woman, while she herself fell from it.
But when her husband was forced to die, as people were saying, she took many hundredweights out of the palace and brought them to her house.
As for these [?], since we do not know the truth, we do not wish to record their number.
For they were said to be very numerous, along with many possessions belonging to the empire. When the emperor learned about these things, he would not let her leave the palace, saying:
“Stay here as our mother, and be at ease, and let me be at ease too. We will do whatever you command.”
And so she remained in the palace, bitter, crushed, troubled, mourning, and lamenting over her life:
Her life, in which she had been brought low, despised, and abandoned by everyone, and had become like someone who did not exist, though she was alive.
Tiberius, then, at the beginning of his tenure as Caesar, began giving gifts lavishly to everyone.
Whenever he went out of the palace to pray or to go anywhere else, he would scatter gifts to the right and left, as at a consul’s inauguration.
Even when he was at sea aboard a warship, boats would come rushing from every direction.
He would scatter gifts to all of them, as at a consul’s inauguration, until he received rebukes and reprimands from the emperors for distributing so much.
Eventually they sent and took the keys of the treasury away from him and set aside gold for his administration. In this way they restrained him from giving such lavish and numerous gifts.
But after he became emperor and gained authority, and, as people say, saw the accumulated imperial treasures, he again began bringing them out and distributing them extravagantly and generously.
Thus, when he began giving his accession gift, which the Romans call the donative,
consisting of nine darics [?], which an emperor gives generously to all the troops when he first becomes emperor,
he sent eight hundredweights to those stationed in the East against the Persians for their donative.
And again, wishing to pour out his gifts still more lavishly and abundantly, he did something that no emperor had ever done: he ordered the entire body of lawyers to come before him.
Although they were very numerous, he gave each of them fifteen or twenty, or ten or twelve, or more.
He also ordered all the physicians to come in, and they all received generously. Then came the silver dealers and bankers.
To some, whenever it occurred to him, he would give a pound apiece, or fifty or sixty darics.
Then came the imperial agents, the [?], the [?], and those in other services, while he said:
“Why is all this gold hoarded here, while the whole world is choking with hunger?” And so he would bring it out and distribute it without restraint.
In the end, however, after he had become emperor in full authority, he closed his hand completely, giving no one relief and accepting no [?].
Now, while this God-loving Caesar was being pressed every day by John the patriarch about the dissenters—that is, the orthodox—one day
he put him under oath before God to tell him whether they were heretics or not. Although the patriarch was very partial, when he was put under oath he could not lie.
Instead, he answered him, saying, “In truth, they are not heretics, and their belief is sound.”
“But they flee from us and from the church and are unwilling to share communion with us.” Then he answered him, “If you yourself have testified about them
that they are believers and Christians, why, then, are you pressuring me to become like Diocletian—Diocletian—a persecutor of Christians?
Go, sit down, and be quiet. Our wars with the barbarians are enough for us. Do not bring wars upon us against our own people.”
Now when Emperor Tiberius, also called Constantine, received the imperial crown, he immediately ordered a procession to the church so that he could go and pray,
while Justin was still alive. When he entered the church, the entire city gathered to see him,
together with the countless foreigners who were there. After praising the emperor as usual, they turned to shouting, “May the bones of the Arians be dug up!
May the bones of all the heretics be dug up! Likewise those of the pagans! May the Christian faith grow!”
When he heard these things [?], together with those very first cries they had shouted to him about the Arians, he was deeply upset. But there in the church he gave no sign of it.
Instead, he prayed, laid down the offering he had brought according to the custom of new emperors, and returned to the palace.
He immediately ordered an investigation and the arrest of those identified as having shouted to him in the church about the Arians.
He had taken it into his head that they were shouting because of him and against him, and that they had shouted this at him because they thought he was secretly an Arian.
For many people secretly harbored just such a suspicion. A short time earlier,
a large crowd of Goths had assembled, together with the wives of those who had gone down to fight the Persians. These women too were numerous and were Arians.
They shouted to him to give them a church for their worship. Wishing not to upset them, he sent them this reply: “Go away; we will look into it and speak with the patriarch.”
Thus, before he put on the crown, a rumor spread throughout the city that the Caesar was an Arian. For this reason, those concerned for the churches gathered and shouted these things to him.
When they were arrested at his command and brought before him, he received them with great anger, saying, “What Arian trait have you seen in me,
that you insulted me and shouted at me about the Arians?” Only after they had gone to great lengths to appease him were they released, and even then with difficulty.
Then, because of this incident, he ordered an edict to be issued and posted in the city, requiring the arrest of the Arians and all the Montanists, [?], and Sabbatians.
That is, as follows. Many began to be arrested and imprisoned by people who had found opportunities to extort money openly and fearlessly from others.
Thus they paid out money lavishly to secure their safety.
As a result, many of the orthodox were also arrested along with them and imprisoned under harsh conditions for many days.
They too were required to give money in the same way, and only then were they released and allowed to leave, one by one.
In that very year when Emperor Tiberius became emperor in his own right, he made a great distribution of gifts as consul.
According to what he himself and everyone else said, he distributed seventy [?] seventy-two hundredweights,
besides silver, robes of pure silk, and other things. He enriched the rich and the idlers, but did nothing to benefit the poor.
But when Sophia became angry with him and reproached him, saying, “What we have gathered and stored up with so much effort and care,
you scatter to the winds as though with a winnowing fork!” he said to her:
“What you gathered through injustice, plunder, and robbery, I am determined to dispose of so that none of it remains in my palace.”
Before this, he had ordered that a quarter of the public taxes be remitted everywhere. And again, after he became emperor,
because Justin had imposed a charge of four darics on each loaf of the state bread allowance established by Emperor Constantine, and these payments were being collected,
Emperor Tiberius himself ordered that the entire amount be returned to everyone who had paid it. He also performed another act of mercy as soon as he became Caesar.
For a levy had been imposed on ships and all merchants, requiring them to give one sextarius from every jar.
This amounted to many hundreds upon hundreds of pounds, and everywhere they exacted it with oppression and great financial loss.
When they made him [?], he ordered that this too be removed and abolished. So this too was discontinued.
These were the things he did immediately at the beginning of his reign. But where his course would ultimately lead will become known at the end.
Another proof that he was a Christian was this: whereas Justin had placed on the dies for his darics
a certain image that many people likened to Aphrodite, he ordered that his own coinage should bear a cross instead.
For, as was reported, it had appeared to him in a revelation some time before.
At that time, persecution of the heresies had been ordered and set in motion. In that onslaught, as though by a powerful dragnet,
the congregations of the orthodox were also swept up. They first attacked John, who was called “the overseer of the pagans,”
the bishop of Ephesus, who had lived in the imperial capital for many years.
They seized him and everyone with him and took them away and confined them in the prison called the Cancella,
after the many imprisonments and other periods of exile that he had endured on numerous occasions.
They were imprisoned and afflicted during the days of the Nativity celebrations, confined in a room where water seeped from all four sides.
Even when the rain from the sky stopped, water continued dripping from above in every part of it for two days, because it was a hollowed-out vault.
Thus they lived there as though in a lake, constantly getting up and bailing out the water.
They lay there on the biers used for burying the dead, because they had nowhere to lay their heads.
Despite all this hardship, every day, morning and evening, bishops, metropolitans, church advocates, and church advocates were sent to dispute with them.
But grace was their companion and did not allow them to give way. Instead, openly and without fear,
they stood up for the truth of the orthodox faith and fought against them.
From then on, those dyophysite persecutors resorted to insults and threats against them when they were defeated.
Every day they assembled groups of patriarchal attendants, stewards, stewards, and other clergy, as well as laypeople, against them.
They spent eighteen days in prison, during the consular celebration for which the emperor distributed largesse.
And because John would not do what they wanted, even in words alone, they sentenced him to leave the city.
And so they released them from prison. They rejoiced and thanked God that they had been found worthy, again and again, to suffer for his name.
Even the seat that John had and used to sit on because he suffered from pain in his feet—the patriarch Eutychius sent men and seized it from him.
Many other things happened, of which we have recorded a few small examples as reminders.
After Bishop John and those with him were released from prison, a band assembled on the following day.
This was the troop of persecutors—or, perhaps more appropriately, a gang, a gang of robbers.
They assembled against the congregation of the orthodox, which used to gather on Sundays in the great imperial house of Marinus, Marinus.
When the whole congregation had assembled, they entered, fell upon them, and seized many of them.
They entered like pagans, laid hold of the altar, overturned it, and broke it. They spilled the consecrated elements that were on it and scattered and dispersed the Eucharistic offering.
They dragged away the clergy and the remaining laypeople, after tearing apart and overturning the whole church and taking down the images of the blessed Severus and Theodosius.
Carrying these behind their heads as a mockery, they went through the public streets.
They took them all away and confined them in the prison where the earlier prisoners had been held.
The others, the greater part of the people whom they had seized, they stripped and let go. They snatched and stole everything that fell into their hands and went away.
Some days later, Eutychius sent for them and had them brought up to the bishop’s residence, where he argued with them at length.
He released them on sureties. Eventually, when the merciful emperor learned of these things, he rebuked him, and he desisted somewhat for a time.
As for Eutychius, Eutychius the patriarch, when he was recalled after John’s death and returned, they praised him,
saying that he was righteous, worked miracles, and saw visions. He himself also wrote and spread these claims.
When he returned, although the inquiry into his deposition by John, who had expelled him, had not been properly conducted, he went up and sat on the throne of the church.
His excommunication had neither been examined nor lifted. Because of this, many broke away and withdrew from communion with him,
as from an excommunicated man whose deposition had been carried out by the man who had died, and who had in turn deposed that man. Yet in the end he returned and took his seat,
accepting that man’s ordinations and everything he had done without examination or inquiry, solely so that, by whatever means, he might occupy the throne.
Again, the second scandal that afterward befell the whole church in connection with him—the whole church in connection with it [?]:
A few days later, he heard about some people who had been caught up in error, apparently through the teaching of John the Grammarian of Alexandria.
As we also explained concerning this subject in the preceding book, he used to argue and say that these human bodies do not rise at the resurrection,
but that other bodies come into being and rise in their place. He himself turned aside and became engulfed in this error.
He assumed the character of those who deny the resurrection in this way, and began debating and arguing that this was indeed the case, and that this body does not rise,
but that another comes into being and rises in its place. Some of his bishops, along with clergy and others, disputed with him about these things,
but he fought all the more insistently to maintain that this was so, even composing a treatise setting out this opinion.
He had it copied into volumes and sent it to noblewomen, so that they would read it and become his disciples. He said and did other things like these, behaving like a fool,
so that many now regarded him as a deranged man who had lost his mind. Indeed, as finally became plainly evident in him, a demon used to come upon him
and throw him down and crush him. Twice, while he was standing at the altar in the Great Church, it convulsed him in full view of the whole congregation.
They picked him up and hurriedly carried him out. It happened once again in the church of the blessed Mother of God in Chalkoprateia.
And, as people reported, it also battered him many times in the bishop’s residence. Those who wanted to cover up for him
said that excessive fasting and keeping vigil stirred up a bodily humor in him, and that this rose and collected in his temples, making him dizzy and throwing him down,
and that he did not have a demon. But many others would reply to such people, “Can a bodily humor really cry out and crush him,
and foam and go into convulsions?” From then on, everything he did appeared to everyone to be the behavior of someone whose mind had been confused and darkened by an evil spirit.
For he also used inappropriate words and indulged in laughter that was out of keeping with his position, along with other things of this sort.
He also produced a book in which, from beginning to end, he amassed material in support of the confession of two natures after the union,
while censuring all the true fathers who would not join him in blaspheming by professing a quaternity instead of the Holy Trinity.
He sent this book around to households so that they would become his disciples. Everyone who read it laughed and jeered at him as at a man who had become deranged and lost his mind.
Throughout the city they were saying, “This man, whom people used to say performed mighty works and miracles, has lost his senses.”
Now this Eutychius Eutychus, when he came in and took possession of the episcopal throne of the imperial city, became firmly established and was praised at the outset,
as we have also related many things about him in the immediately preceding accounts. He was also received with honor by the merciful emperor Tiberius.
But arrogance, conceit, and boasting immediately took hold of him, so that he even overstepped the bounds of his position and spoke extravagantly and foolishly.
As a result, everyone began talking about him and laughing at him as a man deficient in understanding.
He produced a large book in support of two natures, as we have also related. Through it, the character of his foolishness became even more apparent to everyone.
He began sending this book around to prominent households and pressing women of senatorial rank and men, especially those opposed to two natures,
that they should read it and accept what was written in it, confidently confessing two natures after the union.
For, he said, anyone who does not confess this is a Eutychian heretic.
And so everyone, even his own supporters, mocked him and sent his document back to him.
Then the powerful Eutychius, becoming puffed up again, went on to display his zeal against the phrase, “You who were crucified for us.”
He threatened and disputed with anyone who, as he put it, dared to say, “You who were crucified for us.”
Now the well-known large communities of nuns had been driven out of Antioch at the beginning of the persecution,
and since then had been living in various places in the imperial capital, conducting their worship according to the customary Eastern tradition,
with the words, “You who were crucified for us, have mercy on us.” Because of this, he himself went to them with his clergy and began preaching and teaching them. He also threatened them.
And because, in the days of the victorious Justin, when he launched a persecution against them and everyone else, some of them had submitted while others had refused to be persuaded,
they all gathered together as one, clothed themselves in courageous zeal, and stood against him, saying, “It is enough that you forced us to change and lose our faith.
But we will never agree to deny God, who was crucified, suffered, and died for us, even if we face the sword, the cross, or the fire.”
Thus they all together clamored and raised an uproar against him with passion and force. When his clergy saw their boldness and the intensity of their zeal—
for they were saying these things to his face—they said to him, “Get up, my lord, let us go. It is time for the liturgy.”
So he got up and left the place, without achieving among them what he wanted [?].
Finally, he wrote a lengthy treatise, teaching, stirring up trouble, and threatening, and sent it to them. But they would not accept it, saying,
“We are women and know nothing of disputation. But we will not depart from the tradition of the Eastern fathers, even in the face of death.”
News of this confrontation spread throughout the city and the palace and reached the emperor. Everyone criticized him. As a result, he cooled down a little and kept quiet.
But in the fourth year after Eutychius took office, he set himself against the orthodox with bitter resentment, just as he had at the beginning, sending men to seize, abduct, and imprison them.
He overturned altars everywhere and took down whatever images were found. Everything that could be found was seized and stolen,
whether liturgical equipment, vestments, curtains, books, funds, or vessels—
in short, absolutely everything that could be found wherever they went, in open robbery.
In this way they seized men, priests and bishops, and confined them in prison under bitter hardship,
for as long as they wished. There they were subjected to further extortion. Those who had nothing borrowed money and paid.
Even when they were thus released and allowed to leave, they recovered absolutely nothing of what had originally been seized from them.
And if they still had nothing to give, they were sent into exile and again confined in monasteries under great hardship.
But the distinguished Eutychius used to go in to the merciful Tiberius and maliciously accuse the whole community of believers, without the restraints imposed by the fear of God.
And while all the heretical groups of the Arians, the Macedonians, and the Sabbatians, who were his own people,
and the Manichaeans, Marcionites, Marcianists, and followers of Montanus and Montius [?] were all living peacefully,
with no one troubling them, only the true believers were being persecuted and plundered,
and were being sent into various places of exile, to distant cities and to various islands in the sea,
while they were subjected to every kind of suffering from harsh bonds and confinement in cramped prisons, and to hunger, thirst, and every kind of trial.
Thus, if divine grace had not visited and strengthened them, no one among them would have survived, as it is written concerning the tribulation that is to come at the end.
Now, while the victorious emperor was caught up in the turmoil of wars that surrounded him on every side, this bishop Eutychius went in every day,
and kept agitating against the Diacrinomeni, while the emperor told him, “Do not trouble me with these matters. The ordeal of the wars in which I am involved is enough for me.
At your own risk, go and do as you wish in the affairs of the church. You know what you are doing. I am free of the sin.”
Because of this, without fear of either God or the emperor, the persecution spread and grew—a persecution for the sake of plunder, not for the cause of the faith.
Consequently, to gain people everywhere and in every region who would persecute as he did, he did not hesitate to write to every region, every place, and all the great cities,
so that there too they would follow his example and stir up a wicked persecution against all the Diacrinomeni everywhere.
These men too, driven by the desire to seize and plunder property and to commit open robbery,
used the faith as a pretext and, together with the rest of their party, stirred up persecution in every place and every region,
while the victorious emperor, because of the ordeals of the wars surrounding him, paid no attention and allowed no complaint or petition to be brought before him.
Let this therefore be known to everyone who later encounters these chapters of the history: it is in keeping with the exact truth
that we write in this way, and not with any thought of hostility toward the distinguished patriarch Eutychius.
Indeed, we have fallen short of the truth, even if we have related one part in a hundred. We have not put these things on record out of an eagerness to insult and ridicule.
Nor, again, do we say or write these things about the serene emperor out of flattery. Rather, in everything we strive to be advocates of the truth.
For when Emperor Tiberius was a young man, before the hairs of his beard had even appeared, he and I were constantly together,
and with the others we attended upon Justin, now at rest. Since that time I have been thoroughly familiar with his habits and conduct.
Even now, when he has been deemed worthy to stand at the height of imperial power, as everyone now knows beyond dispute,
he has remained just the same, continuing unwaveringly in the same generosity and humility, without becoming puffed up like a young lad who holds imperial power.
He commanded that no one should be killed or plundered, as his predecessor had done, who had spattered himself and his hands with innocent blood.
But for the present he conducts himself generously and humbly—up to this third year of his reign, apart from the four years during which he was Caesar.
For the present, up to this point, he continues in this way, although many grumble about him, saying that he is quiet and mild and inspires no fear. Yet for the present he conducts himself peaceably.
Now this Emperor Tiberius, who was also called Constantine, while Justin was still alive and they were living in the great palace, the Authentikon,
when he was Caesar, lived in cramped quarters in one wing of the palace.
Even when Justin died, Sophia his wife remained in that same palace, the Authentikon, and he could not get her to leave.
Nor would she allow him to move in and live there. Since he was cramped for space after becoming sole emperor,
especially after his wife came to him with her two daughters, and since he did not wish to use force against Empress Sophia or put pressure on her
so that he could move into the great imperial residence, he was compelled to demolish the whole northern wing of the palace and build himself a palace.
He therefore demolished and tore down many large buildings and undertook this construction on a massive scale, also destroying the beautiful garden in the middle of the palace,
which had served as a place of recreation for the emperors. He planted massive buildings in it, demolishing in every direction, extending the site, and building on a grand scale.
He also built a new, massive bathhouse and substantial stables for horses higher up within the palace itself, along with many other things.
Now, after Emperor Justin had become deeply involved in persecuting and disturbing the church, and also in plundering and pillaging,
and that terrible chastisement had been sent upon him, other signs of wrath from heaven were also seen in his case.
For he wished to turn his former house, which was in the area of the western and northern quarter of the city, at the Deuteron, into a palace.
He too demolished many houses, built and made a hippodrome, and carried out substantial construction. He planted gardens containing a mixture of every kind of plant, and so on.
Then he gave orders, and they erected statues of himself and his wife—that is, large bronze images.
A short time after they had been erected and put in place, a strong wind arose and knocked them down. They were found with the backs of their heads embedded in the ground.
Many considered this a sign of wrath and of their downfall. Afterward he again gave orders and began erecting a pharos for himself,
that is, a massive tower at the Zeuxippus, on the seashore on its eastern side, on the eastern side of the city.
He ordered it to be hollow, with stairs so that people could climb it, broad and strong, built with loads of massive dressed stones—
massive dressed stones fastened with iron and firmly set in lead. It was built and rose to a great height, approaching completion.
While it was being built, some of the city's inhabitants wrote a paper and fastened it to a panel on it, as follows:
“Build your tower, build it! Raise it as high as you can, and climb up and stand on top of it.
Consider, look, and see the east and the west, the north and the south: look, they have been devastated and utterly destroyed in your days.”
But he died without completing it. It was said that a dispute arose between Tiberius and Sophia, because she told him to finish it.
But he said, “I will not complete it. It is up to you to complete it.”
“For you to complete it.” She, thinking that he was certainly building it for himself and supervising it, said:
“If you do not want to do it for the one who built it, do it for yourself.” He became angry and swore, “I will supervise neither this nor anything else.”
But when he saw that the great loads of large stones it contained would be useful to him for the building he had begun in the palace, he gave orders, and it was demolished down to its foundations.
He carried all its stones to the palace and to the Church of the Forty Martyrs, which he had been building
for a long time. It was said that many hundredweight of gold had been spent on it.
Now, from the time when the merciful Tiberius took his seat as Caesar during the lifetime of Emperor Justin,
because Justin himself had fallen under the affliction of various illnesses, the Caesar prepared for wars on every side.
At first, in the struggle against the Persians, he was threatened on every side, together with all the other barbarian peoples who had risen against the mighty Roman Empire.
After Justin’s death, they pressed him still harder, especially the accursed peoples of the Slavs
and those hairy people called Avars. This happened especially after he became emperor,
as the news and reports pouring in upon him from everywhere gave him no respite, even for a short time.
Many people, both great and small, grieved for him, saying, “The empire has come to this man amid severe trials and evil days.”
Day and night he was plunged into struggle and anxiety, gathering troops from everywhere and sending them in every direction to the many wars.
For Emperor Tiberius was compelled to gather and bring barbarian peoples from the West, some of whom were followers of the teachings of the wicked Arius,
to send them against the Persians, while their wives and children remained in the imperial city. Then they asked Emperor Tiberius
to set aside and give them a church in the city itself, where their wives and children and those of them who remained in the city could gather.
The emperor sought a way to satisfy them, so that they too would exert themselves with all their strength on behalf of the Roman state
and fight against its enemies. He told them, “We will look into it and speak to the patriarch.”
Because of this promise and this noncommittal answer he had given them, without firmly settling the matter for them,
everyone came to believe and say that the emperor was an Arian, sharing the beliefs of those who had asked him for a church, but concealing his convictions.
Thus, when he went to church for the festival, many people shouted, “Let the bones of the Arians be dug up!”
“Let the bones of the—let the bones of the Arians be dug up!” When he heard these cries, he knew that they were shouting against him.
He was deeply disturbed. When he returned to the palace, he sent and arrested many of those who had shouted, saying to them,
“What have you seen in me that you shouted against me as an Arian and insulted me in church?” In their fear, they gave him an evasive answer.
