But because he wanted to free himself from this suspicion, he ordered that the Arians be persecuted.
So these investigators of the church, taking the command as a pretext, rushed about like wolves.
They attacked not only those against whom orders had been given, but also those against whom no orders had been given: namely, the Montanists, [?], Macedonians, Sabbatians, and the rest.
They even included the orthodox among them, attacking them all alike and openly plundering them.
This continued until the emperor heard about these things, rebuked them, and threatened them severely.
In the second year after Emperor Tiberius became emperor, the wicked pagans of Baalbek, that is, Heliopolis,
who have openly been servants of Satan from the beginning—against the Christians, who are few and poor there among them,
while they themselves all constantly revel extravagantly in wealth and high status, whenever they find an opportunity,
they scheme to destroy them and wipe out their memory from among them. They dared to mock Christ himself as well as his faithful,
and they also dared to inflict many other evils on the Christians. When these things became known to the emperor,
he gave orders to the man who had previously been sent east by Justin because of the rebellion and insurrection raised by the Jews and Samaritans in Palestine.
This man had gone down and subdued them, putting some to the sword, crucifying and destroying others, and subjecting them to harsh rule. His name was Theophilus.
The emperor therefore gave him orders, and he went from Palestine to Heliopolis against the pagans and arrested many of them.
He exacted punishment from some of them in proportion to their insolence, humiliating, crucifying, and killing them.
As he tortured them and demanded that they disclose the other pagans who shared their error, they disclosed to him many others like themselves,
naming them individually, in every region and city. They were present in most of the cities of the East, and especially in Antioch the Great.
As for the others, he wrote to the governors and sent orders for the individuals named to be arrested and sent to him.
They named a certain Rufinus [?], the chief priest in Antioch. Theophilus himself had also sent one of his men to arrest him.
He learned that Rufinus was not there, but had gone to Edessa to Anatolius, the governor and deputy prefect,
that is, the man acting in the prefect’s place. The man who had gone there asked the governor and the bishop to give him written authorization to take with him.
They gave him some of their own men, along with the church’s legal advocate, and sent him to Edessa, so that if he found Rufinus, he could arrest him there.
When those who had been sent reached Edessa, they learned that Rufinus was there. At night they went and surrounded the house to arrest him.
It happened that the pagans there were celebrating a festival of Zeus, and they had gathered with Rufinus to offer sacrifices.
When they realized that the house was surrounded and that they were about to be arrested, they panicked and all fled.
But when Rufinus realized that he had no way of escape, [?], he drew a knife and struck himself in the heart.
He also [?] his belly [?], and he fell down and died. But there was an old man afflicted with gout who could not escape,
and an old woman whom they found there when they entered, together with Rufinus, who lay stabbed and dying, and all the equipment for the sacrifices.
They seized those whom they found and threatened them with death unless they told the truth about who all the people gathered there were.
But if they told the truth, they would live and not die. In their terror, they identified them all,
including Anatolius, the governor and deputy prefect, who had been with them. He, however, thought he could devise tricks, which proved of no help to him.
He went and wrapped himself in a cloak, as though he had just come in from outside after a journey. He put on leather leggings and shoes—traveling shoes.
He went to [?], the bishop of the city. When the bishop heard that the governor had come, he became alarmed and said, “Why has the governor come now, at this unusual hour?”
When he entered, he said to him, “I have only just come in from a journey. I was spending the night in such-and-such a village,
and a dispute arose among us about the meaning of a certain passage of Scripture.
That is why I have come to you before going to my official residence, so that you can explain it to me.” He did this as a trick, so that the bishop would testify for him

that he had come to him straight from a journey. Thus, even if people said that he had been with those who performed the sacrifices during the night, he could counter this with the excuse he had contrived.
But as it is written, “The Lord is a God of knowledge, and schemes cannot stand before him,” so this man's schemes did not hold up. For immediately, as he was coming down from the bishop's residence,
those who had been sent met him, arrested him, and said to him, “Welcome, my lord prefect! We have great need of Your Excellency.
Please provide sureties for a hundred pounds [?], guaranteeing that you will appear in Antioch within ten days.”
He began arguing and said, “I have only just come in from a journey, and the bishop is my witness.” But they said to him, “Do not make excuses, my lord governor.
Last night you performed a sacrifice to Zeus with Rufinus and the others in your company, and here stand those who accuse you.”
When he began making threats, as though exercising his authority, and said, “You are obstructing government business,”
they said to him, “Do not threaten us, my lord governor. No, by the life of Your Excellency, you will not leave here until you have provided sureties.”
So, when he was pressed and realized that there was no escape, he agreed and provided sureties that he would go up to Antioch immediately, together with them and the officers of the court.
When they reached Antioch and the records of the proceedings at Edessa concerning those discovered there had been read out, he and his secretary were arrested and questioned.
They offered false excuses. Finally, however, when his secretary, whose name was Theodore, was subjected to torture and severe flogging, he made a deposition revealing everything.
As has been said, he also made a deposition against Gregory, the patriarch there, and Eulogius, who was likewise from there and later came to be in Alexandria,
stating that they had sacrificed a boy with them at night in Daphne. He said that, immediately when they sacrificed him, the whole city suddenly shook and trembled.
When these things were heard in the city, the whole city was shaken and thrown into turmoil. All kinds of outcries arose, and the church was closed.

Gregory did not dare come down from the bishop's residence. Nor was permission given for the liturgy to be celebrated in the church, or for the customary consecration of chrism on the Thursday of the Mysteries.
While conflicting voices were crying out, we inquire into all these matters through their written records or through testimony concerning them.
For, as everyone was saying, reports upon reports concerning these matters reached the emperor, and these things were being discussed everywhere.
In the end, it was thought that these things had been concealed out of regard for the Christian order, so that the priesthood would not be disgraced and reviled.
Now Anatolius had an image of our Lord set up in his house, wishing to deceive people, since he had persuaded them that he was a Christian.
He took many people with him and went to show it to them. While he was showing it to them, the image turned around, with its back facing outward
and its face inward toward the wall, so that terror fell upon everyone who saw it. When Anatolius himself saw this, he turned it around and set it upright.
Suddenly it turned around again, with its back facing outward. This happened three times.
When they examined it closely, an image of Apollo was discovered inside it, behind its back, skillfully made so that it was neither recognizable nor visible.
Then the governor’s officers threw him to the ground, kicked him, and dragged him by his hair to the praetorium, reporting all these things.
Consequently, as is reported, he himself also made a deposition concerning everything.
Theodore, his secretary, after exposing the bishops and the others, died while being held under guard in one prison after another.
Many thought, and it was said, that he had actually been murdered so that his deposition would be suppressed. But we do not testify to this either.
Many other things happened there that exceed both what can be recounted and the limits of this book.
When news of these events in Antioch reached the imperial capital along with the official reports, the whole city, and the merciful emperor himself,
were shaken, troubled, and distressed, together with the entire senate. These things were being discussed in every quarter of the city.
Then those pagans were summoned and arrived. The emperor ordered that men from among the magistrates and lawyers should sit in judgment over them
and investigate the truth of the affair. He charged them and put them under oath to judge without partiality or favoritism.
For many days they sat investigating the affair in the great imperial building called the Palace of Placidius.
Everything they did was conducted in secret, and not one of these things was disclosed.
They took care that no one should learn of them, and nothing was communicated outside. Everyone thought that bribery was at work and was concealing the truth.
Although many had been identified as adherents of paganism, the people of the city thought that the judges had released whomever they wished—those who had given gold—
and had unjustly condemned whomever they wished, and that the investigation into the pagans had grown lax and been neglected.
This impression grew especially strong because the emperor himself had left the matter alone and gone away to Proconnesus, and the affair had not been investigated and exposed before everyone’s eyes.
There was much grumbling in the city, because people thought that the affair had been covered up through gold and allowed to pass, and that it had now been dismissed,
that the case against the pagans had been dropped, and that they themselves had been released. Suddenly, however, some people ran and gathered in the city’s Mese and began shouting.
“May the judges’ bones be dug up! May the pagans’ bones be dug up! May the faith of the Christians grow!”
“May the judges’ bones be dug up!”—that is, the judges who had been trying them, because they thought that those judges had accepted bribes and mishandled the case.
As they shouted these cries and ran through the middle of the city, people ran from every quarter of the city and joined them.
They became a great crowd, fired with zeal for Christianity—more and more for Christianity [?]—numbering over a hundred thousand.
The entire city was thrown into turmoil, and the shops were closed, along with all the silversmiths’ shops.
Silversmiths’ shops. Even Jews, Samaritans, and the rest of the heretics ran from every direction and mingled with the crowd.
They were preparing to burn the city and steal what others had made. But the whole Christian population rushed furiously to the church against the bishop,
heaping many different, vile insults on him, insults unfit to be set down in an account.
For they believed that he was looking after the pagans’ interests, on account of the man from Antioch and the man from Alexandria, who had been spoken against as involved in paganism.
He had gone in and pleaded for the affair to be covered up and allowed to pass. For this reason they were even threatening to kill him.
When the bishop’s residence had been surrounded on every side, the crowd was ready to burn it down, had they not been restrained out of concern for the church.
The Jews and heretics were threatening to burn the church as well, as they later admitted before the prefect.
They knocked down one of the church’s legal advocates who came out to confront them and gave him a bitter time.
Then they all ran to Placidia, where the pagans were being tried, insulting the judges, who were patricians and officials,
and the rest of the clerks and lawyers, threatening to kill them too.
When they reached Placidius—Placidus [?]—they tore out doors and windows, smashed benches and chests, and entered the courtyard, raging over the pagans.
When they broke open one chest and found it full of hundred-pound weights of gold, they [?], when they saw them, drew back.
The man guarding them, wanting to calm their fury and thinking that they would immediately seize them, said to them,
“My lords, my lord, do not be agitated. If you want gold, here is gold.”
But the great crowd shouted as though with one mouth, saying, “We are not robbers; we are Christians.
We have gathered for Christ, and we want to exact vengeance on the pagans on behalf of Christianity. You look after your gold: we will not touch it.”
They smashed everything they encountered, even the statues—the statues—all that they found, whoever they represented: they pulled them down and smashed them.
Then they found two of the pagans imprisoned there, a man and a woman. They seized them and ran to the seashore.
They took possession of a boat and seized the executioner who served the city, saying to him, “Set a fire and burn them.”
Since he was afraid of the prefect, they themselves threw them into the boat and set it on fire. They threw the executioner in with them as well.
He managed to leap out of the fire and fell into the sea. Although he was badly burned, he did not die. The others, however, were burned and drowned in the sea.
The countless crowds that gathered after these events rushed off and broke open all the prisons.
They broke down the doors and brought out everyone who was imprisoned, shouting, “The pagans are being released! Why are the Christians imprisoned?”
Likewise, they also rushed to the praetor’s headquarters and broke down the doors, the [?], and all the chests containing the documents

concerning the Christians. They brought them out, tore them up, and threw them all away. They also brought out everyone who had been imprisoned. Then they rushed from there to the prefect’s headquarters.
When he heard, he came outside to meet them, while they were in an uproar and shouting, “May the bones of the pagans be dug up!”
Although he was widely said to be a pagan, he too began shouting with them, “May the bones of the pagans be dug up, and may the Christian faith grow!”
“Your zeal is good! Look, I too am shouting with you. For you know that it was not I who tried the pagans.
I was not even entrusted with the matter, nor were they tried at my headquarters. So do not be in an uproar.”
With these words he managed to restrain their fury, so that they would not, as they were preparing to do, lay [?] hands on him and burn down his headquarters.
After this they began shouting at him again, “Come out with us to Proconnesus immediately!” In his fear he said, “I will come out.”
He was thus hurried into boarding his ship without the usual ceremony, and without even wearing his official dress,
trying to escape the fury of that whole limitless crowd. So he hurried out to the emperor.
He informed him about these events, and that more than twenty thousand of them had decided to come out here.
While he was still speaking, they arrived, shouting all sorts of cries. Along with these, they were making accusations and saying,
“Why was the investigation of the pagans corrupted and covered up? Why did a bribe of gold—gold—circulate and conceal the truth?”
Along with this, while they were shouting about the pagans, they also began shouting abuse at the Arians, with a different purpose.
As a result, the whole palace was alarmed. Things were being said that are not fit to be put in writing.
Then the emperor sent them an order: “Do not be in an uproar. Go back into the city. We will come in immediately and do what you wish.
We will not neglect the matter.” Thus the crowd was pacified, and the force of their savage fury subsided.
They returned to the city, and the riot died down, while they waited for the emperor’s arrival and the fulfillment of his promise.
The emperor then gave orders, and a considerable force of armed men was assembled, so that, if they rioted again, he could order the sword to be used against them. Afterward he entered the city.
He ordered that there should be a [?]. When the people had gathered and come up and had begun shouting confused cries at him, he sent them this message: “Be quiet and peaceful,
knowing that everyone is repaid according to his deeds. So remain free of disturbance and disorder.”
Immediately upon entering, before these things, he had dismissed Sebastian the prefect. He appointed another man as prefect, Dionysius [?].
whose name was Julian. He instructed this man to begin arresting them and subjecting them to torture, and to investigate who the others were.
As soon as he began making arrests and questioning them, he found that many of them were Jews, while others were Samaritans, Montanists, and members of other groups.
The prefect, acting prudently so as not to provoke a conflict against himself arising from the Christians’ zeal, began arresting these people and questioning them under flogging:
“Even if the Christians were stirred by zeal to uphold Christianity,
you murderous Jews and misguided heretics—what zeal led you to riot and get mixed up with them?”
They all admitted this: “When we saw a large crowd, we went in among them so that we could get something for ourselves and plunder.” And [?] they also admitted this:
“We were preparing to burn the Christians’ churches, thinking that they would be arrested and subjected to torture, while we would remain unidentified.”
Along with this, they confessed other crimes under flogging. He sentenced some of these men to death by crucifixion, [?] and others to be executed.
Others he sent to various places of exile, so that no Christian could find fault with this or say anything
except, “These people are being punished justly—indeed, justly.” Then he began arresting Christians,
but he treated them mercifully. They were led around the city as a show of intimidation.
And so that their backs would not be seen without wounds, they staged a procession for them.
He ordered—ordered—that red ochre should be rubbed on their backs, so that their backs would appear to have been flayed by lashes,
especially those of the little boys, of whom there were many among them. Some of them were even laughing as they rode mules and were taken around the city.
One of them was arrested and brought in to stand before the prefect. He asked him, “What is your occupation, and who are you?” He replied, “I am a Christian, a shopkeeper.”
He said—he said to him, “A shopkeeper! Since you are a shopkeeper, why were you found in the riot instead of staying quietly in your shop?
“For this reason we order you to be flogged.” When they seized him to flog him, he said:
“By the emperor’s head and life, if I am being flogged for Christ, you may subject me not only to the strokes of whips and scraping combs,
but afterward take—take my head as well, by the head of Emperor Tiberius!” When the prefect heard this, he was alarmed and said:
“This man wants to become a martyr at my hands! Who—who am I? Am I Trajan? Send him out!”
And so he sent him out without—without his receiving a blow. Then he went in and persuaded the emperor to decree an amnesty—an amnesty—for the Christians,
and to order that Christians should no longer be arrested, since it was out of burning zeal that they had gathered and shouted.
The merciful emperor ordered that their offense should be forgiven and that they should no longer be arrested.
Thus the Christians were pardoned. But Jews continued to be arrested and tried whenever they were found.
After all these things, when the serene Emperor Tiberius wanted to show that he had not neglected, and was not neglecting, matters pertaining to the fear of God,
He ordered all the officials and all the senators to assemble together: all the patricians and all the former consuls,
the illustrious officials, the former prefects, the deputy prefects, and the rest of the entire senate, to assemble together in the prefect’s praetorium,
and to have all the records of proceedings against the pagans, whether in the East or in the West, read before them.
He issued an order that anyone who failed to appear should have his belt of office cut off. Thus, under this stern command, they all assembled together and sat throughout the day,
from morning until evening, fasting and exhausted. All the records of proceedings were read before them, and the first person they condemned to death
was Anatolius, whom the account mentioned above, who had formerly been governor and deputy prefect at Edessa.
First, after tortures to the point of death, he was thrown to the wild beasts. After they had savagely mangled him, he was then taken away and crucified.
Before this, another man, his associate, whose name was Theodore—they had served the demons together in all the practices of paganism—
had undergone many bitter tortures, and he too confessed many things.
To keep him for further tortures and questioning about others, he was sent to be imprisoned and held in the praetor’s praetorium. That very night he died there.
As many supposed, it was thought that he had killed himself, because a death sentence was about to be issued against him too.
Because he had sacrificed to demons after baptism, a sentence was issued against him that his body should be burned even though he was dead.
Others, however, out of natural compassion, neglected to do this. But he ordered that he should receive the burial of a donkey: he was to be dragged away and thrown outside.
This man, then, was in addition to those two whom the crowd burned, a man and a woman. That man was the son of this Theodore.
These, then, died in this way, besides many others who had been arrested and imprisoned and were being prepared for torture and interrogation.
There were also others whom men had been sent to find in Syria, Asia, and everywhere else, so that they might be arrested and brought to the imperial capital.
Later, many others were named, and every day more were arrested and added to them, until all the prisons were filled with them.
Clergy of the churches were also named, arrested, and accused of many evil pagan practices.
Sentence was passed against them that they should be thrown to the wild beasts and afterward burned with fire. Thus they received here the punishment they deserved.
But as for there, knowledge of the sentence awaiting them belongs only to that awesome Judge of righteousness.
When so many people had been named and arrested, the judges appointed over them were overwhelmed by their numbers.
Eventually they were removed from the praetorium of the city prefect, who was himself suspected of being one of them, and handed over to the praetor.
From then on, the judges sat and conducted trials in his praetorium. Finally, they sat and conducted trials in the public prison, until the death of Emperor Tiberius.
When Maurice succeeded him as emperor, he too displayed the same zeal. He ordered that the pagans who presented themselves as Christians in name should be tried and investigated,
though in practice they worshiped idols. Thus they are tried every day and receive the recompense for their deeds, both here and hereafter.
An account of the suffering and affliction of Eustochius, who was formerly bishop of Jerusalem.
Because he stood against the pagans with fierce zeal and rebuked them, they devised schemes against him, with unjust pretexts and false accusations.
When he was tried here in the imperial city by unjust judges, who were themselves secret pagans, they unjustly deposed him from his bishopric.
After he was deposed, he did not give himself over to wandering here and there. Instead, he immediately went and took a cell at the monastery of Saint Sergius in Hormizdas.
Of Hormizdas. He shut himself up in it for eighteen years. The emperors themselves and the chamberlains,
and the entire senatorial body, both men and women, regarded him as a righteous man and constantly went to pay their respects to him.
For he was an old man, dignified with his white hair, clear in his speech and teaching, and well versed in the Holy Scriptures.
Now, in the third year of the reign of the victorious Tiberius, after he became emperor, Satan filled the heart of one of Eustochius’s servants during the night.
He took a silver lamp that was burning before Eustochius, raised it, and struck him with it, smashing his skull.
As Eustochius cried out, “Alas!” and said, “Why this, brother?” he struck him again in the belly with his spike—with its spike—and tore it open, spilling out his intestines.
He died immediately. When the rest of his servants began shouting and wailing, the guards stationed below them heard,
and ran upstairs at the sound of their cries. When they reached out to seize him, he drew a knife and struck one of them.
Another drew his sword, struck him on the shoulder, and brought him down. Thus they managed to subdue him. Suddenly there was an uproar and shouting.
A great crowd of people, groaning, ran from every direction to see that dreadful and distressing sight.
The news reached the emperor while he was outside in the [?] at the Hebdomon. Immediately, without delay, he ordered [?] and came in.
When he saw him dead, he wailed and wept like a woman over the husband of her youth, together with the others who saw him—a sight filled with bitter anguish.
At his command, that murderous servant was handed over to the prefect to die a hideous and bitter death. Then the emperor immediately departed.
The servant was thrown to the wild beasts. After they had bitten and mangled him, both his hands and both his feet were cut off.
Then his trunk, together with his hands and feet, was thrown into a boat, which was burned and sank in the sea.
He received the reward for his work, and what is written was fulfilled in him: “Woe to the evil, wicked man, for he will be repaid for what his hands have done.”
Now, when the instruction of the pagans took place in the days of Emperor Justinian, in the four regions of Asia, Caria, Phrygia, and Lydia,
the beginning was first made, with God’s help, in the mountain district of Tralles in Asia.
Many thousands within the territory of this city were turned away from the error of idol worship, and twenty-four churches were established,
and four monasteries were newly built among them. The first was this great monastery, whose story this account has undertaken to relate.
It was built in a village called Darira, in those rugged mountains, on the site of a great and famous pagan temple.
Under his authority, as some elderly men among them told us, were [?] fifteen hundred pagan temples throughout all these provinces.
They said that every year they gathered under its authority, learning and receiving from him rules for how their priests and all the pagan peoples everywhere should conduct themselves.
Then, through a revelation from God, John, who was mentioned above, uprooted this very temple down to its foundations,
and firmly built in its place this monastery called Arira, among the high, rugged mountains. It stands among all these churches.
He also built these three other monasteries: one above it in those mountains, and two below it,
placing them under its authority. He built the monastery itself solidly and spaciously, at great expense,
with funds given to him by Emperor Justinian, together with funds for all these other churches and monasteries.
The emperor gave orders and issued three pragmatic decrees, so that this great monastery should have authority over all these churches and monasteries,
instructing them, watching over them, and regulating all their activities.
From its very beginning, Satan envied this monastery and raised up trials and fierce opposition against it from every side.
The demons that had long lived and rested there, over the blood of the sacrifices offered to them there, openly—
on those sacrifices they used to settle like flies on festering sores. And so they were seen openly fighting and displaying themselves,
as when, at the very beginning of its construction, they lifted one of the builders, a certain cleric, into the air and threw him down onto a cliff,
and from there another cliff below it, still more rugged, received him.
John himself stood with the others, watching him as he flew and fell headfirst, face downward, striking one cliff after another.
He fell farther and struck a rock in the river. The height from which he fell was no less than a thousand cubits.
As they watched him falling, they cried, “Lord, have mercy!” They thought that his very brains were spilling out and being splashed over all the cliffs he struck,
and that all his entrails were being dragged across them. Wailing, they ran to gather up even what remained of his bones and bury them, but they found him sitting upright.
He looked at them. When they saw that he was alive, they were astonished and rejoiced, giving thanks to God, who had rescued him from a bitter death
through the schemes of the wicked demons. Christ had not even allowed him to suffer a wound, except that his nostrils were slightly scratched.
Everyone who saw and heard of the miracle that our Lord Jesus had performed was amazed.
After the year in which the construction of the monastery of Arira was completed, which was in the sixth year, the bishop of Tralles was stirred by envy against the monastery.
He swore, saying, “I will make it an estate belonging to my church, and I will live in it all summer.”
He also quarreled with John himself. Then he went up to Emperor Justinian—Justin [?]—to lodge a complaint against him.
When he went in, he informed the emperor about it and urged him to order that he himself should have authority and command over it, and that John should not come near it,
When the emperor heard these things from him, he said to him, “You did not enter your church or your city without Christ, yet you entered without John's direction and permission.
For you could not administer the church—the church to which you were appointed without any right.
Yet you wanted to seize my monastery, which was built with my knowledge and by my command—was built [?]!” Then he ordered that he should not leave the imperial city before John arrived.
After some time John also came in, and the emperor informed him of everything that had been said—had been said to him by the bishop—and of everything he himself had answered him.
He ordered John himself to go out and administer the city's church and its hospices, and forbade the bishop to do anything without John's permission.
For he also stirred up many other trials and acts of opposition against that monastery and against the twenty-four new churches
that John himself had recently built and established around that monastery, among the pagans whom he had baptized and made Christians, in the mountains near the city of Tralles.
But God in his mercy brought to nothing all the evil one's malice against them and preserved them for the praise of his name to this very day.
Now while Patriarch Eutychius was uttering deadly threats against the orthodox party and threatening them with solemn oaths,
“I will not leave a single one of them in this city, or in its surroundings, or in the other cities,” and while he was making these threats and menaces,
his end suddenly overtook him, and he received his disgrace. On that day all his plans came to nothing and perished, along with all his threats and menaces.
He had gone to great lengths in denying the resurrection of bodies and opposing the words, “You were crucified for us.”
There were very many things that deserved to be included in the accounts about him, but because of their number we have refrained from recounting them all.
When Eutychius departed from this world on the fifth day of the month of April, the man seized to take his place after him was
John the deacon, who had served as treasurer to John of Sirimis, Eutychius's predecessor. He was an ascetic, devoted to fasting and keeping vigil,
who continually lived in seclusion in a cell in the Great Church itself. This man was taken and asked whether he would even listen to the proposal of becoming its head.
When he resisted, Emperor Tiberius ordered that he should be taken to the palace and kept there under guard.
The emperor and the entire senate pressed him, and only with great difficulty were they able to persuade him.
He solemnly declared, “I will not abandon my rule, and I will not meet with anyone before the ninth hour.”
After much had happened, he was ordained. They said that he maintained this same practice, receiving no one before the ninth hour, according to his former custom.
People marveled at him, saying that he lay on his face praying all day, although he was weak and dried up like a piece of wood.
Now those who, in the days of Eutychius, had been accustomed to attack orthodox people like robbers under the pretext of religion,
and heretics as well, and to seize their possessions, began, as usual, asking him to give them permission, as his predecessor had done,
to go and plunder people, drag them away, and bring them to prison. But when he learned of these things, he said to them,
“Go, sit down, and keep quiet. I will not allow you to go and attack and plunder people, causing God and his holy church to be blasphemed.”
They said to him, “Eutychius gave us these orders.” He said to them, “But I command that there be peace and tranquility in my days.”
“But if you are using Eutychius as an excuse, go to him now, and [?] whatever he commands you, you will do.”
There were many remarkable things that could have been written about him, but to avoid an excessively long account, we have limited the stories about him to a few.
Now while Count Maurice was in command of the armies in the East, he took counsel with Mundhir, king of the Arabs, that they should invade Persian territory together.
After traveling for several days, they reached a place opposite Beth Aramaye, where the city of the Persian king was, and found that the bridge ahead of them had been cut—
the bridge over which they had hoped to cross and capture the royal city. Over this, however, they fell into a quarrel with each other,
because Maurice suspected Mundhir of having sent word to the Persians, who had dismantled the bridge.
And so, having become enemies and quarreled with each other, they returned without accomplishing anything.
From then on they began writing to Emperor Tiberius against each other. The emperor made great efforts to reconcile them.
When he could not do so, Maurice went up to the emperor and accused Mundhir bitterly and harshly. The emperor accepted the accusation and was filled with fierce anger against Mundhir.
He began devising a way to trap him and have him arrested and brought to the imperial capital.
Then Magnus, the Syrian curator, who was Mundhir’s friend and patron, and whom Mundhir trusted because he represented him before the emperor,
wishing to win the emperor’s favor, said to him, “If you command it, I will bring him here to you in chains.”
The emperor was pleased and sent him off. He traveled down to the East by the imperial post, to his village called Hawarin,
which he had also made into a city, surrounding it with a wall and building a church in it. It was on the pretext of consecrating this church that he had gone down.
When he went down, he also took the patriarch of Antioch with him, so that they might more effectively deceive Mundhir into coming.
Then he deceitfully sent word to Mundhir: “Since I have come for the dedication of this church and am weary from the journey—
otherwise I would have come myself to pay you my respects—and since I long to see you in good health, I ask you to come to me at once,
without bringing a large body of troops with you. I ask you to stay with me for a few days so that we may rest together,
and so that you will not incur great expenses for a large army. Instead, come yourself with only a few men.”
When Mundhir received the message from Magnus, he was delighted. Immediately, without hesitation and with complete confidence, he came to him as to a dear friend, without a large army,
having no suspicion of him at all. Magnus, meanwhile, took care not to reveal his wicked deceit and welcomed him cheerfully.
He gave orders for a banquet to be prepared and said, “Dismiss those who came with you.” Mundhir said to him, “Look, as you commanded, I have not come with a large army.
When I return, I cannot travel without an escort, even a small one.” He said to him, “Dismiss them,
and when you leave, send for them, and they will come.” But Mundhir, being a man of great understanding, was displeased with what was happening.
He began to grow afraid and sent word to his army to withdraw a little and wait for him. When they had dispersed,
Magnus secretly ordered the troops with him to get ready, along with the duke who had been ordered to accompany Magnus.
Then, toward evening, he began to say to him, “My lord patrician, accusations have been brought against you before the emperor,
and he has ordered you to go up to him, put his mind at ease, and convince him that nothing that was said—that was said about you—is true.”
Then Mundhir answered him, saying, “After all these hardships, I do not think it right that accusations against me should be accepted.
For I am the emperor’s servant, and I do not refuse to go up.
But at this time I cannot abandon my camp and let the Persian Arabs come and take my wives and children captive
and take everything I have.” Then the armed Roman troops appeared, and Magnus threatened him, saying,
“If you do not go up willingly, I will put you in irons, mount you on a donkey, and send you off like that.” When the plot was revealed to him, and he saw that Magnus had stripped him of his army,
imprisoned him, and handed him over to the Roman troops to guard him, he was humbled and subdued like a lion of the wilderness caught in a trap.
When his army learned of this, they surrounded the fortress and prepared to burn it. But when they saw that the Romans had come out into the open and prepared for battle, they withdrew.
With the Romans surrounding him, they brought him out to go up under heavy guard. He reached the imperial capital.
When he entered, the emperor ordered him to stay where he had stayed before. An allowance was assigned to him and those with him.
He remained like this, without being received in audience. One of his wives, two of his sons, and one of his daughters were with him.
Now Mundhir’s four sons, especially the eldest, whose name was Nu’man—a man more cunning and better prepared for war than Mundhir himself—
gathered their armies and attacked Magnus’s fortress, for he too had gone up to the emperor.
Without taking people captive, killing them, or setting fires, they looted and carried off everything: gold and silver,
bronze and iron, all articles of wool or linen, grain, wine, and oil.
They seized all the herds of livestock of every kind that fell into their hands, and all the herds of cattle,
and all the flocks of sheep and goats. The Arab armies swept through and plundered all the surrounding villages of Arabia and Syria.
They gathered possessions and livestock in immeasurable quantities. They withdrew deep into the wilderness and pitched a large camp there.
They divided the plunder, remaining alert and ready for battle, keeping watch on every side.
They kept going out, plundering, seizing things, and bringing them into the wilderness, until the whole eastern region, as far as the sea, trembled before them.
People fled to the cities and did not dare show themselves before them.
So when the rulers of the region and the army commanders sent word to them, asking, “Why are you doing all these things in this way?” they too sent word back:
Why did the emperor lead our father away like a captive, after all these labors, victories, and feats of courage for which he toiled and fought on his behalf?
He has cut off our allowances, and we have nothing to live on. That is why we are forced to do these things. It is enough that we are not killing or burning.

Then, finally, they went against the city of Bostra and surrounded it. They said to its inhabitants, “Give us our father’s weapons and the rest of the property belonging to his kingship that is deposited with you.
Otherwise, we will uproot, burn, and kill everything we can, both in your city and throughout its territory.”
When the duke, a famous and well-known man, heard this, he became angry, gathered his army, and marched out.
He looked down on them as Arabs. But they drew up their forces against him, overpowered him, and killed him and many of his soldiers.
When the inhabitants of that city saw this, they were shaken. They sent word to them: “Stop the fighting. We will give you what belongs to you.
Take it in peace.” So they brought out their father’s property to them. They took it and returned to the desert, to their encampment.
Yet they did not give up plundering and raiding for a long time.
For when Tiberius heard these things about the sons of Mundhir, he was deeply embittered.
He again sent Magnus to make Mundhir’s brother king of the Arabs in his place,
and, if he could, to subdue and capture Mundhir’s sons, whether through treachery, persuasion and disturbances, or battle.
The governors of the cities and the dukes were also ordered to accompany him with a large army, and so he went down with a great show of force.
First he appointed Mundhir’s brother king, but he died after twenty days. Finally, [?] troops [?] for them, for him, while [?] deceitfully.
He also administered matters of ordination. Later, when Paul, who had been patriarch of Antioch, arrived, they administered these matters together.
Thus, when Theodosius had grown old and very infirm, and could no longer stand and offer the Eucharist,
he instructed and authorized Longinus, who was still a priest, to stand in his place. He offered the Eucharist on his behalf for the rest of his life.
He also directed that he should become bishop of the people who had become disciples and were called the Nobades.
In what follows, we will also bring the account concerning them to remembrance.
In the company of Pope Theodosius there was an elderly man, an accomplished priest, named Julian.
Spiritual zeal entered this man concerning that pagan people, [?] the man who was on the eastern border of Thebes, in the interior of Egypt.
This people was not even subject to the Roman Empire, but actually received tribute so that it would not invade Egypt and carry its inhabitants off captive.
As the blessed Julian was concerned for that people, he went in and informed the late Empress Theodora, asking her to take an interest in that people’s conversion.
Because the empress was burning with zeal for God, she received this gladly.
She promised to do everything necessary so that this people might turn away from the error of idol worship.
In her joy, she informed the victorious Emperor Justinian of this. She undertook to send the blessed Julian there and was making arrangements to do so.
But when the emperor heard that she was intent on sending someone there from among those opposed to the council, he was not pleased.
He devised a plan to write to his own bishops in Thebes, so that they would go in, make disciples of them, and establish the council’s name there.
Then he too became zealous, and hurriedly sent envoys there ahead of her, with gold, baptismal garments, and gifts of honor for the king of that people.
He also sent letters to the duke of the Thebaid, instructing him to look after his own envoy and convey him to that people.
When the empress herself learned of these things, she acted energetically and cunningly, preparing letters to the duke of the Thebaid and sending out an imperial courier.
“Since the emperor and I have decided to send an envoy to the people of the Nobades, I too am now sending a blessed man named Julian.
And I want this man of mine to reach that people before the emperor’s envoy. Know, then, that if you arrange for his envoy to enter there before this man of mine,
and do not delay him with excuses until this blessed man of mine arrives and is conveyed across and enters, you will not remain alive. Instead, I will send there and have your head taken off.”
After the duke of the Thebaid had received these instructions, the emperor’s envoy also reached him. He gave him lodging and said to him, “Be patient,
for we are looking for pack animals and making them ready, and we are preparing men who know the desert. Then you can take them and go in.”
Thus he lodged him and kept him waiting until the envoys arrived—the envoys of the compassionate empress.
They found the pack animals and the men ready, and that very day, without delay, they took the pack animals, as though by force, and went on ahead.
Meanwhile, he sent word to the emperor’s envoy: “You should know that, after I had made preparations for you and was just about to send you word, the empress’s envoys arrived.
They descended on me by force, took the pack animals, and crossed over on their journey. You know better than I do how much the empress is to be feared.
For this reason, I did not dare oppose them. But wait for me a little longer, until I make fresh preparations for you, so that you too can travel in peace.”
When he learned this, he tore his clothes, uttering many threats and blasphemies.
Then, after some days, he too set out and went on afterward, unaware of the trick that had been played on him.
For when the blessed Julian and the envoys with him reached the country, they sent word to the king and the nobles, informing them of their arrival.
They sent a military force to meet them, welcomed them joyfully, and brought them into their country to their king. He too received them warmly.
Julian also handed over the empress’s letters, which were read and their meaning made known. They also received magnificent gifts of honor and many baptismal garments,
and everything in abundance. Immediately, rejoicing, they gave themselves over and renounced all the error of their ancestors.
They acknowledged the God of the Christians, saying, “He is the one true God, and there is no other besides him.”
After he had instructed them at length and taught them, he informed them, told them beforehand, and also taught them this in advance:
“Because various disputes have arisen among Christians concerning the faith,
For this reason, when the blessed Theodosius was also pressed to accept it and would not agree, the emperor removed him from his see.
The empress, however, welcomed him and rejoiced in him, because he had stood firm in the orthodox faith and had left his see for its sake.
For this reason she sent us to you, so that you too would follow Pope Theodosius, be baptized in his faith, and preserve his truth.
The emperor has also sent envoys to you, and they too are coming after us. And they instructed them how to receive them and give them an answer.
When they had been strengthened in all these things, the emperor’s envoy also arrived. He too entered and gave their king letters and gifts of honor.
They too began to instruct them, as they had been commanded, saying, “Our emperor, the emperor of the Romans, sends you this message:
‘If you are becoming Christians, join the church and those who hold to it, and do not go astray after those who have been expelled from the church.’”
When the king of the Nobades and his nobles heard this, they answered them, saying, “We accept the honor bestowed by the emperor of the Romans,
and we too send him honor. But we do not accept his faith. Rather, if we are deemed worthy to become Christians,
we will follow Pope Theodosius, whom the emperor drove out and expelled from his church because he would not accept the emperor’s corrupt faith.
If we are fleeing paganism and error, we will not agree to fall once again into a corrupt faith.”
Thus they dismissed the envoys, having put these very things in writing. The blessed Julian remained with them for two years, enduring great hardship from the burning heat.
He used to relate that from the third hour until the tenth, stripped and wrapped in a linen cloth, he would go into caves filled with water and sit there together with all the people of the country.
Nothing but his nose would be above the water. Yet he persevered, made disciples, and baptized the king, his nobles, and the many people with him.
He had also brought with him a bishop from the Thebaid, an elderly man named Theodore.
After teaching them and putting their affairs in order, he entrusted them to that bishop, left them, and reached Constantinople.
In our presence and theirs, he was received by the empress with great honor, while he recounted things about that numerous people—
things so remarkable and so numerous that, because of their number, we refrain from writing them down and confine ourselves to these few details.
On the day of Pope Theodosius’s departure, then, he remembered that people.
This was especially so because the blessed Julian, who had made them disciples, had also died a short time before, and Empress Theodora had also gone to her rest.
He directed that the blessed Longinus should go there, as a diligent man capable of fully converting them and strengthening them in Christianity.
Immediately after the pope’s death, Longinus became bishop for that place and prepared to leave.
When he had put his belongings aboard a ship to depart, there appeared men of whom it is written, “Their teeth are spears and arrows,
and their tongue is like a sharp sword.” They went in and said to the emperor, “You should know that Longinus has become a bishop,
and that he is an enemy of our palace. He has put his belongings aboard a ship to depart.”
“And if he goes,” they said, “since he is an influential man, and enters that nation, he will immediately stir them up to war and to taking captives in Roman territory.”
“Now, therefore,” they said, “give orders for him to be arrested.” When the king learned these things, he became angry and ordered his arrest. They went and brought his belongings off the ship.
Thus he was not allowed to leave. After that he remained for three years, waiting for an opportunity.
Finally, when he realized that he was being watched and was not being allowed to leave, he changed his appearance by putting a wig on his head.
He was very bald. Then, taking two young men with him, he escaped, and God delivered him.
He went and entered that country, where he was received with great honor and great joy. Once again he made disciples of them all, enlightening and teaching them.
He established a church there, appointed clergy, and taught the order of worship and all the practices of Christianity.
When he escaped and the king learned of it, the king became extremely angry. He ordered all the sea crossings to be seized and all the roads to be guarded.
Letters were sent to every region, but all these measures proved useless.
Longinus persuaded the king of that nation to send a chief ambassador to the Roman emperor with gifts and tokens of honor.
When he was received and publicly honored, and so forth, he expressed his gratitude to Longinus, saying:
“Although we were Christians in name, we did not learn what Christianity meant in practice until Longinus came among us.”
While he related many great things about him, the emperor remained bitter toward him, though he said nothing.
When Longinus had spent about six years in that country, Satan, who envies good things,
envied him and sought a way to make him flee and drive him out of there, and to use him as a cause of disorder, division, and ruin in the church.
He arranged for letters to be written to him by the head of the clergy of Alexandria, Theodosius the archpriest,
and by Theodore, his sister’s son, the archdeacon, calling on him to leave that country
and come to the region around Alexandria, so that they could make him their pope and he could help the church. This became the beginning of the trouble and division.
When Longinus received these letters, he was stirred up and burned with intense zeal, setting aside all fear of death.
He began preparing to leave that country, intending to carry out and fulfill what these letters instructed him to do.
When the king and all his nobles learned of this, they gathered and tried to prevent him from leaving. But he showed them the letters, saying:
“The matter for which I have been instructed to leave concerns the communion of the whole church, and I cannot refuse to go.”
They continued arguing with him, mourning and weeping as they said, “Once again we will be left as orphans without a father, as we were before.”
Thus, with sorrow and bitter mourning, they let him go and gave him provisions.
He departed and came to Theodore, the aged bishop of Philae in Upper Thebes. He showed him the letters and consulted him about what had been written.
He was asking him to go with him if possible, but he could not because of his very advanced age.
For it was nearly fifty years since he had been made bishop by Timothy, the predecessor of the blessed Theodosius.
He too agreed to the contents of the letters and gave Longinus a document authorizing him to act in his place, agreeing to everything he would do.
So he set out and came to Mareotis, where he had been directed by letter. He was considering what to do.
He was trembling and afraid that his arrival in Roman territory after his escape might become known, and that he would be arrested and suffer a terrible death. This made his heart tremble.
Now two bishops, John from the monastery of Mar Bassus and George the Urtayan, who had been ordained at that time but had not yet been permitted to exercise his episcopal office,
were sent at that time by the eastern synod to Longinus and to Theodore of Philae, who was mentioned above,
concerning the reception of Paul of Antioch after his ordeal and his escape: whether they agreed to receive him and enter into communion with him.
As it happened, when they were preparing to enter his country to visit him, they learned that he had left his country and gone down to Egypt, so they followed him.
Following reports of his whereabouts, they went and found him in Libya, outside Alexandria, at a place called Mareotis.
He welcomed them joyfully. When he read the letters, he rejoiced over them, saying, “God has brought you at a good time.
Indeed, he has sent you now especially for this purpose: to lend us a hand in establishing the church.
For this is also why I myself, when I received a letter, set out from a distant country and came here, so that there might be a patriarch in Alexandria.”
But they said, “How can we appoint a patriarch without the authorization of our own patriarch?
Rather, if this is what you wish to do, he too should be present. He is not far away, and we will go and bring him.” After much discussion between them,
they went and brought Paul the patriarch from nearby, as is reported, dressed in Roman clothing, to the region of Libya.
They found Longinus traveling about, making inquiries and diligently seeking a man suitable for the rank of chief bishop.
When they found him, they went together to the desert of the solitary monks, inland beyond the blessed Mar Menas, called Rhamnin.
They found the abbot there, a virtuous man named Theodore, who was Syrian by birth.
They began speaking to him, urging him to offer himself to become pope in Alexandria.
When he heard this, he was distressed and tried to excuse himself and escape, even resorting to oaths.
He stood firm in his decision, until they bound him under an anathema if he refused this or spoke. So they seized him by force, against his will, while he wept and wailed,
and Longinus himself and these two bishops ordained him, while Paul, as they swore, did not [?] join them in his ordination.

For he had not yet been absolved and received back after the lapse he had suffered. In the end, however, although he did not take part in his ordination, he agreed to the remaining matters, accepted him, and entered into communion with him.
And, as is reported, they even exchanged synodical letters with one another as the patriarchs of Antioch and Alexandria.

Thus, when they all thought, and thought that all of them [?] the great undertaking, they acted and proceeded in accordance with the canons, the unity, and the established order of the churches of Syria and Alexandria.
Because [?] and because a bishop had been appointed for them without the knowledge of the Alexandrians, which was improper, the outcome proved disastrous for them all,
and for the whole church in the East and throughout Egypt, bringing trials, confusion, disputes, schisms, and divisions.
It became a cause of many evils, also for the individuals themselves, each one of them personally,
and also brought the unruly populace of Alexandria to insolence and a ferocity without order or restraint.
When, therefore, the Alexandrians finally received the letters of Longinus and the bishops with him, and also those of Theodore himself, concerning everything they had done,
announcing that Theodore had become their patriarch—he himself also addressed them in synodical letters,
which first taught the truth of the faith and the other appropriate matters, since he was now writing to them as his own church—
he also offered an excuse, saying, “Because of fear of those who hold power, and so that no disturbance might be stirred up, we did not enter the city.”
“And everything took place in canonical order, with your consent and decree,” and much else besides.
Thus, when the leaders of the clergy, those already mentioned above, and the rest of the others learned all these things,
they became agitated and disturbed and were roused to anger over everything that had happened. They also stirred up, incited, and disturbed all the rest of the clergy.
They drove them to frenzy and barbarous ferocity against Longinus and Theodore, whom he had appointed,
and against Paul, on whose account especially they had become so savagely enraged, and the others with them.
They rejected them, insulted them, and repudiated them, stirring up disturbances and strife against them in the church and in the city,
and saying in chanting, disorderly voices, “Let us all gather now, immediately and without delay, and appoint a pope for ourselves here, from among us and in our midst.”
These men were again inciting and stirring up trouble [?], so that they might appoint one of their own number, Andronicus, who was mentioned above.
Thus they themselves, as has been said, would henceforth exercise authority and leadership and control all the administration of the church of Alexandria.
But when they saw and realized that neither the clergy nor the citizens approved of him or wanted him, because shortly before
even a demon had reportedly manifested itself in him, he then indicated that he himself was now asking not to be appointed.
Thus, when they saw that this plan had failed and that there was now no possibility of appointing one of themselves,
they cunningly devised a scheme to appoint some insignificant, inferior man, arranging that he should possess only the title and outward appearance of office,
while, through his ignorance and simplicity, he would be excluded from all administration and everything appropriate to leadership of this kind,
so that they themselves could give him orders, manipulate him, and administer affairs, while he would be unable to give them orders.
This they actually carried out and accomplished. They chose and brought forward an elderly deacon of middling rank, a simple, uneducated man named Peter.
This man had also been among the companions of the blessed Theodosius during his exile.
When they decided to do this, they had only one bishop available, whose name was John. Canonical accusations were also being pursued against him.
So, in their haste, they hurried in and brought in two visiting bishops who had previously been ordained by the blessed Jacob for Syria:
both had the same name, Antoninus and Antoninus. They seized them by force and made the previously mentioned deacon Peter
a second bishop at that very time in Tronion, after they had accepted that he had received the synodical letters of Theodore, the first bishop.

Without judging and examining the matter in an orderly and canonical way—whether the first bishop had been appointed in an orderly and proper way, and whether according to the canons or contrary to the canons—
they were stirred by bitter resentment and the bonds of injustice, with anger commanding them and brutish cunning—brutishness and cunning—directing them with barbaric violence.
They made, installed, and named a second bishop in the very same see, out of resentment against the first, bringing disturbance, confusion, division, and conflict upon the whole church.
And indeed, it stands visibly demonstrated in practice that this happened according to the pleasure and will of the devil, who brought these things about and carried them out.
Like Pharaoh’s people and a people of foreign speech, they rose up and launched into all this confusion, disorder, and barbarity,
without allowing even a single consideration of good order into their minds, so as to judge and examine whether it was proper or improper
as the first bishop supposed they had learned had happened [?]; and then they launched into all this barbaric savagery, so as to set another man over him.
Yet they did not restrain the violence of their brutishness with restraints—with restraints of their brutishness [?]—of the fear of God,
nor did they consider within themselves the evils, divisions, conflicts, factions, clashes, and disturbances that would arise from this in the church of God.
Indeed, just as they had planned, this became visible, happened, and was fulfilled. This evil, conflict, and warfare took hold between the two parties and continues to this day.
It has been about eight years since then, years that need the lamentations of the sorrowful prophet Jeremiah to mourn over them,
over the wars that occurred and the evils that sprang up, over the hatred that took hold, over the unrelenting hostility that darkened the hearts of many,
so that they would not reflect on all these evils and cease their insults, abuse, and bitter oppression of one another.
Just as someone whose eyes are weak and dim cannot easily see clearly and gaze at the sun’s rays,
and someone burning with a violent fever cannot perform any action like a healthy person, so too those who are swept away by the passion of anger
and drawn into the violence of furious zeal cannot judge and examine what is proper before carrying out their actions.
Likewise, those who are drunk with anger and bewildered by rage and hostile zeal cannot think of or do anything right at all.
This is what actually happened to the learned Alexandrian clergy, who were not deficient even in knowledge,
if only the storm of rage had not disturbed them and anger had not bewildered them. They became an example of this scriptural saying,
concerning those tossed among the waves by winds and storms: “They reeled and staggered like drunken men, and all their wisdom perished.”
How, now, in these matters they acted hastily and savagely, without regard for ecclesiastical order:
When they received the synodical letter of the man who had become their bishop from among orthodox people and members of their communion, although, as they themselves complained,
time had not allowed his appointment to take place by their vote [?], they nevertheless descended into utter savagery over this.
They were driven to distraction by the rush of their anger and sought to conceal their transgression, on account of which they had, as they supposed, been passed over in these matters:

because they had been passed over and that first man had been appointed without their vote, they themselves, thinking themselves so very wise, rushed to appoint Peter as a second bishop at the same time and in the same see.
If indeed it was right for them to do this, then throughout the ten years that had intervened after the death of the blessed Theodosius,
they should have done it without dispute and appointed a bishop for themselves—not after learning that Theodore had become their bishop first.
They issued a decree [?] born of anger, as though intent on quarrelling, contention, and the division of the church.
They rushed to appoint Peter as the second bishop, so that people would immediately regard him as an adulterer who had entered into adultery with his fellow's wife.
How, again, at their urging, the man who had come into office unlawfully and without canonical order—whom two of them had thus appointed contrary to ecclesiastical laws—
was earnestly urged by them, as if to confirm his position, to proceed to appoint bishops, seventy in number, as is reported.
Even if someone had been looking for laborers to work the land, it would have been difficult for him to find that many ready and gather them all at one time.
And what can we say about those chosen to shepherd Christ's rational flock, which he commanded the blessed Peter to shepherd?

Moreover, according to the apostolic command and teaching addressed to Timothy, even the appointment of priests should take place through selection, investigation, and extensive examination. How much more must this be said of chief priests!
But just as the beginning of this undertaking was confused, disorderly, and entirely lacking in propriety, so too was its conclusion.
Not even then was he restrained from his furious rush of frenzy and savagery, so as to put on Christ's gentleness and humility.
Instead, they cunningly urged him to rush on to divide the church of Syria and Alexandria as well, and to make use of the deposition of Paul—
who had been appointed patriarch of Antioch by order of the blessed Theodosius—unjustly and contrary to the canons, while he was far away.
Not only this: he also pursued accusations against Jacob, bishop of Syria. He did these things not merely informally, but also in a circular letter of his own, which he composed and sent everywhere.
In it he further added, because of the hostility and long-standing hatred they had toward Paul,
a document concerning acts of oppression, murder, and deceit, which Paul himself, they alleged, and others with him had drawn up and presented to the members of the synod.
This document had also been anathematized by those who had been wronged, in the very declaration in the Spirit that they issued concerning this matter to the whole church.

They anathematized those who had done these things, those who had committed the wrongs, and themselves too, if they had done it or had any knowledge of it or involvement in it, secretly or openly, in any way at all, as they declared.
Therefore, let those who encounter these brief records of ours, either now or later, which are being written about this thoroughly confused undertaking, not suppose
that we are recording them unfairly, with exaggerations [?], or [?] entirely contrary to the truth.
Or when we wish to vindicate one side and are eager to heap blame on the other.
But we record a little out of the many things that happened in our own times—that is, in the year 886 of Alexander—
and afterward, without adding anything. We do not, however, promise that we will leave nothing out.
For great confusion, turmoil, and disorder arose through the activity of the murderer of human beings.
We can deal with these things only through brief indications, since we have set them all down in a confused and disordered mass.
Now Theodore, who is said to have been made bishop first in Alexandria by Longinus and the others, against his will,
when he learned that the Alexandrians had reached such a degree of cunning and brutality that they would accept neither him nor his letters,
but had instead made and appointed in his place the Peter mentioned afterward, entirely outside canonical order,
withdrew into solitude and remained in the order of his former way of life. He was not at all disturbed by what had happened, saying, “Let there be neither division nor strife on my account.
For I have no concern except to live in peace of soul, as I have lived until now.”
And so, for the time being, he remained undisturbed. Eventually, however, many turned to follow him.
In the city, in the deserts, in Egypt, in Thebais, and in the Thebaid, he also established [?] in his name and performed ordinations.
Now, in the second book, we gave a detailed account of the lapse concerning the hope of unity that befell the blessed Paul and those with him, together with this.
But now we must make known and record the empty notion held by the Alexandrians, who in a brutal rush appointed Peter the Second to the throne of their church:
namely, that he allegedly entered the region of Libya with his bishops and, together with Longinus, ordained Theodore. This is empty and false.
For Longinus himself, in one of his letters, refuted this notion and made a declaration [?] with many oaths
that he had not been present at Theodore’s appointment, and that it had happened neither at his word nor with his knowledge.
For in their brutal haste they had, they said, appointed Peter for this purpose: that he should carry out his deposition presumptuously and without canonical order.
Yet his own priesthood was still, according to the canons, subject to censure, unstable, and unconfirmed.

It had come about barbarously, through a furious rush, and not according to the order of the church canons; and he had unlawfully taken his place as the second occupant of the throne after another had been designated for it.
For they also fabricated accusations against the blessed Jacob, and not merely informally, but also in writings and in a letter [?], an encyclical—that is, a circular letter.

They did these things while the persons concerned were far away. They had not been summoned according to the provisions of the canons or accused in person, but were nevertheless rejected, as though by the authority
of their actions. From this point onward, division and bitter strife arose between Syria and Alexandria, and were deliberately prepared and established.
There was also a severe division arising from the passion of longstanding hostility and the bitter resentment they had long held toward Paul.
As for this elder Jacob, it was neither unfamiliar nor far-fetched to speak about him and his simplicity and innocence.
What is written about the brothers—that is, the holy disciples in the days of the blessed apostles—is that they praised the Lord with purity of heart.
So this man too, along with his simplicity and innocence, was adorned with spiritual zeal and with struggles and labors for the church, from his youth to his old age,
while he was being pulled along by others—unscrupulous and cunning men who attached themselves to him and tried to turn him as they wished,
so that through him and by using him as a pretext they could accomplish all their wishes. Thus they pulled the old man this way and that in his childlike innocence,
tugging him about and turning him around. This happened also in the affair of Paul, whom he, together with the others, had previously made patriarch in Antioch the Great—
that is, their own patriarch and their superior. Afterward they acted freely and without his authorization, even after he had appointed him,
so that eventually others reproached them, saying, “You ought not to do anything without the consent of your patriarch.”
When many of them heard this, these words greatly disturbed them and did not please them at all.
Even so, they did not stop doing everything according to their own wishes. These things continued in this way for some time.
Afterward, ostensibly for the purpose of unity, Paul and the others were summoned to come to the imperial city.
When they arrived, entered, and were received by the emperor, they engaged in countless discussions, with many changes of position, over a prolonged period of more than two years.
We have already made known some of the main points of these discussions in the second book, which precedes this one. For now, however, we have decided to pass over the matter quickly.
Finally Paul himself and three others with him, having trusted the oaths and decisions of the rulers concerning unity,
were caught, in their hope for unity, in the evil lapse of communion with those who professed two natures.
After innumerable things had been said and done in the meantime, as related earlier, they were all sent into exile.
Then Paul, disregarding his own life, fled from the episcopal residence and escaped from the hands of his enemies.
He hurried to the regions of Syria and drew up not just one but two written declarations of repentance addressed to the eastern synod.
He continued pleading for about three years, more or less. Then the blessed Jacob himself and his synod received him into communion by a formal decision and according to canonical order.
And so Jacob wrote many letters here to the imperial city, to Antioch, and to the other regions:
“You should know that we have received our blessed patriarch, Mar Paul, into spiritual communion, and we have shared communion together.
Everyone who receives him receives us, and everyone who does not receive him does not receive us.” But again, a short time later, through the working of the Evil One,
various causes of dispute arose among them, which, out of respect for the dignity of their religious calling, we shall pass over in silence.
Thus division and hatred continued between the two parties for some time.
Both parties were blamed for the confused and disorderly events in Alexandria, and the blessed Jacob especially,
since he wrote everywhere against Peter II, whom they had appointed there, saying that he had become a new Gaianus in Alexandria, bringing turmoil to the church.
He also wrote three letters on the same subject to our humble self, along with many others.
But as for Peter, whom certain people, so to speak, used as a means of carrying out and fulfilling their own wishes:
They took him like a picture painted on a wall and made him bishop of Alexandria, after another had already been appointed before him.
And it was not enough for them that his ordination was unlawful, unstable, and unconfirmed,
and that he gathered people indiscriminately, whether young or old, and irregularly made a [?] of seventy bishops, along with the rest of the clergy.
They also dragged him into another savage deed, so that he rushed to divide the church of Syria and Alexandria,

and tyrannically dared to undertake the deposition of Paul of Antioch, unlawfully and contrary to ecclesiastical regulations and canons, although he himself was unlawfully appointed. Nor was he restrained from this insolence.
Instead, so that they might stir up unrest, hatred, and accusations against him, he drew up a petition of false accusations against him as well as against others,
and through such insolence, tyranny, and arrogance, he would resemble a drunken man who had lost his way in his drunkenness and understood nothing,
at the urging of those who had set him up like an image for these purposes. He put these things into circular letters and sent them everywhere.
The rest of the things of this kind that he brought about, causing divisions in the church, also produced many great disputes,
and there was endless turmoil between Syria and Alexandria, brought about deceitfully and savagely.
For, as we explained above, the innocent old man Jacob was being dragged along by those energetic men who had attached themselves to him,
as they schemed to find a pretext and an outlet for their hatred and their resentment toward Paul, which had arisen through the influence of the murderer.
So they kept urging the old man to go to Alexandria, ostensibly persuading him to bring about unity between the Alexandrians and Syria,
although they knew perfectly well that the Alexandrians had a longstanding hatred and implacable hostility toward Paul because of envy.
They managed to ensnare the old man in his simplicity, lead him away, and bring him into Alexandria almost secretly,
although many who learned that he was preparing to go wrote and solemnly warned him not to go into Alexandria alone in this manner,
lest, by being harassed and ensnared in these men's hatred, he should cause further divisions and disputes between Egypt and Syria, and the growth of evil should gain strength.
But they would not be persuaded. They led him away and brought him into Alexandria, and he fell among a people of foreign speech, as it is written.
Then they forced him, under pressure, into communion with Peter, by whom he had been reviled both in writing and orally,
and called a new Gaianus who had arisen to throw the church of God into turmoil.
Again they subjected and humbled him, making him also draw up a petition in the form of a document of union,
and present it to the very man whom he had censured and reviled, saying that he was nothing but an adulterer who had seized his neighbor's wife and committed adultery with her,
since another orthodox man had already been appointed and named, and there had also been one or another orthodox man before him and after him.
And these men, out of hatred for Paul and in order to find grounds for cutting him off and deposing him, closed their eyes to absolutely everything.
They turned to Peter, whom they had been insulting in this way as a new Gaianus, having, as has been said, trampled on every obligation.
They condoned every violation of the canons for which they had previously been accusing Peter, and agreed with him in everything.
They put their signatures to every violation of canon law that he had committed, and especially to the deposition of Paul, patriarch of Antioch.
This had been carried out boldly and tyrannically, outside all canonical bounds, by Peter and his party while they were far away, before Jacob and his party came to them.
When they heard of it, they heard this with pleasure, and the passion of their hatred found relief when it was put into action.
And even though it had been done by others, it delighted them and pleased them greatly, since they thought that the yoke of their patriarch Paul had been lifted from their necks.
They also gave their written assent and signatures to it. But the elder Jacob presented a plea that this deposition should take place without a sentence of anathema.
So, when the blessed Jacob and those with him had completed their confused proceedings in Alexandria—
which became a cause of upheaval, disturbance, division, and conflict for the whole church in Syria—having agreed to and signed everything that Peter had done, then, as they were leaving there,
they asked him to have three of his bishops accompany them to Syria, as witnesses and confirmation of the reversal they had made.
And so they all departed together, so that all Syria, so to speak, was astonished and alarmed at their arrival.
On their departure, when they began to relate the substance of their proceedings and the deposition of Paul that they had carried out without canonical justification,
great division, schism, and confusion immediately spread through and took hold of the whole church of the faithful everywhere throughout Syria.
Many agreed with what the elder Jacob had done in Alexandria. For one reason—for one reason in Alexandria [?]—
