because of him and because they had long been attached to him; and for another, because they thought that a sound and complete union had been achieved in Alexandria.
Others, however, immediately broke away, turned back, and repudiated all the proceedings they had carried out there, finding fault with Jacob and his party and complaining against them.
First, because he himself had been finding fault with Peter and insulting him and those who had appointed him, calling him a new Gaianus,
whom the Alexandrians had appointed—had appointed—to disturb the church, and saying that he was outside the canons, a nobody, and a stranger to the priesthood,
and an adulterer. Yet after all this, he went in, agreed, and submitted to the man whom he had been rejecting and insulting, and entered into communion with him—not merely in an ordinary way,
but even presenting him with a formal petition. Those three bishops who accompanied him carried it with them and secretly showed it to many,
saying, “Here is the formal petition that Father Jacob drew up and presented to Pope Peter.”
This was done secretly, since neither he nor those with him thought that what they had drawn up had the form of a petition. Rather, they said, “We have drawn up a document of union.”
Were it not for the length of the narrative, we would also have included it here in its proper place.
So once again pain was added to pain, and disaster to disaster, also at this time, in the year eight hundred and eighty-seven.
It overtook the whole persecuted and harassed church of the faithful in all the regions mentioned above, through division, disputes, schisms, sufferings, and evils—
this division that arose between Jacob and Paul, spread, and took hold like a bitter gangrene, without any fear of God.
Bishops, clergy, large and small monastic communities, and the rest of the people of the churches in the cities and villages of these regions attached themselves to one or the other of them.
Each faction rushed against the other to harm and overthrow it, exchanging insults and abuse,
with unrestrained, savage attacks, tearing one another down, oppressing and dividing the people, and splitting the church into opposing sides.
They tore the congregations apart, so that each person would break away from his neighbor and oppose him, and enlarge his own faction.
Through his own supporters, each of them did everything he could to divide many people, make them stumble, split them apart, and draw them to himself.
And so both factions were filled and inflamed with a spirit of opposition, without the discipline and judgment of the fear of God,
which would lead them to turn back from these evils and stop dividing, disturbing, and throwing God's church into confusion.
Instead, he drove them into this pattern of murderous hatred, hostility, insults, and abuse against one another—
he who asked to sift them like wheat—and into mocking and ridiculing one another,
in ways that no one would dare to speak or mock even against pagans, Jews, or heretics, not even someone exceedingly savage and beastlike.
And all this happened although, in matters of faith, there was no difference or deviation between them.
When, therefore, they had reached this whole state of frenzy and unrestrained savagery—not only these two men themselves, Paul and Jacob,
but also the factions following each of them—all Syria and the remaining regions were now divided, split apart, thrown into confusion, and bewildered.
Some of them agreed with and accepted Jacob and everything he had done in Alexandria, while others attached themselves to Paul's party,
rejecting Jacob and everything he had done in Alexandria, criticizing him and saying that he had done everything contrary to canonical order,
especially the great monasteries and the rest. While these things held sway everywhere in such a beastlike, savage, and disorderly manner,
Paul himself continually sent messages to Jacob through many people: “Why has all this turmoil arisen in God's church?
Let us come together, and let the matters between us be examined according to the canons and the law.
If I am condemned by the canons, I will accept three penalties for every single sentence and canonical penalty.
And if the guilt instead rests with you, even then I will accept the penalty in your place.”
But those surrounding the innocent old man Jacob would not let him yield at all and agree to see Paul and speak with him.
For they knew that they could not stand against him, and they knew that with his very first word he would rightly condemn them.
But Jacob said, “I have agreed with and accepted the Alexandrians, and I have established unity with them in writing.”
And I do not turn away from them. Without them, he does not see me, nor do I see him.
For Mundhir son of Harith, king of the Arabs, a faithful, zealous, and diligent man,
had long been working hard and appealing to both parties to cease their anger and fighting,
to approach one another, talk, and make peace with one another. But Jacob’s followers would not listen to him.
Paul himself was appealing both to Mundhir and to many others for the matters stirred up among them by Satan to be investigated and examined.
For a long time, ever since the days of his father Harith, they had regarded the elder Jacob as a great man, and later they had also come to regard Paul in this way.
But when they reached this degree of deceit, brutality, and division against one another, and Jacob’s party would not agree to come to terms,
division then arose among all the Arab forces as well. Many of them were scandalized; some followed Paul, and others followed Jacob.
Because of the strife and turmoil that prevailed everywhere, especially throughout Syria, Longinus and his companions, together with Theodore, who had become patriarch from among them,
went to the land of Egypt and from there came down to the eastern regions of Syria, to Paul’s followers,
so that together they could discuss the dispute with Jacob’s followers and, if possible, resolve the quarrel and the evil that the Evil One had stirred up among them.
Theodore remained quietly in the city of Tyre, while Longinus went down as far as the camp of the house of Harith son of Jabala, to Mundhir son of Harith.
When he had conversed with him and carefully explained the whole truth to him, King Mundhir again worked to bring them together and reconcile them.
But Jacob’s followers would not listen to him at all. Eventually, however, they held a gathering at the monastery of Mar Hanina in the desert:
a considerable number of Jacob’s party, with Jacob himself among them, and one of the bishops, named John, who resided in that monastery and belonged to it.
A deceitful message was sent to Longinus and his companions: “Since the elder Mar Jacob has come here and wishes to speak with you, set out quickly and come here.
The three of us—you, he, and I—will be alone together, and we will talk so that we may resolve the quarrel and put an end to the turmoil.”
When Longinus received a letter of this kind, he gladly got up and set out with others, and they arrived there.
When they entered, they took him and brought him in, placing him in the middle of a considerable crowd of monks, laypeople, lawyers, legal advocates, and their officials [?], and the rest.
When Longinus saw the [?], he said to John, the very man who had invited him, “What is this deception you have practiced on me?
You wrote me a lie: ‘The elder is here alone; come, so that the three of us can talk.’ Where is the elder, and what is this crowd?”
When he said this, one of the monks produced a written accusation against him and said, “Take this, read it, and give an answer to it.”
But he replied, “Since I have been invited through deceit and lies, I will neither read it nor give an answer to anyone.”
Then, when he tried to leave, they laid hands on him and held him, saying, “You will not leave without reading it.
Otherwise, we will read it ourselves, and you must listen.” When they began to read, he put his fingers in both ears so that he would not hear.
When they began dragging him this way and that, he began shouting, “Help! I have a king! Why am I being treacherously killed?”
When a disturbance broke out, a quarrel flared up, and a disorderly uproar arose there, the disaster of murder very nearly occurred.
Then, while shouting for help, he tore himself free and got out from among them. He escaped from their hands and fled without seeing Jacob.
And many such evils, through the manifest activity of demons, everywhere among them, in every
against one another, unceasingly and senselessly, he rejoiced and exulted with all his dark demons in the destruction and turmoil
of the believers. These things deserved lamentation and the bitter pain of sobbing,
which at this time arose among the believers in the church of God through the envy and activity of the devil, and were being committed unceasingly by both sides.
Thus these great and renowned monasteries in the West and the East became divided, split apart, and thrown into turmoil.
They grew bold in fighting and battling against one another, and would grow still bolder, until boundless evil would be practiced among them,
murders would occur, and many would be arrested by the judges and taken to great Antioch, bound in irons and shackled with chains.
They would be thrown into prison, and the honorable habit, which had not been preserved honorably, would be despised and mocked by pagans, Jews, and heretics,
as they were bound in irons, shackled with chains, brought to court, and required to give accounts like murderers:
elderly monks with long beards and trailing robes, put in collars, standing before judges and being questioned about murders.
Who would not tremble, beat his breast, and howl over these calamities, mourning like a jackal and making lamentation like an ostrich,
over the salt that had not only lost its flavor but had also become rotten and been rejected, and was thus thrown outside and trampled by people?
As for the others who had split into opposing factions, one faction from each group remained in the monasteries themselves.
The other faction, which left, would go and take possession of a place, naming the place they occupied after the monastery from which they had departed.
They continually and thoughtlessly prepared themselves for deadly conflict against one another.
There was also a great assembly of many heads of monasteries, along with many other assemblies that had previously taken place in various locations,
and also this later assembly, when they deliberated and prepared themselves against Paul’s party. They appointed three men from among themselves who were bold and ready for battle.

They gave them a written commission on their behalf and sent them to the elder Jacob and the others with him, stirring them up, preparing them, and urging them on through the document they had composed.
We would have included this document too, were it not for its length. It demanded that they take vigorous action and appoint a patriarch for themselves in place of Paul.
They also asked them what they would decide concerning the ordinations Paul had performed, and also concerning the Tritheists and the rest. The elder had himself also undertaken this very matter.
He gave orders, and an assembly was held at the monastery of Mar Hanina. When they began discussing the matters, some of the bishops would not agree,
saying, “Paul the patriarch is alive and has not been condemned under the canons. How can we now talk like senseless fools?”
appoint another patriarch while he was still alive, and come under canonical censure. And so, when they did not agree, he called it off and dissolved the assembly.
Then, after they had been prevented from appointing a patriarch, the blessed Jacob was suddenly seized by an idea.
Taking bishops and eight others with him, he hurried off toward Alexandria.
Many people formed various opinions about him. Some thought that he was going there to appoint a patriarch together with Damian, who was there.
Others said that he was going to establish unity with Paul's followers.
Since he concealed his thoughts from everyone, the purpose of his undertaking was not known for certain.
But God, from whose eyes nothing is hidden, and who looks to the help of his creation—while they were traveling along the road,
they reached the great monastery on the border of Egypt called the Monastery of Cassian. There, as is reported, one of the bishops accompanying him suddenly died.
He had been the abbot of the monastery of Qartmin. The old man rose and offered the Eucharist for him, in his memory.
Then there was also his syncellus, Sergius, who was said to have become a bishop himself.
He suddenly fell ill and died. Afterward, the old man himself also fell ill for three days and died.
Then, after him, his attendant died as well. All these suddenly died, one after another, within twelve days.
This left people in astonishment, great uncertainty, and conflicting thoughts.
When this became known to the Alexandrians, Damian and the others hurried there after the old man's death. They wanted to take his body, but the monks of that monastery would not allow it.
Astonishment and amazement seized them over everything that had happened: how the blessed Jacob and his companions had suddenly been snatched away.
Many were reasoning within themselves that perhaps he had devised something improper, and was going to stir up still greater turmoil in the church,
or was planning to appoint a patriarch, and God had restrained him so that the soul of that man of God would not be lost.
Because the death of the blessed Jacob and his companions had been so sudden, those who had no concern for the harm to their own souls did not refrain from saying
that some of Paul's followers had gone out at his command and lain in wait for Father Jacob on the road, and had beaten them with clubs
and pelted them with stones, and that this was how he had gone on to die in Egypt. This was not merely a lie, but a very wicked one.
For, as though eager to add to the harm to their own souls and to make the scandal greater, they spread the story everywhere,
so as to unsettle many and cause them to stumble, and to wound the consciences of the faithful, intending, as they thought, to bring others down and enlarge their own faction.
They were neither disturbed nor grieved at the loss and ruin of their own souls, behaving so recklessly through such slanderous accusations of murder, without any fear of God.
At this same time, three envoys—the patrician Theodore, and John and Peter, the consuls—
were more devoted than anyone else to Patriarch Paul and fought on his behalf—that is, these consuls.
To such an extent that they were more eager to hold gatherings every day and speak on his behalf than to attend to all public affairs, so to speak.
Abba Jacob himself also went to them with many others, and things were said among them that exceed the bounds of a narrative and the limits of a book.
Neither side could persuade the other. And so, in distress, the two sides broke up and went away from one another.
Besides this, in every city they entered, they raised the same question again.
And because, for the most part, throughout all the regions east of the Euphrates, and even as far as Persia,
they supported the blessed Jacob rather than Paul, they were not persuaded at all and did not yield to the envoys.
And so they came up and arrived here in the imperial city, offended and reviling all the Easterners.
Now all the tribes of the Arabs had supported the blessed Jacob from the beginning.
But even during the lifetime of the elder al-Harith, Paul used to go there and take refuge with them, and they were edified by him too, because of his orderly conduct, humility, and teaching.
This was even more so after al-Harith’s death, when both sides met among them and received one another lovingly.
There, in the Arab camp itself, they all supported both men, Paul and Jacob.
But in the end, when Satan stirred up discord between them, all the Arabs were distressed.
Especially their king al-Mundhir, together with his brothers, his sons, and the others, pleaded with the elder Jacob
that they should draw near to one another and unite. But he would not be persuaded by them to receive Paul and unite with him, using the Alexandrians as his excuse.
He said, “If they do not receive him, neither will I receive him.” And so all the Arabs were offended and distressed.
Whenever Paul went to them, they received him and took communion from him. And whenever Jacob came, they did the same.
This continued until Jacob forbade them to take communion from Paul. And so they all remained offended, troubled, and bewildered until the death of the elder Jacob.
After his death, most of them followed him. Some followed Paul’s party, while others continued to receive both.
They were all alike grieved and troubled over this alien division and dispute that had arisen among them.
Especially he himself, and especially al-Mundhir their king, who continually pleaded with both sides to make peace with one another.
But envy, hatred, and hostility, coming from Satan and from those who advised both sides according to his will, did not allow them to find relief and make peace again, even until death.
And so, while the elder Jacob was still engaged in this conflict and had directed his journey toward Alexandria, God, who knows everything,
foreseeing what would benefit him, appointed his end on the road, as we have already related many times above.
Again, when accusations were made in many letters by John the Chalcedonian, bishop of Alexandria, against the orthodox clergy,
an order was issued, and they were arrested and brought up to the imperial city. They arrived in the month of May in the year eight hundred and ninety.
So when they went to Eutychius the patriarch, he treated them arrogantly and sent word to them outside:
“Since, on that previous occasion when I released you, you promised me that you would receive communion, go in now and receive communion.
Then you may come in to me and see me.” When they heard this, they sent word to him: “We did not promise you that we would receive communion
unless the Council of Chalcedon was rejected.” Then he became angry with them and gave orders, and they went away, were separated, and were [?] in monasteries.
Theodosius, the head of the church of Alexandria, was confined in the monastery of Beth-Salentaria. After they confined him, he fell ill and died at a good old age,
and all the Alexandrians grieved deeply over him, especially those who were confined.
This happened after they had once been summoned and had gone in for a debate with Eutychius the patriarch.
They said to him, “We will not speak with you unless the emperor or the senate acts as mediator.”
After much had happened, they were sent back to those monasteries, each to the place where he had been confined.
While they were again waiting to be summoned and to go in for a debate, their leader died, as has been said.
Even now, they are all confined in those monasteries and carefully guarded.
Meanwhile, the furnace of the Babylonians was being heated still more fiercely and blazing between these two parties, the followers of Paul and the followers of Jacob,
through flimsy pretexts, empty suppositions, and the agitation of certain people who, driven by envy and longstanding hatred,
were stirring up trouble and disturbing the pure and weary soul of the aged Jacob, so that he would enter into opposition against Paul.
Insults and abuse, beyond every limit and all proper order, without restraint and without the checks imposed by the fear of God,
were being hurled at one another by both parties—not only during the lifetime of the aged Jacob, but even after God's will had been fulfilled concerning him
and he had escaped this oppressive and troubled life and departed from the world. These same things, with further additions and mutual anathemas,
were being savagely stirred up and set in motion everywhere, in every region and every province, in the East and in the West,
until, as it is written, “We became a reproach to our neighbors, a mockery and a derision to those around us.”
For when the illustrious patrician Mundhir was summoned and went up to the emperor and was received with great honor,
he clothed himself in courageous and God-fearing zeal against all these evils that he saw being committed
against one another by people who shared the same faith and communion. Then he gathered both parties together
and began to rebuke, admonish, and reproach them for all these evils, divisions, and disputes that had arisen among them.
He advised them to abandon their divisions, stop fighting and quarreling, and make peace with one another,
especially because they shared the same faith.
For from the very beginning Paul had been working, advising, and urging the individuals Paul and Jacob to make peace with one another and live in love.
The journey up of the illustrious Mundhir took place in the year eight hundred and ninety-one, on the eighth of the month of February. He was received with great ceremony and boundless honor
by the merciful Emperor Tiberius, who honored him with distinctions, great gifts, and royal presents.
He did everything he wanted for him and gave him everything he requested. He also took both his sons into his service and deemed him worthy of the royal crown.
When, therefore, the victorious Mundhir had accomplished everything he wanted with the emperor,
he convened an assembly of the prominent men of both parties, together with the Alexandrians, on the second day of March of that same year.
He urged them to make peace with one another and to put an end to and extinguish everything that Satan had stirred up among them.
Many things beyond recounting were raised and discussed among them, now not by two parties but by three:
the followers of Jacob, the followers of Paul, and also the Alexandrians, addressing one another, with our humble selves also present among them.
Since there were many discerning men in both parties, and they were deeply distressed over everything that the troublemakers
among those three parties already mentioned were doing deceitfully and brutally, [?],
and they welcomed peace and the ending of all these evils, they all came together as one and gave pledges that there would be unity among them.
An arrangement began to take shape, so that all the hostilities Satan had stirred up among them might be quieted, examined, and brought to an end.
Everyone agreed to this, and a document was drawn up among them concerning unity and the ending and abolition of all the divisions and disputes that had arisen among them,
and providing that all the archbishops, bishops, clergy, monks of all the monasteries, and laypeople who had been divided should accept one another,
and that all together they should enter into unity with one another without dispute. Thus a prayer for union was offered by the priests of both parties and also by the Alexandrians.
Unity came about, and everyone thanked God for driving the Evil One from their midst, together with everything that belonged to him and came from him.
Everyone gave a pledge that he would take care to bring all the members of his party who were physically absent into this union that had been established.
But there were some troublemakers and agitators who, filled with the filth of the wicked one, were very angry and did not rejoice at the peace that had come about.
Since the gathering of the assemblies of leaders and prominent men had taken place in the presence of King Mundhir,
and had not required the attendance of the entire body of the people, especially because the whole body had not been considered and summoned,
some people turned to opposition and to undoing and abolishing what had happened. They gathered, drew up [?], wrote, and stirred up unrest.
Throughout Syria and in Alexandria they stirred up many people to maintain their faction, not to join together, and not to accept what had taken place.
This delighted Satan and all his black demons. The assembly, however, was dismissed in peace and joy,
with everyone acknowledging the kindness of God and also that of the victorious Mundhir.
Before the events we have just related, this Damian had irregularly become pope in Alexandria after Peter; he too became a cause of conflict, division, and strife.
Thus Damian too, like that man, was shown to stand outside all church order, as an undisciplined man lacking sense.
He conceived a vain and senseless plan and went to Syria to appoint and install a patriarch in Antioch,
in place of Paul while he was still alive, and in violation of every canonical boundary—just as he himself and his predecessor had come to office.
For they had come after another man had already been appointed and given the title, namely Theodore, who had written synodical letters to Alexandria.
But the Alexandrians acted presumptuously and, stirred by a surge of anger, behaved savagely and barbarously and appointed a certain Peter, a deacon, a simple and uneducated man.
They acted in his name as they pleased, so that there were now two patriarchs on one throne at the same time.
Consequently, many called Peter and Damian, his successor, adulterers who had entered and committed adultery with another man's wife.
So Damian planned to cover up the disgrace he suffered from everyone because he and his predecessor had come to office while Theodore, who preceded Peter, was still alive.
Damian therefore devised this scheme: to appoint another man over Paul in Syria too, while Paul was still alive, so that a parallel to their own disgrace might be found.
When he went out and summoned the bishops of Syria, he urged them to agree with him and appoint a patriarch in Antioch.
Some of the bishops raised objections on canonical grounds, saying, “Since Paul has not been summoned, tried, convicted of wrongdoing, condemned, and canonically deposed,
we will not agree to appoint another man over him. We would not only be condemned under the canons, but also excommunicated.”
Others, however, sided with Damian and agreed with him to appoint another patriarch.
When they pressured one or two men to accept appointment, these men likewise raised objections, each saying, “While the man is alive,
and has not been canonically summoned, tried, condemned, and deposed, I will not take office and be elevated above him, perhaps only to be deposed myself in the end.”
Finally they found a certain worthless man like themselves, named Severus. Damian took him along with two other bishops,
and they entered Antioch by night. They secretly sent word to the caretaker of the church called the Cassian Church
and promised to give him eighteen gold coins if he would open it for them, so that they could enter by night and ordain him there.
When the caretaker accepted the arrangement and gave them his word, they felt confident and prepared to enter by night and carry out their wishes.
Some people learned of the scheme they were preparing to carry out. They immediately went and informed the city's patriarch, who at once sent men to arrest them.
They surrounded the house on every side, entered, and arrested three monks among them.

Damian hurried away, and the bishops and the rest of his companions went down into the hollow beneath the house, that is, the cesspit. Through the opening where the cesspit emptied, beneath the latrines,
with their whole bodies and all their clothing soaked, smeared, and rolled in all the filth of that cesspit, and wallowing in it,
they got out, escaped, and fled without being arrested: Damian, Sergius the Anphitor—that is, the [?]—George Sarcabinus, and the bishops with him.
And what they had been preparing to do to the others—being more ashamed of their [?] among the thorns than of his frustrating their schemes.
As for the monks who had been arrested, they brought them before the patriarch. He gave orders, and they were suspended and brutally tortured.
They confessed everything they had been preparing to do. When they confessed concerning Damian and his companions, orders were sent everywhere for their arrest, but they escaped and were not caught.
Those who had been arrested also confessed concerning the sacristan. He came and confessed, and he suffered even greater tortures than they did and was stripped of his possessions.
When Damian fled, he secretly went up to Constantinople, before that gathering for unity took place.
Through the efforts of people who wanted peace, he came at night to the illustrious Mundhir, and they spoke with one another.
He promised that he would work for peace, seek it, and agree to it. After being seen by only a few people, he fled and departed for Alexandria.
For, as has been said, he also appointed bishops in the imperial city.
Now, as for the Alexandrian clergy, after the gathering had taken place and dispersed, since they were being held by order together with some prominent laypeople,
because of the affair concerning the faith in the imperial city, the illustrious Mundhir went in and petitioned the merciful Emperor Tiberius on their behalf, and he released them.
An order was issued for them, and he also did great things for them in recognition of the unity they had established.
So they departed joyfully, boarded a ship, and went to their own city. After this, the illustrious Mundhir himself asked that he too be allowed to leave.
He also petitioned the merciful emperor concerning peace for the church and an end to the persecution of Christians.
He promised him under oath that, if he could obtain a respite from the wars, he would immediately establish peace. With this promise, he allowed him to leave with great honors,
and royal gifts of much gold and silver, splendid clothing, saddles, many gold [?], and weapons.
Along with all these things, he also bestowed a royal crown on him. This had never happened before, nor had it been granted to any of the Arab kings before him.
They had only been permitted to wear a circlet. Thus he was allowed to leave and departed with pomp and great joy.
When he reached Antioch, he was welcomed there too. Trusting in the emperor’s goodwill, his promises, and his oaths concerning the unity of the church,
he informed the patriarch of the city and the others that the emperor had ordered the persecution to stop.
The patriarch immediately gave orders, and letters were written to all the provincial governors, directing that no one should dare to carry out persecution,
because the emperor had given orders and wished to establish peace. Thus the persecution stopped for a short time. But when this
became known to the believers in two natures in the imperial city, they were stirred to great anger against Mundhir. Without delay, they went in and accused him bitterly before the emperor.
But the God-loving emperor would not listen to them. Now, while Mundhir himself was on the road, his enemies, the Arabs allied with the Persians, thought
that he was spending a long time in the imperial city. Seeing that he was far away, the Arabs and Persians gathered and headed toward his territory and his land, against his sons and brothers,
to fall upon them, devastate their land, and take them captive. As they prepared to confront one another, Mundhir himself suddenly arrived.
Suddenly, when they were not expecting it, he came out against them, fell upon them, and struck them down until he had finished them off. Only a few of them fled and escaped his sword.
So he returned rejoicing and brought back all their plunder. He won greater acclaim than anyone else, and his name was greatly praised.
But the zealous Damian the Syrian, who happened to be in Alexandria at that time—the same man mentioned above—
when he arrived in Alexandria and was reproached by some people over Paul, then, as though seeking to please people rather than God,
or to work for the peace of the church, went back on his word and broke his promises to the illustrious Mundhir
and to the rest of the believers from both sides who had appealed to him. He turned around and became Paul's opponent.
He wrote condemnations, insults, and harsh abuse against him. He was not content merely to employ these himself,
but also wrote them all in an encyclical letter—that is, a circular letter—and sent it to Syria and everywhere within his jurisdiction and outside it.
His letters were delivered especially to disruptive and savage men, men yoked to Satan, running and working alongside him,
who did not gather with Christ but, running in the opposite direction, scattered far and wide. These men zealously stirred up agitation and turmoil,
created divisions, provoked quarrels, and caused disputes, conflicts, abuse, and everything that pleases the devil, even more than before.
He also brought about these deeds of his—and perhaps it is not improper to say Satan's as well—among the clergy who had been present at that assembly for union held in the imperial capital,
so that they too, along with him, would lie to the Holy Spirit and go back on their word after they had received relief and been released
and had escaped their distress through Mundhir's care, because they had promised unity before him and a large gathering and had united.
They had also put this in writing under their own names. It was precisely because of this that they had been released and had come out of custody and prison.
But they turned back and acted falsely like their fathers—that is, like their father Damian, who was worthy of them, and they of him.
Thus, when King Mundhir returned from fighting his enemies
and learned of their change and their turning from truth to boundless falsehood, he was distressed and grieved.
At the same time, he was astonished and especially appalled by Damian's encyclical letters, which were not far removed from every kind of wickedness.
So Mundhir did not neglect to write to each of them by name, reminding them and reproaching them for their false dealing with God, with him, and with the whole church.
But because of their shame and their dishonesty, they could neither accept his letters nor write him a reply. And so he was brought to grief,
while, especially for these reasons, the furnace of wrath was being stoked, blazing and flaring up
against the whole church of the believers. There was a still greater increase in divisions, quarrels, insults, abuse, and conflicts,
which continually blazed fiercely between the two sides, without restraint and without fear of righteous judgment.
So, while the letters of the powerful Damian of Alexandria were circulating in the East and he was giving disruptive men an opportunity,
Some men acted presumptuously, so that, contrary to the proper order, a second patriarch bearing the title of Antioch—although the first had not been shown to have been canonically condemned—
would be appointed by them over him, making the affair a laughingstock and an object of ridicule to mockers, who said:
“It was necessary for two patriarchs to bear that title in Antioch, just as there are three in Alexandria besides the patriarch of the Synodites, so that they would not reproach one another!”
Thus everything among the faithful was being conducted perversely, oppressively, and confusedly, without order, because of their disputes.
For in the year eight hundred and ninety and eighty-two [?], the bishops, abbots, and clergy of the blessed Jacob,
after his death, arrived at this decision: they appointed and installed as patriarch a young layman named Peter,
the son of Paul, from the city of Callinicum. The blessed Jacob himself, while still alive, had twice wanted to appoint this man.
Others, too, after the blessed man's death, had again wanted to appoint him. But he would not be persuaded and refused, saying:
“I will not agree to be placed over a man who has not been canonically summoned, condemned, and lawfully deposed, and in the end be excommunicated and cast out of the church myself.”
Now, however, he was finally persuaded. As is reported, he went to Alexandria and was ordained by Damian and the others,
and was named patriarch of Antioch over Paul, although Paul was still alive and had not been condemned and removed by a synod.
The church of the faithful was in this state of corruption and confusion, brought about entirely through the activity of the Accuser and pleasing to him.
After this, all the abbots who had agreed to this action took counsel together and assembled.
They all drew up letters bearing their own signatures to John, bishop of Ephesus, who was residing in the imperial city,
inviting him into unity and communion with themselves and with the patriarch they had appointed, although they did not even tell him plainly what the man's name was.
Because he maintained a position between the two parties, he was reproached equally by both,

while he mourned and grieved over the breach that had arisen between them through the envy and hatred of the Alexandrians, and over the divisions and disputes throughout the whole church of the faithful.
He advised and admonished them and solemnly warned them, while absolutely refusing to allow himself to be drawn into standing with one party and fighting against the other.

When he received these letters, he was moved to tears and bitter sorrow over this further increase in the corruption and confusion of the church of the faithful, and he was not even inclined to write.
A year earlier, too, they had drawn up other letters inviting him to stand with them, as though in battle, against the other party.
He had neglected to send them a reply. They reproached him for this in their letter, and for this reason he was compelled to write them an answer containing a stern rebuke,
asking how, when they themselves had acted entirely outside canonical order in what they had done, they could invite him into union and communion.
Were it not for their great length and the bulk of their contents, we would have included here both the letters they all sent him and his letters to them.
Let this, then, be known to both parties, who, through the activity of a spirit of hostility, acted presumptuously against one another,
and to everyone else: that these accounts by our humble self of what was stirred up and done among them, and which we have brought into a written record,
We have set this down to uphold the truth, reproaching and rebuking both sides equally. We have not written these things to side with some people against others,
even if we seem, here and there, to direct our criticisms and accusations at each side in turn.
This concerns the hostility and disorder with which they have treated one another savagely and unlawfully.
We mourn and grieve over these things, and our eyes stream with tears
over the offenses, destruction, schisms, quarrels, divisions, disputes, insults, and abuse that have arisen and been carried on among us, to the murderer's delight.
We too have been compelled to speak out against these things by the anguish of our hearts, grieving
that although we are partners and fellow believers, we have been driven, for certain unworthy reasons,
to plunge recklessly and without restraint into all these evils. We had also written about these things personally to the individuals concerned from the beginning,
and especially to the hardworking elder Jacob, until the day of his death, in these terms: “I, insignificant as I am, follow the laws of the church,
and since I see no offense against the faith, I withdraw neither from communion with you nor from communion with Paul.
For you are engaged in conflict with one another over canonical accusations that may be either true or false.
As for the other things that have been done or are being done among you in a disorderly and improper way, outside the boundaries of the church,
whether you have resorted to excommunication and uncanonical deposition against Paul's party, or Paul himself has done so against you or against the Alexandrians,
or the Alexandrians have acted against you or against Paul outside the order or bounds of the canons, I have no share or involvement whatsoever in any of these unlawful acts,
until they have all been judged, examined, and established through canonical judgment and lawful investigation before a synod,
so that it becomes known which acts conform to and agree with the laws of the church, and which are far removed and alien from proper order.”
These things, then, are found written personally in more than ten of my letters to the blessed Jacob during his lifetime, and to the others.
Although these things cause me great sorrow and unceasing pain in my heart, I have borne blame and even hostility from both sides.
I call as my witness the one who examines the kidneys and the heart: I have not aligned myself with one side against the other, but have remained in the middle until now,
distressed, groaning, and grieving over all these evils that have occurred through the activity of the one who asked to sift us like wheat.
But Paul himself, the patriarch of these evil days, when he saw storms rising on every side,
went away to live in hiding in a cave, as is reported, in the rugged mountains of Isauria. He has now been there for four years.
He has shown himself to no one except the few who attend to his affairs. He writes to no one and receives letters from no one.
As a result, many have grumbled against him and criticized him for hiding himself away like this and neglecting all this conflict that is raging everywhere on his account.
He did not even appear or speak when some energetic men in Syria appointed another man in his place. Instead, he remains in silence and hiding to this very hour.
Now Theodore, whom we mentioned above as having been made patriarch in Alexandria by Longinus and the others, according to his custom, since he had formerly been a monk,
continued to live quietly in Alexandria itself, openly occupying a monastery and residing there. Many people gathered around him.
Because of his humility and quietness, no one harassed him or drove him out of the city, even though he was opposed to Damian, who succeeded Peter.

Instead, they left him alone because of his gentleness and quietness, and because he used to say, “As for me, it does not matter to me. Let there be no disturbance or division in the church on my account.”
After some time, however, he became resentful toward Paul and Longinus and their associates, because Paul had hidden himself away and neglected everything,
while Longinus, in turn, had been sent farther inland, beyond the people of the Nobatae, among whom he had been living,
to another great people, many stages farther inland, whom the Greeks call the Alodians, and who are thought to be Ethiopians.
God helped him, and he spoke to their king, all his nobles, and all the peoples under his rule. We also set down accounts of these events in their proper order.
But now let us bring the narrative back to its original subject, the account of Theodore that we began to write.
Let us return, since, when we wanted to explain what occupied Paul and Longinus, the narrative strayed and turned to another subject.
Theodore, then, became distressed and troubled over them, saying, “They came and plunged me into trouble and brought me out of the desert,
and now they have abandoned and neglected me. They have not even asked whether I am alive or dead.” Indeed, he wrote many letters of complaint,
to Syria, to us as well, and to many people in the imperial city. These letters were full of accusations, grumbling, and complaints.
He sent them through a certain blessed stylite who had been with him in the desert, a virtuous man, and another man who accompanied him, a priest named George.

We received these men with their letters and comforted them at length. We also wrote accusations against Paul and his associates on their account. Then a fierce persecution overtook us, and we were seized.
They left the city, and we did not see them again. Later he himself wrote to us with this same complaint,
the reasons for which we did not think it right to include in the written record, but rather to cover them in silence and pass over them.
Now, through the arrival of the blessed Julian, who, as we also explained above, through the efforts of the late Empress Theodora,
had previously been sent to the great people called the Nobatae, he made disciples of their king and his nobles,
and of most of the peoples under his rule, within two years. He then departed from there, entrusting that whole people to a certain Bishop Theodore, a very elderly man,
who lived in the city called Philae, which is in the inner Thebaid, on the border of the country just mentioned.
This bishop would go in, visit them, instruct them, and return to his city.
They continued like this for about eighteen years, more or less, until Longinus changed his appearance and went in among them,
and once again made disciples, instructed and taught them, and baptized the rest of those among them who remained unbaptized.
He spent six years among them. Envoys were also sent by their king and came to the imperial city,
They spent a long time in their company, praising, exalting, and thanking Longinus greatly.
For when the people of the Alodians learned about the conversion of these peoples, the Nobadians,
their king sent word to the king of the Nobadians to send him the bishop who had taught and baptized them, so that he might also instruct and baptize these people.
But when Longinus received letters from the Alexandrians, he quickly left for Roman territory and encountered all these trials described above, one after another.
Then afterward, with much labor and great hardship, the king there finally managed to send messengers, who took him and brought him to them.
The Alexandrians, prompted by Satan’s envy, were also trying to stir up that king and all his people and turn them against him, so that they would not receive him.
They also sent him the decree of Longinus’s deposition, which they had carried out unjustly, contrary to the requirements of the canons. But they paid no attention to them and did not accept them.
They said, “We will receive no one else except our spiritual father, who gave us new birth through spiritual rebirth.
We consider everything his enemies say against him to be lies.” Thus they turned them away and did not receive them.
So when the Alexandrians learned that the king of the Alodians had sent a second delegation
to the king of the Nobadians, asking him to send Longinus, who had instructed them, they acted out of envy rather than zeal.
They sent messengers to that people to undermine Longinus, so that the people would accept and be instructed in the corruption and violation of church law that they themselves had committed.
They eagerly and diligently composed a letter to them against Longinus, neither fearing God nor giving thought to justice.
Drunk with envy and hatred, they did not take to heart that it was ungodly, toward a misguided and pagan people
who had asked to turn to Christianity and learn the fear of God, immediately, before anything necessary for their instruction,
to send them letters containing corruption, stumbling blocks, and insults from Christians against Christians.
But, as has been said, their minds were darkened and their understanding blinded, so that they did not comprehend.
Instead of instruction in the fear of God, they eagerly sought first to lay down hostility for these people as a foundation for stumbling.
They loaded and filled letters with accusations against Longinus and sent them to the people with two bishops from among those whom they had appointed contrary to church law,
and some others, writing: “Because we have learned that you asked for Longinus—Longinus [?], whom we learned was among the Nobadians [?]—to be sent to you to baptize you,
we have therefore sent two bishops and others to inform you that you must not be baptized by him.
For he is a heretic, and he has been deposed. He is not permitted to exercise the priestly office or to baptize anyone.”
Along with many other things, they wrote them corrupting words instead of exhortations for their instruction.
But the Lord brought Nabal’s punishment back upon his own head. As it is written, the nations that had not known the law of righteousness attained the law of righteousness,
and they became a law to themselves. But Israel, which pursued righteousness, did not attain it. Thus it was fulfilled in these people.
so that they would be rebuked and repudiated by the pagan people and would not be accepted, but would return dejected and ashamed.
They said these things to them: “We do not know who you are. We do not accept you, and we will not receive baptism from you.
Instead, we accept the man who baptized the people of the Nobades, and we will receive baptism from him. We do not accept the things you say against him.
For we see that you are his enemies and that you say these things against him out of envy.
Go away! Leave our country, lest you die a miserable death.” And so they left that place, without either they themselves
or anything they had said being accepted at all. This was through the action of God, who saw their crooked intentions and their hostile zeal.
Now when the king of the Alodians [?] sent envoys to the king of the Nobades,
asking him to send Bishop Longinus to instruct and baptize him and his people,
it became clearly apparent that, by God's grace, provision was being made for the conversion of that people.
The Lord stirred the spirit of Longinus to go and enter their country. And while they were thus [?] distressed over his departure from them,
the king, his nobles, and his leaders sent him off with men who knew the desert. But he and those with him fell ill.
And, as he reports in his letter, among the animals accompanying him in the desert, seventeen camels died from the scorching desert heat, along with the others.
Besides these things, there was also a people [?] and another kingdom between these two kingdoms, whose inhabitants are called the Makurites.

When their king learned that Longinus had set out on his journey, Satan, in his envy, stirred him to station guards at all the crossings of his kingdom—his kingdom—on every road, on every mountain, and in the plains,
as far as the Red Sea, to seize Longinus and obstruct the salvation of that great people, the Alodians.
Of the Alodians. And so God concealed him and blinded the eyes of those who were seeking to seize him. He passed among them and went on, and they did not see him.
When he reached the borders of the kingdom to which he was traveling and the king learned of it, he sent one of his nobles to meet him, as Longinus reports in his letter.
His name was Itiqia. He welcomed him and escorted him through the country with honor and great ceremony.
When he arrived, the king himself went out to meet him and welcomed him with great joy.
When he entered and spoke the word of God to him and all his nobles, they opened their minds and received it joyfully.
Within a few days they were instructed, and the king and all his nobles were baptized. Afterward, many of the people were baptized in succession.
And so, as that king was glad and rejoiced [?], he wrote a letter of thanks [?] to the king of the Nobades [?], which reads as follows [?].
“Your love is remembered, my lord and brother Orfiulo, for you have now shown yourself to be my true kinsman,
not only in body but also in spirit, since you sent here to me our common spiritual father.
He showed me the way of truth and the true light of Christ our God, and he baptized me, my nobles, and all my people.
And in everything the work of Christ is growing. I trust in the holy God that I too will take care to do what will give you relief.
And I will drive your enemies out of your country. For the enemy is not yours alone, but mine as well.
For your country is also mine, and your people are my people. So do not lose heart, but be courageous and strong.
For I do not neglect you or your country, especially now that I have become a Christian through the hands of my father, the holy Abba Longinus.
Since there is a need, prepare what is required for church worship for us. For I expect you to send these things to me with care.
And I myself will make the reply—your reply. But I did not wish to write down the day on which I celebrate the feast, lest [?] my letters be intercepted.
Only be free from anxiety, and be courageous and strong, because Christ is with us.
These things, then, were written by that new confessor, the king of the Alodians, to the king of the Nobadians.
And again, here is also a short excerpt from the letter that the blessed Longinus wrote from that country
and sent to the king of the Nobadians, asking him to send it [?] to Alexandria, which he also did. The passage from the letter reads as follows:
But so that I do not recount distressing things to you and make the letter too long, I have left all these matters aside,
and I write to tell you the second matter, which brings joy to all of you who are truly Christians and steadfast in the orthodox faith.
I rejoice, and I will rejoice with you all. You too, in the same way, rejoice, and rejoice with me.
For he who desires every person to live, and does not desire the death of a sinner like me, forgot all my sins
and remembered his own mercy and grace. He opened the door of his mercy to me and rescued me from those who were hunting my life.
He brought me through their midst and blinded their eyes, so that they did not see me. Yet we were not beyond his love for humanity and his discipline.
For everyone who was with my weak self fell ill, from the greatest to the least, with my humble self being the first to become ill.
Indeed, it was right that I should be disciplined first, since I am responsible for many sins and for the transgressions into which I have fallen.
Not only did we fall ill and despair of our deliverance, but even the animals with us were dying,
unable to endure the burning heat and thirst of the mountains and the foulness of the water. Seventeen of our camels died.
When the king of the Alodians learned that I had resolved to go to him, he sent one of his officials, whose name was Itika.
He brought me into his country with great ceremony. When we reached the riverbank, we boarded a boat.
When the king learned of this, he rejoiced. He himself came out to meet us and welcomed us with great joy.
By the grace of God, we instructed and baptized him, his nobles, and all his people. And the work of God grows every day.

But there are also some people from among the Aksumites who have fallen into the sickness of Julian's doctrine of an illusory appearance, and who say that Christ suffered in a body incapable of suffering and not subject to death.
We made the exact teaching of the faith known to them and required them to anathematize the heresy in writing, and we received them on the basis of a written declaration.
And again, after other matters: And so that all the provinces may learn and, rejoicing spiritually with you,
may offer thanksgiving and praise to our God, who loves humanity, for all these indescribable gifts of his,
and so that the fathers may take care to have bishops sent here who can labor and serve in this divine work, which is pleasing to God and to human beings,
in which they have confidence, and which is being well managed. For those who are hastening here for salvation number a thousand thousands, to the glory of Christ, the Savior of us all.
And believe me when I say that a merely human thought arose in me a little while ago: not to write to anyone.
But when I consider the danger facing those who make negligent use of these spiritual gifts, I have turned to this brief letter addressed to your spiritual love.
For I have not desired silver or gold or clothing, and God, who examines human hearts, is my witness.
He knows my circumstances: I lack my daily bread and even a leaf of greens, and I long even to see them with my own eyes.
It is enough for me to make this much known. These things, then, were written by the holy Longinus.
But excerpts from them were copied out [?] and sent from the country of the Alodians to the king of the Nobadians, with a letter asking him to send them to Alexandria.
When he finally received them, he sent his letters to Alexandria, to the patriarch Theodore, who had consecrated Longinus,
and the king himself also wrote him a letter describing the whole course of Longinus's journey and the remoteness of the country,
the trials and opposition that had arisen against him, and the help that had come to him through God's grace, together with the other things that he wrote about with wonder.
They are as follows. Letter of the king of the Nobadians to Theodore of Alexandria.
Before everything else, I greet you most warmly in Christ, blessed fathers.
I also think you should know this: seven months ago the king of the great people of the Alodians sent here,
that is, Ethiopia, of Ethiopia [?], and took my holy father, Bishop Longinus, to baptize him.
This indeed took place, as the king and that same holy father of mine wrote to me.
When I first spoke here to my father about this matter, he immediately accepted readily and willingly, and his blessedness promised to undertake it.
Every day he urged me on, saying, 'We must not neglect this undertaking, because it belongs to God.'

Because of the wicked schemes of the ruler between us, namely the king of the Makurites, I sent my holy father to the king of the Blemmyes, so that he might send him there by routes farther inland than his territory.
But the aforementioned Makurite—Makurite [?]—also learned of it and stationed his guards throughout every part of his kingdom, in the mountains and on the plains,
and as far as the Red Sea, seeking to seize my father in order to put an end to that good work of God, as my father wrote to me here.
He endured great hardship and bitter trials, both spiritual and bodily, in the country of the Blemmyes, of the Blemmyes [?]. Added to these were great distress and deprivation.
Yet even so, the wicked schemes of the adversary could not hold back my holy father's readiness for God's work.
Instead, the Lord our God himself made straight the roads and paths of my holy father, so that he could traverse long roads and pass difficult guard posts.
Although his baggage train [?] of camels and other animals was lost, God helped him, and he escaped and reached the country.
He was welcomed joyfully by the king and all the people. He made disciples of the king and everyone with him and baptized them, as is related in the letter he sent here.
Know this also: how closely God, the Lord of all, accompanied my father, and how he went in with him, so that you may marvel at the great wonder he performed for him.
When my maternal uncle the king and his fathers, the kings, used to send an embassy to that kingdom,
the envoy would remain there for eight or ten years, and only then would he return here.
But when my holy father entered that country, within two hundred days he sent us an embassy from that king,
whereas many of our earlier envoys never returned here at all.
And so as not to prolong the account in this letter, my father sent letters to me here for me to send on to you.
I have now sent them through his envoy. They contain everything that happened to him and everything he did.
These are the things his letter made known, which you too are to make known there.
For it is not fitting for Your Blessedness to conceal and neglect all these matters.
Rather, it is especially fitting for Your Holiness to help my holy father with your holy prayers.
We place this extract from the letter of the king of the Nobadians here to confirm the account, since in it he bears witness to the whole divine undertaking.
He also wrote two other letters on the subject. We have refrained from including these because of the length of the account.
And because the power of this whole undertaking and this divine activity is made known to everyone who reads these two letters, those of the bishop and the king,
we therefore thought it best not to expand the account of these things any further with words of our own.
Instead, with thanksgiving and wonder, let us recall, even now, in connection with these things, the saying of our Savior:
“Truly I tell you, this good news of the kingdom will be proclaimed among all nations, and then the end will come.”
These things thus took place with God's help in the year eight hundred and ninety-one, and we set them down as a memorial.
Now, we have already mentioned Paul's concealment according to what was believed at the time, since many thought that he was hiding in a cave in the mountains of Isauria.
But now, as the events that finally occurred make known and show, those who wish to investigate say
that during those four years when he was not seen and was thought to be hiding in the mountains of Isauria, he was actually hiding in the mountains of the imperial city.
Although we were living in that city, this was not made known or revealed to us until the very end of his life.
His confidants thought that his burial had been concealed from us, or from most people, and had been revealed to only three people.
But those deluded men had forgotten the Lord’s saying: “There is nothing hidden that will not be revealed.”
Theodore, who through Longinus had become bishop in Alexandria, had received no communication at all from Paul for these four years.
Although he had written to him many times, he had not even received an answer to his letters from him.
Moreover, Longinus had gone to those peoples who had become Christians in the interior of Ethiopia.
Theodore was left without consolation on any side, until he felt compelled to consider writing a circular letter to the whole of Paul’s party.
In it he complained and grumbled about him, because he had neglected him and treated him with such contempt. He sent it through two of his priests, who arrived in the imperial city.
When this became known to everyone, and especially when they heard the complaints and grumbling of these priests,
many were distressed and reproached him. They wrote to him where he was thought to be, but he was not found.
So, with much persuasion and encouragement, they were sent to the island of Cyprus, where some of his bishops were staying.
They then returned and came to Theodore, having accomplished nothing. This distressed him still further, so that in the end he himself set out and went to Cyprus.
For when Pope Theodore saw that he received no communication through either his letters or the people he sent,
he finally boarded a ship and went to the island of Cyprus, but did not find him. He did, however, find some of his bishops.
After many things had happened and disputes had arisen between them, and Paul had still not revealed himself to him, two bishops agreed to go with him to Alexandria.
So he returned, distressed, because he did not believe that Paul was not there or in Cilicia, yet Paul had not appeared to him. But, as finally became known,
throughout those four years when he was not seen, and people circulated reports that he was hiding in caves in the mountains of Cilicia and Isauria,
he was secretly hiding in the imperial city. This was known and disclosed to only a few people.
There his end overtook him, which we are also recording explicitly in our account of him.
For, as we explained above, during these four years, when Paul was thought to be hiding in the eastern regions,
he was on the mountain by the imperial city. At his death this was revealed and became known to everyone.
Those who looked after his affairs tried to conceal even his death, so that it would not become known, even though he was mortal.
For, as was said and also became known, he had gone up to the city with the knowledge of some of his followers,
and had been hiding with some of them throughout that entire period already mentioned. Suddenly he fell seriously ill,
and shortly afterward he died. Great consternation and an intense, terrible fear fell upon those
with whom he had been hiding, or who had known of it: [?] those in authority might hear of it, and they would be put in danger because of him.
And so they sent for and brought only three of the priests who recognized him, and demanded solemn oaths from them,
that they would not let people know that he was Patriarch Paul.
Instead, they instructed them that, if the matter attracted attention, they should say that a stranger named Christopher had come to this city and died.
This is what these three did. They took him away at night, covered up, and brought him to a convent of women for burial.
When the nuns heard this, they became alarmed and said, “We do not accept a dead man at night, in the dark,
when we do not know who he is, or whether this involves the blood of someone murdered, so that we might find ourselves in danger.”
But the men pleaded with them at length, saying, “He is a great and righteous man, and a stranger. Do not be afraid.”
When they had been persuaded to receive him, the men brought him in with his face covered.
While they were hurrying and bustling about to lower him into the pit, the nuns began to argue, saying, “If things really are as you say,
and your words are true, that this is a great and righteous man, let us perform the service over him according to the prescribed order.
Uncover his face so that we may see him, draw near, and receive a blessing from him. Then you may lower him into the grave.”
But they hurriedly bound him up and buried him, saying, “Let us lower him now and be on our way, for we are in a hurry.”
And so they buried him with the burial of a donkey, in a confused rush, and left. This caused those nuns to fall into great anxiety.
They numbered more than a hundred and fifty. From them spread reports of doubts and many conjectures,
not only in that city and in Syria, but also in Alexandria and everywhere else, as the matter became known. Paul’s death was being discussed everywhere,
while these men were still brazenly insisting and swearing that it was someone else who had died, and not Mar Paul, our patriarch.
There was much grumbling and agitation among all the orthodox people of the city who recognized him,
because the secret of his death had been revealed to three of them and concealed from the rest. In the end, many no longer remembered even him with affection,
especially when they learned that his arrival, his stay in the city, and his death had been concealed from them and revealed to only three of them.
Meanwhile, his confidants were still swearing with practiced deceit that Paul was not dead, but alive.
They did this, as they thought best, so that his opponents would not rejoice. And so this dispute continued for an entire year,
and his name was proclaimed as that of a living person in the diptychs of the living, supposedly to prevent his death from becoming known and confirmed, although everyone already knew.
Now, concerning the end and departure of these two blessed men—I mean Jacob and Paul—whose dispute and conflict with one another
caused a great schism and bitter division in the persecuted church of the faithful, anyone who reflects on it is left in great astonishment and dismay
at how disgracefully, suddenly, and obscurely they were taken from this life here and departed from this world.
Earlier, when the blessed Jacob, in the very heat of their quarrel and dispute,
had taken two other bishops with him, along with the rest of the monks, they hurried off at a rapid pace for Alexandria.
The reason for this journey of his was hidden from many, and many people had numerous ideas and a host of thoughts about it.

And because the one who alone cares for the welfare of his creation perhaps saw and knew that Jacob’s journey would benefit neither the church nor Jacob himself, he checked, hindered, and stopped his journey.
Some people spread a report about him and everyone with him that, after they had put out to sea and begun their voyage, a severe storm struck them,
and their ship sank, and they all died at sea, and their bodies were not found. This was not definitely established for people.
Others, however, who are eager to speak on his behalf, say that although a storm did indeed strike them,
their ship did not sink. Instead, they were driven ashore and landed in Egyptian territory, and entered a monastery in the desert called the Monastery of Cassian.
After they entered that monastery, they say, within three days the two bishops died first, and then the venerable Jacob himself,
and one other person from among his attendants—all four of them together,
one after another. But which of these accounts is true, God knows. We have not learned the exact truth of these matters.
Then, after about two or three years, what happened concerning Paul at his death was likewise confused and contrary to every rule of proper order,
like all the things of which we reported a little out of much in the preceding chapter—done in secret, or so those who did them thought.
What should we think and write about these things, except to cry out to God with the prophet in sorrow and sobbing, and say:
“Even if our sins testify against us, Lord, have mercy for your name’s sake, because your grace is great, and we have sinned against you.”
After the deaths of Jacob and Paul, then, these parties that had arisen from each of them began discussing unity with one another.
They did not gather to speak with one another properly, with an attitude of humility and fear of God, but arrogantly and deceitfully.
Each party thought that it was the head and its counterpart was subordinate, and that it was lofty, exalted, pure, and free from all blame; and it sought to subdue and subject its counterpart.
Each party blamed the other for all these evils, rifts, and divisions.
Each exalted itself over the other, and each was making moves to receive the other as repentant toward itself and bring it into submission,
according to the teaching and cunning of the devil, who schemed and set them against one another. And so their undertaking did not succeed.
This Peter, who had been irregularly forced forward by some people and had become patriarch in Syria while Paul was still alive,
was reproached first by his own conscience and then by many people, because he had uncanonically occupied another man’s throne while that man was still physically alive.
When at last the two parties began discussing union with one another, and the whole party of Paul was disputing against Peter
because he had taken a position over Paul while Paul was alive, he began to say—whether as a pretext, or sincerely, or with deceitful cunning:
“Let there be no dispute on my account,” he said. “I ask to be excused, and I will go and live quietly. Let the parties unite with one another.
Let them appoint someone else who is acceptable to both parties, and let there be unity between them.”
Many were pleased with what he was saying, since his words bore an appearance of humility and peace,
but others spoke reproachfully against him and even rebuked him to his face, saying,
“You are saying these things deceitfully and cunningly, not sincerely from a pure heart,
but because you know that your supporters, who appointed you, will not let you go. Besides, you are making Alexandria your excuse.”
When he heard these things, along with much else, from many people, in order to show that he was indeed sincerely striving for unity,
he got up, took some of his supporters, and entered Alexandria, ostensibly to urge them toward unity with Damian, whom they too had appointed as their head.
Many matters were raised and discussed between them, and, in accordance with the apostolic saying quoted above,
“whether in pretense or in truth,” he was seen to speak and argue at length about unity. But they opposed him and did not accept what he said.
Thus, as was to be expected, he left there in disgrace. Some thought that this had been skillfully and strategically arranged.
For God, who examines the mind and heart, knows the truth of these things.
Indeed, because they departed from there on peaceful terms with one another, it was suspected that he had gone in and come out under a pretense.
For even afterward he persisted in the dispute, saying, “I will do nothing without the Alexandrians.”
After all these things, then, the assemblies of both parties—that is, the bishops, monks, and the rest—
spent a certain period, about a whole year, contending and meeting in various places,
going back and forth, sending messages to one another, and making burdensome and harsh demands on one another.
As we explained above, they made demands on one another arrogantly and imperiously, rather than fraternally and lovingly,
first through individuals from each side, and afterward through writings directed against one another. And once matters had been settled and established,
some disruptive and contentious people appeared from their own ranks and among them, as well as others who obstructed peace.
They stirred up discord between the parties, and they returned to complete hostility toward one another and tore up the documents they had drawn up between them.
They began circulating writings against one another to the imperial capital, the East, and the West. Each party placed itself among the innocent,
while pursuing the other with insults and everything tending toward condemnation, together with abuse and fabricated falsehoods.
They all also resorted to hostile writings against one another and harsh accusations,
so that these were sent, in the form of records of proceedings, both to us and to many people in the imperial capital.
Not only did they fail to be messengers of peace toward one another, but they continued for the time being in every kind of division, schism, strife, and mutual hostility,
and in all this turmoil that gives satisfaction to Satan, who asked to sift us like wheat.
Thus, through the impetuousness and disorderly conduct of both parties, who approached one another without the discernment that comes from the fear of God,
he also gained strength. And now he leaps and rejoices with all the herds and hordes of his demons, taking his ease in what is happening between the two parties.
These things have continued from their beginning until now, in the year eight hundred and ninety-six.
In this year, a little of the boundless extent of all these boundless troubles was recorded.
The fourth book of the Ecclesiastical History is finished. It contains sixty-one chapters.
Chapters of the fifth book of the Ecclesiastical History. First, concerning those who proclaim gods like the pagans, and so on.
And after twelve chapters concerning these matters, further chapters concerning the reign of the victorious Emperor Maurice.
This should have been placed at the beginning of the book, but was not included there.
1. First chapter: Concerning how the Tritheites began to perform ordinations.
2. Second chapter: Concerning Nisha.
3. Third chapter: Concerning the party of Conon and Eugenius, the leaders of the heresies.
4. Fourth chapter: Concerning Conon's release from exile.
5. Fifth chapter: Concerning the division of the Tritheites into two heresies.
6. Sixth chapter: Concerning the journey of the two of them to the region of Pamphylia to lead people astray, and concerning the death of Eugenius there.
7. Seventh chapter: Concerning what was sent to Conon by John of Asia.
8. Eighth chapter: Concerning the proposal of the Tritheites, who deceitfully and cunningly make a show of wanting to be united, but not sincerely.
9. Ninth chapter: Concerning how they did the very same things both in Alexandria and in Syria.
10. Tenth chapter: Concerning the great book of disputations that the Tritheites produced.
11. Eleventh chapter: Concerning the assembly of the bishops and the bishops of the Tritheites.
12. Twelfth chapter: Concerning one of the Tritheite bishops who returned to orthodoxy.
13. Thirteenth chapter: Concerning the reign of the victorious Maurice, which, in the proper order, ought to have been described at the beginning of the book, had matters not turned out this way.
14. Fourteenth chapter: Concerning Emperor Maurice and the wedding feast he held for himself, and concerning the son whom he afterward fathered in the palace, and related matters.
15. Chapter fifteen: Concerning those who were accustomed, under the pretext of religion, to attack people, plunder them, and steal the property of others,
and did not cease making accusations [?] to the emperor against the orthodox.
16. Sixteenth chapter: Concerning the persecution of the church of the Arians.
17. Seventeenth chapter: Concerning Gregory, bishop of Antioch, his journey up to the imperial capital, and his interrogation by the emperor.

18. Chapter eighteen: Concerning his parents, brothers, sisters, and very numerous relatives, whom Emperor Maurice sent for and brought to him in the imperial capital, and whom he enriched and raised to high rank.
19. Chapter nineteen: Concerning Domitian, metropolitan of the city of Melitene, a relative of the emperor.
20. Chapter twenty: Concerning how Maurice, when he became emperor, found the palace treasuries empty and fell into distress and anxiety.
21. Chapter twenty-one: Concerning the troublemakers, persecutors, and oppressors of others who continually troubled the hearing [?] of Emperor Maurice and the rest of his household.
22. Chapter twenty-two: Concerning the rebuilding of Arabissus, a ruined city in Cappadocia, from which Emperor Maurice's family came.
23. Chapter twenty-three: Concerning the destruction of the city of Arabissus by an earthquake roughly two years after its rebuilding.
The fifth book of the third part of the Ecclesiastical History, concerning the histories of the church, and the rest.
For at first there were two bishops from Cilicia, Conon and Eugenius, the leaders [?] of the heresy. When their heresy was exposed and became known,
they were repeatedly and severely rebuked and admonished, but they did not turn back. This resulted in their condemnation and deposition.
They and Athanasius, the son of Empress Theodora’s daughter, who nurtured and enlarged the heresy through the great quantities of gold he distributed, were plotting together
to find three bishops, as the canon required, so that they could ordain bishops [?]. They began to flatter and trouble John of Ephesus,
who lived in the imperial city and had authority over the administration of all the congregations of the faithful, both there and everywhere else.
They were scheming to bring him under their control through presents and gifts, so that he would be won over to them, join them, and ordain bishops with them.
But he was not won over to them. Instead, he rebuked them severely and argued with them, saying that they were heretics,
and showing them that the Arians, Macedonians, Nestorians, and the other heresies were far less heretical than they were. So, when they could not ridicule and mislead him,
a certain Theonas happened to arrive in the city. He had been made a bishop at the command of Patriarch Theodosius,
but afterward a charge was established against him, and Theodosius deposed him. Thus he was wandering about without an appointment.
They put pressure on this man, and after misleading him with gifts, the two of them, Conon and Eugenius, took him
and ordained many bishops with him. They sent them in every direction to spread their heresy.
For, contrary to order and the canons of the church, by a man who had been deposed from the episcopate,
Conon and Eugenius and their followers, the chief leaders of the heresy of many gods, began appointing bishops, taking indiscriminately anyone who came their way:
