whether young or old, uneducated or learned—in short, absolutely all their disciples and notaries.
They made everyone who was accepted a bishop and dispatched them to various regions and countries, as far as Rome, Corinth, Athens, and Africa,
so that they might establish congregations in the African regions and lead people astray after them. They even tried to lead the patrician Narses in Rome astray.
They brought with them two chosen men from their number, brothers born of the same mother, Phocas and Theodosius, and their efforts were considerable.
But he turned his face away from them and did not receive them. They did, however, lead astray some of his chamberlains and officials, as well as military commanders.
Conon and Eugenius and their followers, the leaders of the heresy, persisted in the imperial city itself, even after they had been excommunicated.
They were [?], arguing and leading people astray. They also pressured many people and went in to complain to the emperor, as though they had been mistreated and wronged.
The emperor himself gave orders to the patriarch of the city to assemble both parties before him, and before him and before his synod,
so that these men, who were all enemies, might argue their cases against one another. We have given an account of all these matters in other books.
They continued doing these things until Emperor Justin launched a severe persecution and sent them into exile in Palestine through Photius—
that is, Conon and Eugenius. Meanwhile, all the rest were traveling about outside the capital, throughout the regions of Syria, Cilicia, Isauria, and Cappadocia,
leading people astray and appointing priests and deacons in churches, monasteries, cities, and villages, until they had led many regions astray and spread their heresy very widely.
Since many people remained attached to Conon, as had long been their custom, because his house was below the palace,
they used to go down in their official shoes and receive communion secretly. Then they would go back up and stand before the emperor without being recognized.
For this reason, and because he presented himself as humble and righteous, many people gathered and petitioned on his behalf.
He was released and left the monastery where he had been confined. He went to a village called Aulas, where he lived in a women's monastery.
From then on, all those who held to their error, especially the people of Cilicia and Isauria,
flocked to him as though he were one of the apostles. They praised him and went still further astray after him.
In the end, however, they split into two heresies and became opponents of one another.
For we have briefly described in the preceding books the error and division of these preachers of many gods, and the causes that brought them to this point.
We have also described the destructive writings expressing the error of John the Grammarian of Alexandria. One of these, the first, led them all astray and drowned them.
They all held to it together, carried it around like the Gospel, and boasted of it. Many things took place in the meantime,
some of which were set down in the accounts. The rest, however, were not collected and recorded because of their overwhelming number.
For the second book by John the Grammarian also reached them eventually—the one that teaches that there is no resurrection for these bodies:
Instead, other bodies come into being, and these come to the resurrection from the dead. This led them still further astray and divided them into two heresies.
Both of these outdo one another in corruption. Thus some of them did not accept that book of the two.
Instead, they argued against it, reviled it, and anathematized it. Others accepted it so fully that they valued it above the books—the books of the prophets and apostles.
Thus they quarreled and rose against one another, divided and separated, and anathematized one another. In their writings they exposed one another's faults in many matters.
And both heresies remain locked in opposition to one another.
Now this region of Pamphylia had belonged to the orthodox from the beginning, with its many large villages and churches,
and its many monasteries for men and women. At the time of the schism of those called Acephali,
that is, the Headless, many of them had broken away and gone out into the region.
Through the zeal and diligence of the orthodox there, however, they had all been converted and come to orthodoxy.
Thus they all alike embraced zeal for the true faith. Orthodox bishops were frequently sent, and they came and visited them,
and put church affairs in order: that is, they consecrated altars, new churches, and monasteries that were being established there.
They also ordained many priests and did whatever else needed to be done.
Thus, to our own knowledge, this wretched Eugenius—wretched Eugenius, who fell into heresy—was himself sent to that region twice, as were other bishops.
Eventually, however, both Conon and Eugenius became eager to go to that region, lead it astray, and add it to their own heresy.
This they diligently set about doing. While they were staying there, Eugenius's end overtook him, and he died there. Conon, however, returned to the imperial city.
Now before their heresy of the Tritheists split in two—that is, the party of Athanasius separating from the party of Conon—Athanasius had made a will concerning his estate.
He made the emperor and empress his heirs. He also freed his slaves and left a legacy to each of them, and to many others.
He also left a considerable amount of gold to Conon himself, all of which was to be distributed through his hands.
For Conon personally, however, he left ten pounds, which he was to receive from his estate in a single payment.
Besides this, he was to receive two pounds every year for as long as he lived.
Athanasius himself sealed this will and kept it, before the division arose between them.
Then, when the division had arisen and they had anathematized one another, and had finally even published writings full of abuse against one another,
Athanasius was considering changing the will and excluding Conon, when he suddenly died.

When the will was opened, it turned out that Conon was receiving what was written in it, even while anathematizing the man who had left it to him. It was for this reason that he came to the imperial city.
Thus, while John of Asia—that is, of Ephesus—was in the city, and was testifying about him,
He sent him this message: “How long will you fail to bear in mind, O wise man, that you are mortal,
and that you are destined to stand with your neck exposed before that dreadful judgment seat of justice, and will be required to give an account for being called ‘Rabbi,’
and for having your hands kissed amid the division of the church of the living God, who gave himself up for her?
Why have you persisted in such complete insensitivity, knowing that all those who belonged to both sides, ours and yours, have gone to God?
Look, until now you and my humble self have remained alive in the body. Let us withdraw from all the cunning that comes from Satan and put on the gentleness and humility of Christ our God.
Let the two of us draw near to one another in love and put an end to this dispute and division. Just as it arose disastrously in our days and in our midst,
so now, while we are still in the body, let us take measures to dismantle the barrier of hostility, so that corruption does not remain like this in the church of God.”
When the other man heard this, he said, “I too desire this.” But he gave no further answer.
Instead, he took the gold that had been left to him and departed for Cilicia. There he delights in his own heresy like a drunkard.
Now, while these people who proclaimed essences, natures, and divinities were being rebuked by everyone, and were even despised in their own hearts,
they often appeared in lambs’ clothing, pleading to be united with the church of the orthodox, from which they had gone out, though they had not belonged to it.
For if they had belonged to it, they would have remained in it. Concealing the deceit in their hearts, they would say that they wanted to be united.
But when they came to speak and were required to turn back and stop speaking of substances and natures in the Trinity,
so that a multiplicity of gods and divinities, as among the pagans, would not enter Christianity through these teachings,
they would immediately flee and withdraw, saying, “We cannot refrain from speaking of a number of essences and natures.”
But this was put to them in reply: “The faith of the church confesses one God, who is known in three persons: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.
Three persons, three names, one divinity, one essence, one nature, one lordship,
and one power, will, kingdom, authority, and dominion in heaven and on earth. One is three, and three are one, without division and without confusion.
And how is it that, while you speak of a number of essences and natures—even if you do not acknowledge it openly—
you seem to want, through these things, to introduce [?] of gods into the catholic church, as among the pagans, while seeking union in appearance and not in truth?
You are scheming and devising ways to deceive the whole church and draw it into your heresy.” Thus, when they had been refuted and put to shame, they would leave.
They did this many times in the imperial city and in other places, deceitfully and not sincerely.
For these very same things were also being done by them many times in Alexandria and Syria.
When they saw that they had been unable to make fools of the people in the imperial city, they went off to Alexandria and drew up a petition.
They artfully set out their confession of faith in it and presented it to Damian, who had succeeded Peter there.
And when he too demanded that they abandon the enumeration of multiple natures and essences,
and also anathematize John the Grammarian and both his books, through which they had been led astray—as for the latter book, concerning bodies not rising again,
they indicated that they anathematized it; but they would not agree to reject or anathematize the first, concerning a plurality of gods.
He, however, pronounced an anathema and expelled them, just as they had also done this many times in Syria.
Finally, when they saw that their schemes were not succeeding, they persisted in that same corruption of heresy, even to the present day.
These men, then, who considered themselves philosophers among the Tritheists, tore out a large book
from the living body of the writings of the holy fathers—passages which they think establish and confirm their heresy within that same heresy of theirs.
These are the things concerning which God's law commands: “You shall not eat flesh torn by wild animals.”
In the same way, they too tear dead limbs from the demonstrations of the holy fathers, so that, as they suppose, they may show that all the fathers
likewise introduce and teach, as they do, an enumeration of many natures and substances—substances, that is, many essences.
By this they are exposed, even if they do not think so, as also teaching and proclaiming, like the pagans, an enumeration of many godheads and gods.
For the followers of Conon and Eugenius, who teach a plurality of gods, in order, as they supposed, to spread and establish their heresy,
appointed numerous bishops and sent them in every direction, so that many of them also remained in the imperial city
and opened large meeting places, because John of the imperial city had supported them from the beginning.
A great many people gathered around them openly and without fear. When John died and Eutychius succeeded him, he sent against those who had split away from the members of his own heresy,
those who deny the resurrection of bodies, and arrested everyone he found there and seized all their liturgical equipment.
He uprooted and demolished their altars, arrested their bishops and the rest, and confined them in monasteries. They remained in them for a long time.
But one of these well-known bishops whom the followers of Conon had appointed in the region of Cilicia, when he recognized and understood the error of their heresy, turned away from them
and submitted a written declaration to the orthodox, anathematized the followers of Conon and their heresy, and joined the company of the faithful.
After the death of Emperor Justinian, which occurred on the fourteenth day of November in the year eight hundred and seventy-six,
after he had reigned for thirty-nine years, Justin, his sister's son, succeeded him and reigned for thirteen years less forty days.
During this time, when an illness of severe chastisement overtook him, he appointed Tiberius Caesar on the seventh day of December
in the year eight hundred and eighty-six. Justin himself bestowed the imperial crown on him during his own lifetime, when he saw that death was pressing upon him.
He installed him as emperor while he himself was still alive, lying in the depths of death. After Tiberius became emperor, he lived alongside him for nine days and then died.
Tiberius held the position of Caesar for four years, and after becoming sole emperor, for another four years less thirty-one days. Then he fell gravely ill with a fatal disease.
When his condition became critical, he in turn appointed Count Maurice the Cappadocian as Caesar, on the fifth day of the month of Ab [?], in the year 893.
A few days earlier, he had come from the eastern region, where he had been appointed chief and commander
over all the commanders of the Roman armies, as is explained to us in the earlier chapters concerning these matters. He also gave him the name Tiberius.
He also made his younger daughter, whose name was Augusta, reign alongside him. He gave her the name Constantina and immediately gave her to Maurice as his wife.
He lived with them for eight days. When he saw that his condition was critical, one day before his death he placed the imperial crown on Maurice.
He departed from this world at the [?] of the Hebdomon. They then brought him into the city, to the palace, and he was buried according to the custom for emperors.
Thus, when the God-loving emperor Maurice had taken his seat on the imperial throne and had appeared and become recognized as sole ruler,
he began administering the affairs belonging to the empire. After some time, when the mourning for Emperor Tiberius had ended,
he made grand preparations and arranged imperial celebrations, with many displays befitting the reign of emperors,
which would not be easy for anyone to describe without considerable effort. Nor does the purpose we have set ourselves allow us to occupy ourselves with these matters,
except to make occasional mention of those among them that are connected with the history of the church, which is the subject of our account.
After the imperial wedding feast had ended, splendid as it was with many gifts and imperial festivities, a pregnancy followed.
In due time a son was born to them in the purple, on the fourth day of the month of Ab [?], in the year 894. They named him Theodosius,
apparently with Theodosius the Younger in mind, who alone, from the time of Constantine's dynasty onward, had been born in the purple.
For he himself did not father another child in the purple, nor did those who became emperors after him:
Marcian, Leo, Zeno, Anastasius, Justin, Justinian, the other Justin, and Tiberius, down to Maurice himself.
Thus, when a son was born to him, many rejoiced over him, especially because other people, who were entirely unfit,
had set their sights on the throne and were plotting to seize the empire by force. On the day of this child's birth, their designs were extinguished and brought to nothing.
So, in the Hippodrome, as the people of the city praised him, they shouted acclamations to him, saying, “God has graciously given you, and you have freed us from servitude to many.”
Immediately, offerings, gifts, and many presents were brought to this child by all the noblemen and noblewomen, the senate, and the rest.
Everyone was devising ways and striving to surpass the others in the magnificence of the gifts they presented with great reverence.
From the very beginning of the reign of the God-loving Maurice, the troublemakers and thieves already mentioned did not cease
stirring him up and agitating him against the orthodox, accusing them of many evil deeds and making false charges against them,
although he himself did not know what beliefs they held or why they were divided against one another.
Thus, as they continually stirred him up and agitated him, he was roused to anger. He sent for the patriarch and ordered him to send men to seize and imprison them so that they could not assemble.
Then John the patriarch was distressed and mourning over the deeds of the pagans:
for afterward, as though through God's intervention, they were thus exposed, revealed, identified, and denounced by one another.
Proceedings were taken against them all—not only those in the imperial city, but also those in every region and city.
As we also explained at length in the preceding chapters, most of the senate were implicated in these things, so that even the emperor himself was shaken,
because these things had happened at the very beginning of his reign, and [?] he would be deprived of his leading officials and would kill and destroy his entire senate.
Then he fell silent, neglected the matter, and covered up the affair [?]. Only a few of them were put to death, while some others went into exile.
The rest remained as they were, left in their positions of leadership and authority. This was why the patriarch was mourning inconsolably.
Thus, when the emperor ordered him to persecute and arrest the orthodox, he answered him with a cry, saying:
“Even God groans at this: after the pagans' paganism was exposed and became known to everyone, we acquitted them, freed them, and let them go.
Now, therefore, having declared these people innocent, are we to persecute, condemn, and kill Christians in their place?
Are these the laws of justice? What do the Dissenters say or do that we should persecute them?
Your Majesty should know that, since the pagans have been acquitted and released, and not one of them has even been removed from his position of authority,
how can I persecute these Christians, who are blameless in their Christianity and consider themselves more faithful than we are?” In this way he stopped the persecution at that time.
But a short time later, after these troublemakers had repeatedly asked to attack the congregations of the faithful and he had not agreed to their demands,
they fabricated pretexts and multiplied accusations against the congregations of the Arians. Their entire band assembled,
and they went to attack—to attack—the church of the Arians, which used to assemble outside the city in the queen's courtyard.
They attacked them while they were assembled and celebrating the Eucharist. They overturned their altar, threw their offering onto the ground, and took all their liturgical equipment,
their books, and everything else that fell into their hands. They dragged them away, brought them in, and imprisoned them within the church's chancel enclosure.
To these people, as also to the others imprisoned there, applies the saying of our Lord:
“Truly I tell you, you will not get out of there until you have paid the last penny.”
For these too are required to pay the last penny of their lives, and only then leave that place.
For when the investigation of the pagans took place, both in the imperial city and in Antioch and everywhere else,
various things were also said against the blessed Gregory of Antioch, so that the whole city rose against him, seeking to burn him.
They shouted, “Into the fire with this man! A Christian patriarch for the city!” along with many other things.
But when the whole affair was covered up, corrupted, and brought to nothing everywhere because of prominent and well-known people, it was hushed up in this way.
He too remained there, although all the people were thoroughly stirred up against him and took offense at him. After some time, however, he prepared himself
to go up to the emperor, and prepared a great quantity of gold and silver objects, and many splendid garments of every kind,
and other things suitable as gifts and marks of honor for the leading members of the senate.
Thus, according to what was said, the cost of his journey amounted to many hundredweights.
When he reached the imperial capital, he lavished his gifts on the entire senate.
With his gifts he soothed and appeased the noblemen and noblewomen, and all the members of the church who were angry with him because of the report of his paganism.
Along with these, he also won over all the relatives of the patriarch, who, when he heard that he had come up, had decided not to associate with him.
Since the patriarch himself would not accept a bribe, those around him were persuaded, and they persuaded him, and he received him.
The emperor too, and the entire senate, received him with honor, and they were all on his side.
Although many had expected that proceedings would be brought against him and that he would not return to his episcopal seat, he was received.
After doing everything he wanted, he was sent away with great honor.
Having resolved to give rest and relief to the people of his city, he asked the emperor to authorize him to build them a hippodrome.
He granted him this too, also giving him funds for building his church of Satan, in which he was to carry out everything he wished and pleased.
Indeed, according to what was said, he even took mime performers with him and brought them down from the imperial capital.
For some this became a matter for laughter, mockery, and ridicule, but for others it was a cause of mourning and grief.
They all said, “Look, in this man our Lord’s saying is fulfilled: ‘If salt loses its taste, with what will it be salted?’” And so on.
For although he had been made head of Christ’s church, he showed himself to be the builder and founder of a church of Satan in Antioch, after all these generations that had passed.
He persevered, worked diligently, and supervised its construction without growing weary—as was mockingly said, with [?].
Immediately, then, at the beginning of his reign, the emperor himself sent for and brought to him his father, an elderly man named Paul,
and his mother, his brother named Peter, and his two sisters, one a widow and the other married to a man named Philippicus.
He first appointed this man count of the Excubitors. Afterward, in his own place, he set him over all the commanders of the Roman armies throughout the East,
giving him authority and sending him to prepare the armies for war against the Persians.
His own father, in turn, he made chief of all the patricians, above the entire senate.
He immediately granted him and his son Peter, the emperor’s own brother, the entire estate of the great patrician Marcellus, the brother of Emperor Justin:
an estate not much smaller than the imperial estate, including his houses, suburban properties, gold, silver, and treasury, and absolutely everything he possessed everywhere.
He also gave his father and mother another house near the church and the palace.
He also gave his sister and his brother-in-law Philippicus a large, strongly built house on the western side of the city, in the place called—called—Zeugma.
That house is also known as the house of [?]. He also gave his other sister, a widow, a large, new, strongly built house,
which likewise belonged to the patrician Peter, who was called Barsymes, who had recently built it. It contained as much as a whole town.

He also bestowed other large and well-known houses belonging to the imperial estate on the rest of his relatives. He gave generously and diligently promoted them, enriched them, and strengthened their position.
Along with others, he distinguished them with high and prominent offices close to the imperial throne, appointing them, securing their positions, and giving them authority.
Since these matters are not the subject of our account, we have passed over them.
Now, as for this distinguished Domitian, Emperor Maurice himself, while he was still a count and had been sent east by Tiberius,
had made him bishop of Melitene in Cappadocia. After Maurice had spent a short time in the East, about two years, more or less,
and had gone up and become emperor, Domitian immediately hurried to him. He became his adviser and confidant, closer to him than anyone else.
He advised him and comforted him in the severe and bitter trials arising from wars with the pagan nation of the Persian Magi,
and also from the barbarous and savage peoples who had come from the farthest reaches of the world and were called Avars,
and the other peoples, the Slavs, who surrounded Emperor Maurice on every side.
In all these matters, the bishop of Melitene comforted and advised the emperor, although he was still a young man.
He was, however, thoroughly steeped in the Chalcedonian outlook and that of Leo's party. As for the many important matters that came rushing to him from every direction,
he presented them to the emperor, persuaded him, and settled them as he wished, even immediately.
Now Emperor Tiberius, who appointed Emperor Maurice as his successor, had recklessly squandered all the treasures of Emperor Justin,
when he rose to take charge of the empire and came to prominence. He found in the treasuries of Justin—the man who had appointed Tiberius himself, appointed him as his successor—
a great quantity of gold that had been unjustly amassed and hidden in his treasure stores. When Tiberius himself saw these treasures, it was as though a spirit of zeal had entered him.
He began bringing it out, scattering it, and distributing it: sometimes compassionately in [?], and sometimes in the customary payments to the army.
At other times he spent it recklessly and without calculation, scattering it as though with a winnowing shovel, until Justin's treasuries were emptied.
This was especially so at the celebration of his consulship, when, as he himself said, he distributed seventy-five hundred-pound weights of gold,

apart from silver and the other imperial outlays that he distributed according to imperial custom, until he was compelled to open Emperor Anastasius's treasure stores, bring out their contents, and distribute them.
But when he departed this world, having appointed Maurice emperor after him, Maurice found the palace swept clean as though with a broom. He was compelled, even if gold was found,
or came to him from public revenues, to hold on to it and tighten his hand, and to withhold a portion from the army and keep it, saying:
“For,” he said, “I do not thresh and scatter, but gather and store up, so that I may contribute toward the peace of the state.”
And so, with this aim, he held back his hand and curtailed many customary gifts, to the point that many people laughed at him, mocked him, and even insulted him in many ways,
and called him a miser, a skinflint, and a hoarder, who could only promote, exalt, and enrich his own relatives,
along with many other things of this kind, which, except for a particular reason, would not have deserved to be recorded by us in the accounts of ecclesiastical history.
Now while the emperor was caught up in the trials and anxieties of the wars that surrounded him on every side,
these agitators, who were moved not by zeal for the faith but used it as a pretext, were eager and intent on plundering houses and seizing other people’s possessions.
They shamelessly schemed to obtain permission and authority over these matters, and they never stopped wearing out the ears of the patriarch and the emperor,
persistently and zealously denouncing and accusing people, especially those who had stumbled over the Council of Chalcedon,
and many others besides, saying, “Look, all these people gather large congregations
and celebrate the Eucharist and perform baptisms in greater numbers than the catholic Church, together with all the heresies of the Arians and the Sabbatians,
the Tetradites, the Montanists, the Marcionites, and the rest of those like them. They disturb and overturn the whole Church.
Grant us authority over them,” they said, “so that we may arrest them, imprison them, torture them, and uproot all their meeting houses.”
But the patriarch, because he was a peaceable and merciful man and knew their deceitfulness and their eagerness for plunder and robbery, rebuked them, saying,
“If you were showing genuine zeal in what you are eager to do, or were concerned to set these people right, your zeal would be good.
But since we know what concerns you—that you are intent on stealing, plundering, and seizing other people’s possessions—go and keep quiet.
For we will not allow persecution to take place in our days. Instead, we teach and admonish as far as we can.”
But these people included not only members of the clergy but also laypeople,
and not only these, but also people who were not sound in their Christianity—physicians and pagans. And because they were eager for plunder,
and also wanted to present themselves as people who, like Christians, were zealous for the Christian faith, whenever they saw that the bishop would not lend himself to their wickedness,
they would not refrain from wearing out the ears of the merciful emperor himself. Some of them were, in fact, imperial physicians.
But the emperor, whose whole activity and all whose thoughts were absorbed in the wars against the barbarians, paid them no attention and would not even give them a hearing, saying,
“Are the foreign wars surrounding us not enough for us? Do you also want to bring internal wars upon us?”
Thus their impetuosity was restrained, and their plans were checked and thwarted.
Now when the God-loving Maurice came to the throne, Tiberius gave instructions concerning his name:
that he too should be called—should be called—Tiberius. But he himself was not pleased to change his original name, which he had received from his parents.
But he also ordered that “Maurice” be inscribed on the stamp of his gold coinage, and so he had all the gold that was minted inscribed in this way.
He was especially eager, before anything else, to rebuild his own city, Arabissus, to restore it, raise it up, and make it famous.
He sent an imperial officer in every direction, who gathered and brought craftsmen skilled in stonework, quarrymen who cut stone, builders, carpenters, and contractors,

and metalworkers and engineers, and workers in all the other trades. He stationed a military unit there so that they would all remain constantly at the work, attending to all the craftsmen in every task.
He first ordered that the church there be torn down and made much more spacious and extensive. A great abundance of gold and silver furnishings,

and splendid vessels for the altar and for the adornment and furnishing of the whole church, he sent in lavish quantities, along with a large altar canopy like those in the other churches of the imperial capital.
He ordered this to be made here of [?], and sent it to be installed there. He also ordered that there should be a large hospice there, with lofty buildings.
Along with these, he also ordered, as befitted a city, a large public bath, long and spacious colonnades, large basilicas, a palace, and a strong wall.
Because of these things, many people spoke against him and complained bitterly, saying:
“To the Roman troops who toil and fight for the state, he cries out every day, saying, ‘I have no gold to distribute to them.’
And now, when so many strong cities in the East and the West have been conquered and devastated by the barbarians,
and he cries out, ‘There is no gold for me to give,’ how is it that hundredweights of gold are [?], which people say are very many in number?”
Since we ourselves do not now know this with certainty, we do not attest to it or set it down in the records of our history merely because it is reported in the talk of many people.
For they were saying, “He sent all these hundredweights of gold to build and establish a city that had never been known or contributed anything to the Roman state.”
For when the city of Arabissus had been built with great care and zeal, and was still being built,
suddenly a great, terrifying, and violent earthquake, in the second year of its construction,
which was the third indiction, struck various places throughout the East and, as though in anger, overturned the whole of Arabissus.
It demolished, as is reported, all the buildings in it, both new and old, so that it became a cause of astonishment to everyone.
Emperor Maurice himself was deeply shaken and distressed, as though the overthrow of his city had come from God through a hidden sign.
Nevertheless, he did not desist from rebuilding and restoring it once again from the beginning.
He kept all the tradespeople who had been gathered for its construction there again, under the former arrangements, to build it and restore it and raise it up anew.
The fifth book of the Ecclesiastical History is finished. It contains twenty-three chapters.
Chapter headings of the sixth book of the history concerning the wars, which are briefly outlined and set down in short accounts in the historical record. They are as follows.
1. The first chapter: Concerning the beginning of the account itself.
2. The second: Concerning the campaign of Marcian the patrician, and what happened to him in the end.
3. The third: Concerning the reason for the emperor's anger against Marcian.
4. The fourth: Concerning what the emperor wrote to Marcian and Mundhir.
5. The fifth: Concerning the arrival of the king of the Persians and his capture of Dara.
6. The sixth: Concerning the capture of Apamea and the other places.
7. The seventh: Concerning the two thousand young women who drowned themselves.
8. Chapter eight: The brief peace that occurred, and Khosrow’s war.
9. The ninth: Concerning the war in Cappadocia and the burning of Melitene.
10. The tenth: Concerning what happened to the Romans in Armenia in the end.
11. The eleventh: Concerning the Armenians—the Persian Armenians—who surrendered to the Romans.
12. The twelfth: Concerning the Roman and Persian envoys who held discussions.
13. The thirteenth: Concerning the devastation that the Persians immediately carried out.
14. Chapter fourteen: On Count Maurice and the rest.
15. Chapter fifteen: On what Maurice did afterward.
16. Chapter sixteen: On Mundhir son of Harith and on Maurice.
17. Chapter seventeen: On the devastation caused by the Persian marzban.
18. Chapter eighteen: On Mundhir’s victory.
19. Chapter nineteen: On the events arising from the captivity at Antioch.
20. Chapter twenty: On the death of Khosrow, king of the Persians.
21. Chapter twenty-one: On Khosrow’s grief over the breaking of the peace.
22. Chapter twenty-two: On Khosrow’s son, who became king after him.
23. Chapter twenty-three: On the reasons why the peace was broken.
24. Chapter twenty-four: On the loathsome people called the Avars, and on the bridge they built.
25. Chapter twenty-five: On the accursed people of the Slavs and the devastation they caused.
26. Chapter twenty-six: On the Persian attack on the city of Tella.
27. Chapter twenty-seven: On Maurice, who fled from battle.
28. Chapter twenty-eight: On the battle that took place in Armenia, and on the victory of Cours.
29. Chapter twenty-nine: On Aphitita, a Persian who pretended to be the king’s son.
30. Chapter thirty: On Sirmium, the great city of the kingdom of the Gepids, which the Avars took by a tight blockade.
31. Chapter thirty-one: On the departure of Narses the sword-bearer.
32. Chapter thirty-two: On how, in the end, when the expected events did not take place, the city of Sirmium was handed over to these barbarians.
33. Chapter thirty-three: On the burning of Sirmium, which happened afterward.
34. Chapter thirty-four: On accounts of many battles, and finally on the battle of Maurice, Maurice [?], and the capture of Arzan.
35. Chapter thirty-five: On another fortress, called Shamkart, which Maurice himself built facing the territory of Sophene.

37. Chapter thirty-seven: On the envoy—the envoys—of the Persians, who was received—who were received—at that time [?] he was sending to our Roman emperor.
38. Chapter thirty-eight: On the Roman envoy’s journey down to speak with the king of the Persians about peace.
39. Chapter thirty-nine: On the Persian envoy who was sent again to the Roman emperor.
40. Chapter forty: On the great devastation that the two states repeatedly inflicted on one another.
41. Chapter forty-one: On the rise and subsequent decline of the leadership of the Roman Arabs.
42. Chapter forty-two: On those Arab leaders who went over and surrendered to the Persians.
43. Chapter forty-three: On certain prominent leaders among the Persian frontier governors who were arrested, taken up, and imprisoned in the imperial capital.
44. Chapter forty-four: Another battle in the year of Trita, and the victory that God gave the Romans.
45. Chapter forty-five: On the repulsive people of the hairy barbarians called Avars.
46. Chapter forty-six: On how the Avars went out and conquered great cities and many fortresses.
47. Chapter forty-seven: On the alarm and panic that arose in Constantinople while we too were there.
48. Chapter forty-eight: On the conquest and devastation of the country by the Slavs.
49. Chapter forty-nine: On the destruction of the city of Anchialus and on its hot springs.
Here end the headings, or chapters.
Book Six of the Third Part of the Ecclesiastical History: On accounts of wars, briefly recorded.
It therefore did not seem to us improper or out of place to append to the ecclesiastical histories a brief account
of the wars and battles, the sword and bloodshed, that occurred in our days, in our days, for the information and knowledge of those who come after us,
if indeed the world still endures. We shall record and make these things known as far as we are able, as far as we understand them, and as we receive them by report.
Through these things we recall the word of our Savior and his life-giving teaching, which teaches us, warns us, and bears witness to us
about the final period, when the world will end, and also about the time of his coming, saying, “When you see all these things happening, know that it has reached the door.”
Look, in our own days we see that all these things have happened and been fulfilled. From now on, we must always await that fearful coming, with great power and abundant glory.
We are making a few brief records of the things that have now happened in the eastern regions.
Let us now begin the account of our history with the illustrious patrician Marcian, a relative of Emperor Justin,
who was one of the military commanders sent to the East at that time.
Burning with zeal for the Christian commonwealth, he gathered his army, went down, and encamped against the city of Nisibis,
which the Persians still hold to this day. He vigorously set about capturing it and built siege works all around it.
Since he also had engineers with him, he set up siege machinery against it, consisting of tall towers and strong [?], and the city was in distress.
Its inhabitants, together with the Persian troops stationed there, despaired of their lives, seeing that it was already as good as captured by the Romans.
While those inside were terrified, those outside were preparing to capture the city and destroy it.
While all the Romans were expecting and preparing to enter it,

suddenly a brutish man named Acacius Archelaus appeared. Emperor Justin had sent him against Marcian, without any regard for what was right, to remove him from his command, cut off his belt of office,
and send him away from the eastern regions. He arrived and presented the order while Marcian and his army were fighting against Nisibis
and expecting to enter and capture the city the following day. The whole army was shaken, and their hands grew slack.
The illustrious Marcian had been working hard and making preparations, and was close to capturing Nisibis. When he heard the order, he said to Acacius,
“Look, you have seen how much toil we have endured in order to capture this city.
Now restrain yourself and grant us just two days. Then immediately do what you have been ordered.
The emperor has the authority to have his command carried out.” But Acacius became angry with him, insulted him, flew into a rage, and laid hold of him in front of all his troops.
He dragged him this way and that, pulled off and cut his belt of office, insulting him as he did so. It was even said that he struck him on the cheek.
Thus the whole army was in uproar, and the hands of the entire force grew slack.
Cursing because they had seen what had been done so unjustly, they took his standard, lowered it, and turned it back.
Immediately the whole army broke camp and fled. They turned back and withdrew far from the city, mourning and grieving over what had happened to their commander, a good and faithful man.
They also grieved because, just when they had expected to enter and take the city, they had turned back without any of their enemies pursuing them
and had become an object of laughter and mockery to those who hated them. But when the Persian army stationed in the city saw these things,
At the sudden rout and retreat of the Romans and the flight of Marcian’s regiment, they were astonished, took courage, armed themselves, and pursued them.
They fell upon the army—the infantry force that had been left behind—and slaughtered and struck down many of them.
And so they returned to their city, laughing and jeering at what had happened to the Romans at their own hands and among themselves.
They immediately wrote and reported all these things to their king, saying, “Hurry and cross into Roman territory at once, because the great gods, the sun and fire, have brought them down.
For at their king’s command they fell upon one another, dismissed Marcian in disgrace, and all fled and went away from our city.”
Now, for the sake of the purpose and orderly progression of these successive accounts, and to explain clearly and accurately the reason for King Justin’s anger,
first against Mundhir son of Harith, and then, because of him, against Marcian, when unjustly and without a fair judgment
he became angry and issued orders against them both, under what influence we do not know—for his anger against Mundhir arose from the following cause:
When Harith, king of the Arabs allied with the Romans, died—the man whose fear and dread had gripped all the Arabs allied with the Persians—and they saw that he was dead,
they despised and looked down on all his sons, his nobles, and his army. They thought that his entire encampment had now been delivered into their hands.
Then they gathered, came, and camped in the territory of Harith’s family, where all their livestock were.
They drove away all their herds of camels. When Mundhir learned of these things, he was deeply embittered.
Burning with fierce zeal, he took all his brothers, his sons, his nobles, and his entire army,
and they suddenly fell upon them, when they had not expected at all that they would dare to stand against them.
They slaughtered and utterly defeated them. When Qabus their king saw the fury of the slaughter inflicted by Mundhir and his army,
who had advanced, gained the upper hand, and already slaughtered his entire army, he mounted and fled with a few men, escaping stripped of their equipment.
Mundhir entered and sat down in his tent, and carried off his entire camp, his baggage train, and all his herds.
He captured and bound even members of his family and some of his nobles. The rest he slaughtered or carried off. He crossed over and pitched his own tent in Qabus’s territory,
three stages away, where all the livestock and all the wealth in which the Arabs allied with the Persians took pride were located.
He kept it pitched there for a long time. When Qabus’s raiding bands came and saw the tent pitched in Qabus’s own territory,
they thought that their king Qabus himself was in it. They confidently entered and plunged into Mundhir’s camp.
His men would seize and kill them, while taking the prominent men among them prisoner. And so, after staying there for some time, as long as they wished,
they returned from there with a great haul of horses, many herds of camels, weapons, and other possessions.
After some time, Qabus went and gathered a large army for himself. He sent word to Mundhir: “Prepare for battle, for we are coming against you.
Although you fell upon us like a band of raiders and imagined that you had defeated us, now we are coming against you openly in battle.”
Mundhir sent them this reply: “Why are you wearing yourselves out? I am coming.” He agreed, made his preparations, and put his words into action.
He suddenly encountered them in the desert, when they were not expecting him. He fell upon them, threw them into confusion, and destroyed most of them. Once again they fled before him.
Since we have already mentioned these things in other accounts, we will now explain the things that happened unjustly, without proper investigation:
what a plot was devised against him after these great triumphs and this immense victory in the two battles.
Mundhir, expecting to be welcomed and praised by the emperor, wrote to him about everything he had done and the full extent of his victory.
After this he wrote asking him to send gold so that he could hire an army, since he thought they were certainly gathering against him again.
When Emperor Justin himself heard that he had written asking him to send gold, he became angry and extremely furious. He insulted him and threatened him harshly.
He resolved to have him killed secretly by treachery.
Then Emperor Justin, as though filled with some spirit of hostility, wrote a letter to the patrician Marcian, intending, as he supposed, to have Mundhir killed secretly.
He wrote as follows: “I have now written to Mundhir the Arab to come to you. See that as soon as he arrives, you take his head without delay and write to us.”
To Mundhir, however, he wrote: “Because there are some urgent matters, I have written to the patrician, the patrician Marcian, to speak with you.
Go to him immediately, without delay, and discuss the matter.” For, as eventually became clear to everyone,
through what seemed to be some intervention by God, the matter was reversed: on the order addressed to Marcian, instructing him to take Mundhir’s head,
Mundhir’s own name was written, while on the one addressed to Mundhir, Marcian’s name was written, as though by mistake.
Thus the imperial courier received both orders, set out, and delivered the orders to the two men according to their written addresses.
So Mundhir received the order for taking his head that was intended for Marcian, while Marcian received Mundhir’s letter, which told him: “Go to Marcian,
for I have written to him to speak with you.” When Mundhir received this and read it, he was deeply shaken and said:
“In return for my labors and hardships on behalf of Roman territory, am I being repaid by having my head cut off?
Did I deserve this?” He was filled with anger, assembled his entire army, and gave them strict instructions to protect him, saying:
“If you see anyone sent to me by the Roman emperor, and they are few in number, seize them and keep them under guard outside the camp.
But if they are many, immediately meet them in battle with all your strength.
Do not believe anything at all that they say to you, or allow them anywhere near the boundaries of your camp.”
Thus all the Arab contingents remained assembled, armed and standing ready, night and day,
keeping watch and preparing to fight anyone among the Romans who might come to them.
When the Persians and their Arabs heard about this and realized that they now had nothing to fear from Mundhir,
And because he did not commit himself to battle on behalf of the Romans, who had sought to kill him, they, for their part, confidently prepared
for the Persians and their Arabs to invade Roman territory. They laid waste and burned—and he burned [?]—and advanced as far as the region of Antioch.
They took a great many captives, and devastated, uprooted, and burned large, strong villages, like cities, in the region of Antioch, and elsewhere.
They took captives and completely destroyed all these regions, and returned to their own country with a great quantity of plunder.
Meanwhile, Mundhir was grieving and mourning over the plot against him and the devastation the enemies had caused, enriching themselves from Roman territory.
He took his army and went out to settle in the desert. Thus, all who heard of the injustice decreed against him, though he had done no wrong,
were deeply distressed. They complained and condemned the orders that had been given thoughtlessly and without a just judgment.
When the emperor heard these things from every side, and also learned that Mundhir had freed himself from all responsibility for Roman affairs,
he sent word to the governors and army commanders in the East to go to him, persuade him, and reconcile him.
But when many of them wrote to him about coming to him, he sent word to each one of them: “You should know
that if any man from anywhere in the whole Roman realm comes to me, I will meet him in battle. Either he will kill me, or I will kill him.
For far be it from me ever again to entrust my life to any man from the Roman realm.
For as far as you and your emperor are concerned, my head has already been taken off. For this,” he said, “was what I deserved from the Romans!”
And so, for a period of two or three years, many appeals were written to him, but he would allow no approach, sending out his command and making it known to everyone.
But there was anger against Marcian because Mundhir had survived and escaped, because the secret had been exposed and revealed, and because the plan had not been carried out.
It had also become clear to everyone that this sentence had been decreed against him unjustly and arrogantly, without any thought of the fear of God.
While King Mundhir was thus acting cautiously and remaining with his entire army, taking every precaution and keeping vigilant against all the magnates and armies of the Roman Empire,
of the Romans, of the empire [?], for a period of about three years, more or less, he nevertheless, as a Christian man, was distressed over Roman territory,
and was filled with anger against the Arabs of the Persians, because they had dared to cross over with the Persian army, laying waste, burning, and taking captives as far as Antioch,
and had returned to their own country with great quantities of plunder and countless captives. He resolved to make peace and fight on behalf of the Roman state.

Letters from the emperor were continually being sent to him through many dignitaries, while the emperor denied responsibility, saying that the order for his death had been written without his knowledge.
But he continued to act cautiously and would not be persuaded to receive the letters, or a single one of the envoys sent to him.
He kept his sword ready against anyone who dared approach the gathering place of his army. Finally, however, he sent word to the patrician Justinian, son of Germanus,
who was the chief and commander over all the officers of the Roman armies throughout the East.
He wrote to him as follows: “From the beginning, I had heard of the Romans’ plots and knew about them.”
But now, through experience, I have learned the truth from this deadly plot that was devised against me as a reward for my efforts.
From now on, I will never agree to entrust myself to any of the Roman leaders.
But as for you, because I know you to be a Christian, a freeborn man who fears God, if you come to the shrine of the blessed Saint Sergius at Resafa,
and send me word, I will come there with my army, armed as for battle.
If I am met with peace and you speak truthfully with me, I will return in peace, and so will you.
But if I find treachery, I trust in the God in whom I believe that I will not give way, nor will my hands fail me.
When the patrician Justinian received this message, he rejoiced greatly. He sent him word: “Do not mistrust me,
for the God of the Christians stands between us. Come on such-and-such a day to the shrine of Saint Sergius, and you will find me there. Do not wear out your army,
for I trust in God that we will part from one another in peace, harmony, and love.”
When Mundhir received this reply, he relaxed and changed his mind. Immediately he set out with a few men and went to him.
When the two of them were together before the resting place of the bones of Saint Sergius, many things too numerous to write down were discussed between them.
They requested and received pledges from one another as they wished, and so they parted from one another with great joy, now confident and at peace.
When these things became known to Emperor Justin and the rest of the senate, they too rejoiced greatly that Mundhir had been won over and reconciled.
Afterward, letters of peace and reconciliation passed between the two sides.
A short time later, the brave and mighty King Mundhir, filled with anger at the insolence of the Arabs allied with the Persians,
and eager to recover and rescue the captives they had taken from Roman territory, secretly gathered his brothers, his entire clan, their sons, and all their forces,
instructing them to prepare immediately and quickly, armed and supplied with provisions, and all to assemble before him on Monday.
When they had assembled and were fully prepared, he revealed his secret to them, saying:
“Immediately, without a single man among us breaking ranks or straying away, let us all together attack Nu'man’s city of al-Hira in Persian territory.
Because of their deeds and their violent aggression against the Christians, God will deliver them into our hands.”
So they all set out eagerly, reached al-Hira, and attacked it suddenly, leaving its inhabitants silent and stunned with great astonishment.
They slaughtered and destroyed the entire army found there. He devastated the city, demolished it, and burned it all except for the churches,
pitching his tent in its center and remaining there for five days. He seized and bound all the Arabs he captured.
He took away all the captives from al-Hira, all the captives whom they had seized and carried off from Roman territory, all their horses, and all their possessions.
He led them away and returned to his own country in great triumph and with a mighty victory. This, above all, added to his glory and wealth.
He distributed gifts and gave abundantly to all the Orthodox monasteries and churches and to the poor, and distinguished himself more than anyone else.
Both kingdoms were repeatedly astonished and amazed at the vigor of the man's mighty deeds and at the victories he achieved.
Now the king of the Persians, with his powerful armies, as soon as he learned that Marcian had fallen and that the army had fled from the city of Nisibis,
immediately arrived and found all the siege machinery and all the engines that Marcian the patrician had prepared against it. Immediately he went and laid siege to Dara.
He took with him all Marcian's siege equipment that had been deployed against Nisibis, brought it, and set it up against the city of Dara.
He had brought craftsmen of every kind with him. First of all, he brought in stonecutters and the others,
to cut through the eastern mountain outside the aqueduct and divert it away from the city.
As people report, they encountered hard rock. They would light a fire against it and afterward pour vinegar over it.
In this way they made it brittle. He set up opposite the city all the siege engines that Marcian had made for use against Nisibis.
He kept besieging it and changing the siege equipment used against it, seeking to capture it, for a period of six months. He also built two siege ramps against it.
The Romans devised means and took action to burn them, while the city remained shut up.
There were commanders in it: John the general, son of Timostratus,
a warlike man, and Sergius son of Zephaniah, who was also a general, and the others.
Sergius, however, as people said, was struck by an arrow and died. Finally, the king of the Persians himself
went up and pitched his tent on the northern mountain above the city. Sitting there, he watched everything that was being done inside it.
He even ordered a siege ramp to be built there, from above, against the great tower that stood higher than all the other towers,
which they called Hercules. Those inside had no means of doing anything about it.
Those outside strengthened the siege ramp and became confident and sure of taking the city. Before these things, when he had already seen how much he had toiled
without shaking the city, he had even ordered a brick wall to be built around it, outside its wall—the city wall—
so that, if the inhabitants happened to come out, it would hold them in check.
When he saw that all his devices had been frustrated, as has been related,
he fell ill and became so agitated that he nearly died. He sent word to the city that they should send someone to him to speak with him.
There was a well-known and distinguished man there, an interpreter for the Romans and the Persians,
whose name was Comitas. The inhabitants sent this man to him. After they had spoken at length together, he told him
to tell the inhabitants to give him five hundred pounds as the city's ransom, and he would withdraw from it.
He who, as he had promised him at the end, when he was confident that the city would not be conquered, did not say—he said this to them. [?]
So when the king saw that the days had passed and that they had scorned him and had not given him an answer—an answer—he became still more enraged and was filled with great anger.
He again attacked the city and strengthened and reinforced the siege mound that he had made last.
Now the Romans, [?], despised him and mocked him, saying, “He himself has been put to shame,” and other things like these.
And so—and so—they neglected the fighting on the wall, especially, and still more especially, because the cold was—was severe and intense.
Intense and severe. They came down from the wall and went inside to eat and drink in the houses.
Inside the houses. But when the Persians saw that the wall had been emptied of the Roman troops, and that the siege mound they had made rose above the wall,

then they prepared themselves, tied timbers together, and leaned them against the wall. The troops crossed—crossed over—and filled the whole—the whole section of the wall. Then they descended into the city.
When a shout suddenly went up, “Look, the city has been captured!” and the Persian force overwhelmed the Romans, [?], they were astonished, shaken, and thrown into confusion.
All of them together ran to the gates—to the gates of the city—to flee from them.
So when the Persians saw how numerous they were, they too became frightened and shaken.
They held back and left the Romans room to flee, so that they would not stand against them.
For when the Romans ran to all the gates, shouting for the keys—the keys—they searched, but the keys could not be found:
the keys, because the commanders had hidden them. So when the Romans saw that the Persian force had grown strong—strong—and that the city was already full,
and that they themselves were hemmed in and trapped on every side and could not escape, then they rallied themselves,
whether for death or for life, and charged the Persian force, cutting them down and throwing them to the ground as reapers do ears of grain.
And these in turn did the same to those. The fighting inside the city became fierce, and they slaughtered one another while the city remained shut up for seven days,
until the city was filled—filled with corpses—and began to stink. Out of necessity they dragged them away and threw them into the river and into cisterns.
So when the Persians saw—were seeing—that they were being slaughtered and could not enter and take possession of the city's plunder,
and were also frightened by the Romans, they fled and went up—up onto the wall. They planned to deal deceitfully with them and toward them,
sending a deceitful message to the Romans: “Why,” they said, “are we slaughtering and destroying—destroying one another like this?
Instead, come, let us give one another our word. Let both sides lay down our weapons and make peace with one another.”
So when the Roman troops despaired—despaired of their lives—and saw that they were trapped in distress,
they agreed, gave their word, and received the others' word, and laid down their weapons. Then they confidently approached one another as though at peace.
But those Romans, [?], now trusted the promise and were without fear.
So that, while confidently [?] in the mighty force of the Persians, the two sides mingled with one another as though at peace.
And when both sides began plundering—plundering the city—then the Persians’ deceit and treachery were revealed.
For they turned against them and acted deceitfully, and broke their word. They seized the Romans and slaughtered the greater part, the great majority of them.
The rest they bound—they bound them one by one—and brought them out to the king.
And with them they brought all the freeborn men and women and the leaders of the city. He gave the order, and they were all drowned.
Then he also ordered everyone who had gold to bring it to him, and that wherever gold or silver was found, it too should come to him.
And in this way gold was gathered—an immense amount of gold was gathered, reportedly exceeding one hundred or two hundred—two hundred hundredweights—and was collected before him.
But because we have no certain knowledge of these matters, we do not want to make a false assertion.
Instead, those things about which we do not—not have certain knowledge, we cover in silence—we cover them.
But the king himself, it is said, when he saw all that gold, summoned the leading men of the city and said to them:
“May the great God of heaven hold you accountable for the blood of all these people who have perished from your side and ours,
“who have perished from ours and yours! I had not been asking you to give even a hundredth part of all this gold now heaped up here as a ransom for your city, so that I would withdraw from it,
“as I also sent word to you through the count, but you paid no attention to me.” When they heard these things—they had heard them—they swore to him, “We have never heard this message.”
He summoned the count to refute them and said to him, “Did I not send them this message through you?” He said, “Yes, my lord.”
He said, “And did you tell them?” He replied, “My lord, I did not tell them, because I was afraid.”
Then, when in anger he had sentenced him to death, he said to him, “Because you have labored on behalf of both empires,
“I will not kill you.” He gave the order, and he was blinded; he had given the order, and both his eyes were blinded.
And so he plundered the city with an immense, indescribable plundering. He took its people captive and emptied it of all its inhabitants.
He left a force of his own men in it and returned to his country with an immense quantity of booty, without—without—without limit:
The silver and gold of the citizens, of the churches, and of the rest. He brought out of it—brought out of it—brought out of it a great quantity of booty and captives.
As for its capture and its surrender—its surrender into the hands of the Assyrians—from its foundation,
from the time of Emperor Anastasius until its capture, the years are calculated to have been seventy-two, more or less.
Now while the Persian king was still encamped against the city of Dara—the city of Dara—and saw that there was no one to check him,
he immediately sent a marzban named Adarmahan against the city of Apamea with a large army.
He too captured fortresses, destroyed and burned large and strongly fortified villages, and went on and reached—reached Apamea.
And because, when the Persian had conquered Antioch, he had encamped against Apamea and pressed it hard, Apamea too had surrendered to him,
after receiving his pledge, the king himself had entered it and had seen in it [?], [?], and had not demolished or burned anything there.
For this reason they trusted him, believing that this time too he would not come and do them harm. With this confidence,
the leading men, the leading men of the city, and the bishop, the bishop, went out to him and paid him honor.
But he deceitfully said to them, “Since the city belongs to us, open the gates for me so that I may enter and see it.”
“And see it.” Since they trusted, trusted him, and did not expect him to do anything evil, they opened the gates for him, and he entered, entered the city.
Immediately he seized control of the gates and began arresting and binding the men and women and plundering the city.
They brought out all the plunder and the entire population and placed them outside the city.
When they had plundered all, all of the city of Apamea, which was full of wealth accumulated over, over long periods of time,
and was much more prosperous than many cities, and had brought out its entire population and all its plunder,
and the bishop, the bishop, along with them, then they set it on fire and burned it completely.
And so they took all, all the captives, and all, all the plunder from it and from the other places, and went down to the king while he was encamped against Dara.
The captives whom he had brought down from it and from the other places were counted before the king: 292,000.
Thus they were divided up and taken into Persian territory. Now after that king had conquered Dara and plundered it, finding there too, there, boundless wealth,
from the other cities, the city, and from everywhere—for people had been fleeing there as to an impregnable fortress—
and they had brought out all its captives, captives beyond counting, he departed and returned, and they departed and returned, to his own country.
Now when the Persian king was drunk with pride, and his mind was carried away by the abundance of the plunder and captives he had taken from Roman territory,
he ordered that two thousand young women be selected from among the captives, women perfect in stature and beauty.
In stature and beauty. When these had been selected according to his command and brought before him,
he ordered that they be adorned in every respect like brides, in splendid and costly clothing, with gold and silver, beads and pearls,
and be sent as a gift of honor to the barbarians beyond his country, who are called Turks and Avars, so that he might win their favor and satisfy them in order to hire them.
When this had been done as he commanded, and they had been magnificently adorned, he assigned a military escort to accompany them, along with two marzbans.
He ordered generous allowances for them, first-rate and generous allowances, and sent them off.
He commanded that they should not be hurried along the road, but should travel at ease and be allowed to rest, “so that,” he said, “they do not waste away and become ugly.”
But those, those young women were tormented not only by separation from their fathers, their brothers, and all their relatives,
But also for their souls, which were being lost to Christianity, and for their bodies, which were being handed over to the brutality, the brutality of the barbarian enemies.
And as they now spoke these things to one another in their own language, all together like sisters, with weeping and lamentations, and again with bitter lamentations,
all of them together asked for death for themselves instead of life.
And all these things passed from them to the other Syrian captives, [?], who were their fellow countrymen, men accompanying the marzbans,
and the others who had been appointed to transport them and attend to them. These things were made known and disclosed by the women to them secretly, as to their fellow countrymen.
Thus, in the end, they became known to everyone, and it was learned from them, who were their fellow countrymen and spoke their language.
For, as they reached about five stages into the territory of these barbarian peoples to whom they were being sent,
and learned that they had reached, had reached those regions to which they were being sent,
they happened to encounter a large and very powerful river, which, it was said, was exceedingly difficult, difficult to cross.
So those who were leading them, having been ordered to let them rest and not drive them hard, camped beside that river for one day.
But all the women themselves took counsel together, and this one strong and courageous resolve arose among them all: to make light of death.
They all ran to one another, took counsel among themselves, and said to one another, “Let us all consider together,
all together, that when we all defile our souls, our souls, with paganism and with the unclean food of animals,
of dead animals and strangled animals, among the barbarians, and lose our Christianity, in the end we will all be handed over to death.
And in the end we will come to a sentence of torment. Now, then, we are all sisters, Christian women and daughters of Christians.
Let us not be divided against one another. Rather, from now on let us all have one will, one soul, one purpose, and one mind.
For all of us—and before our bodies are defiled by the barbarians and our souls polluted, and death overtakes us in the end—

now, while our bodies are pure and our souls are kept from pollution and uncleanness, let us offer him our souls and bodies in purity, for the sake of the name and on account of the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.
Let us hand ourselves over to death now, so that we may be delivered from our enemies and live a life that lasts forever and ever.
Let us live in exchange for the suffering, the sufferings of our souls for a single hour, for the sake of our Christianity, Christianity, and the preservation of the purity of our souls and bodies.”
And so they all bound themselves together by one word, one secret pledge, and one promise, and swore and swore to one another.
And all together, at the same time, they threw themselves, themselves, into that river.
And all together, at the same time, they were all drowned and did not fall into the hands of the barbarians.
Thus this resolve pleased them all equally and was chosen. And while those who were guarding them were watching them, holding [?],
they were devising a plan in secret, now waiting for the right moment, while these men, these men, remained constantly beside them.
And they said to them, “If you permit us, we would like to bathe along the banks of this river.”
Since the men wished to give them relief, as they had been ordered, they allowed them to bathe.
But the women said to them, “We are ashamed to bathe while you stand beside us and watch us.
Instead, move a little distance away from us, and then we will bathe.” So they left them and went some distance away.
Then they all strengthened and encouraged one another, and all signed themselves with the sign in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ,
and all together they threw themselves headlong into that river in a sudden rush and drowned.
When their guards looked into the river, they saw some of them floating and being carried along the river like cork, while others were sinking.
When they ran to the place where the women had asked them for permission to bathe, they saw that not a single one of them was alive.
They all wailed bitterly, running here and there to rescue one of them, but they could not.
Nor could they work out how to escape. But these weak women, who had become strong in Christ, for the sake of their Christian faith
thus entrusted their souls into God's hands and escaped, in spirit and body, the defilement and brutality of the barbarians.
After all these things, there began to be peace in the land of Syria for three years,
with three hundredweight also being given in return for these three years. In Armenia, however, there was to be war between the two sides.
As for the origin of the cause—the submission of the Armenians under Persian rule to the Romans—
we had already given brief accounts in the preceding portions of the ecclesiastical histories. From now on, let us turn our account to what happened afterward.
For the Persian king was carried away by pride because he had captured Dara, and the arrogance of his heart led him astray.
Now confident that he faced no war in the territories of Syria, he gathered his army and confidently set out for Armenia.
He had set his sights on Theodosiopolis, on the border of his own Armenia, and on Caesarea in Cappadocia and the other cities.
He was so confident that, when Theodore the silentiary had been sent to him on an embassy, and he decided to go out to war, he took Theodore with him. When Theodore begged him to release him,
he said to him mockingly, “Come with me to Armenia, and enter Theodosiopolis with me, and bathe and rest there.
Then I will release you.” So he took him along and brought him with him to Armenia, firmly confident that he would enter and capture the city without difficulty.
When the Roman armies learned of these things, although they trembled greatly at the king's name, they made thorough preparations to face him.
When he saw these powerful armies, he was greatly dismayed, for they were said to number more than one hundred and twenty thousand.
When they challenged him and prepared to fight him, he became afraid and turned away from them to advance against another city.
But there too they hurried to confront him, met him, and drove him away from that place as well.
And once they had tested his strength, they grew still bolder against him and despised him. After this, when he saw that things had not turned out as he wished,
he set out into the northern mountains and turned toward Cappadocia, intending to enter and conquer Caesarea.
When the Roman armies saw this, they moved against him and reached Cappadocia ahead of him.
They stood against him and hemmed him in there in the mountains of Cappadocia. They held him back and did not let him pass.
They skirmished with one another for many days, while he did not dare engage them in a pitched battle.
When he saw that they were more numerous and stronger than he was, and that he could not get past them and march on Caesarea,
he became bewildered and deeply troubled. From then on he planned how he might get through and escape to his own country. His Magi, however, reproached him and argued with him.
Then he turned and went out into Cappadocia toward Sebaste, while they were all trembling before the Roman armies.
Out of shame, so that he would not be reproached for having been unable to accomplish any of his plans, he attacked Sebaste and burned it with fire.
For he found neither plunder nor captives, because the whole region had been evacuated before his arrival.
When he passed on from there, he made a retreat and now headed eastward, to escape to his own country if he could.
Afterward, the Roman armies treated him with contempt, having tested his strength; they despised him and grew bold against him.
When he saw that they had surrounded him and were pressing upon him from every side, he was forced to flee hastily to the mountain,
abandoning his entire camp and his pavilion—that is, his tent—and all his equipment and his treasures of gold, silver, and pearls,
and all his splendid royal garments, and to flee empty-handed. Then the Romans hurried in and took possession of his entire camp.
They killed everyone they overtook there and carried off all his equipment and that of his nobles,
as well as the shrine of the fire he worshiped and the horses that carried it and bore it in procession.
People became rich from what they took there. Indeed, some of the Romans who found and took the royal possessions formed a band, took what they had found, and fled.
They were never found or seen again. But those who fled and escaped from the Persian camp
went to the king, weeping and saying, “My lord, the Romans fell upon us and killed many of your servants.
They plundered and carried off our entire camp.” When he heard this, he reportedly answered them, “Leave them alone.”
For he ordered his entire army to surround him and raise a wall of shields for him. He arranged them in ranks.
He rode among them on horseback and pleaded with them, showing them his white hair and saying,
“My brothers and my sons, have pity on my white hair! Go in and fight for the Persian kingdom, so that it will not be mocked and laughed at.
Look, I myself am fighting alongside you like any one of you horsemen.” For his nobles, it is said, were constantly arguing with him, saying:
“Whether we live or die,” they said, “Persia gains a bad name through us, for none of the Persian kings has ever done what you have done,
bringing us here to die in these mountains.” The Romans learned from some of them what was being said among them.
Then those Persians resorted to another maneuver and moved to another side, to flee, to destroy the city.
They came out opposite Melitene. If there had not been jealousy and divisions among the Roman commanders,
and they had agreed with one another, they would have finished him and his entire army there. They had given one another their word, divided their forces, and surrounded him.
They turned toward Justinian the patrician, the son of Germanus, and Justinian became afraid and fled before him. His fellow commanders did not reach him and help him either.
When he saw this, he and his army took heart, grew bold, entered Melitene, and set it on fire.
When the Persian entered the city of Melitene, he immediately gave the order, and the whole city was burned.
When he went out to cross the Euphrates, heading toward his own country, the commanders of the Roman armies sent him this message:
“What you have done—entering and burning the city—is not the proper conduct of a king: to carry out raids and roam about.
For us, who are servants of the king, these things you have done would have been deeply disgraceful if we had committed them,
how much more so for you, who consider yourself not merely a king, but also a king, a king of kings.
For it is not fitting for a king to behave like those who go out on raids, plundering and fleeing, setting fires and burning things.
Rather, a king should take his stand openly in battle, with authority, confidence, and royal dignity.
When he wins, he should triumph as a king, not enter like a thief, cause destruction, steal, and flee.
Instead, get ready, and now let us face one another in open battle, so that it may be clearly known to whom victory and defeat belong.”
When he heard this, he ordered a battle for the next day on the plain east of the city, some distance from it.
Early in the morning, both sides drew up their ranks opposite one another, with only a short distance between them.
They stood in formation, looking at one another, from morning until the sixth hour, and not a man moved from his place.
The king himself stood behind his army, and they watched one another to see who would begin first.
The men who recounted all these things to us, who had been interpreters for the Persians and the Romans, swore to us,
“Finally, three of us spurred our horses and rode out from the Roman ranks into the space between the two sides.
We galloped as far as the front of the Persian ranks and then galloped back again, without approaching them. We did this three times,
making our horses gallop, while both sides turned and watched us. For we had ridden out to provoke them to battle.
